course.title: Corporate Finance: How Businesses Decide
course.description: How a company decides which projects to fund, how to pay for them and how much to give back to its owners, with a learner judging each choice rather than computing it.
course.audience: A capable adult who can read a balance sheet and income statement and has met compound interest, expected value and diversification. They want to judge whether a project, a borrowing, a payout or an acquisition makes sense, using Australian companies and tax where the sources allow.

paragraphs: How a company decides which projects to fund, how to pay for them and how much to give back to its owners, with a learner judging each choice rather than computing it.
outcomes: You'll be able to compare a payment now with a payment later and say what rate makes them equal.
You'll be able to say whether a project creates value, which cash flows belong in the answer, and when IRR or payback gives the wrong one.
You'll be able to explain what a required return is made of, what debt and equity each cost, and why a project needs a rate that matches its own risk.
You'll be able to judge whether a firm should borrow more, pay out cash or buy back shares, and say what a franked dividend is worth to a given shareholder.
You'll be able to find the assumption an answer depends on and check a forecast against what happened to similar projects.
You'll be able to say whether an acquisition price can pay off and what a share price can and cannot tell a manager.
introduction.prerequisites: It builds on Accounting: Reading the Numbers of a Business, Personal Finance and Investing, Economics: Markets and Strategy, Decision Theory, Maths Foundations.

modules.title: Time and value
modules.description: Money now and money later: why waiting has a price, how to turn a stream of future cash into a value today, and where the value of a long stream sits.

modules.title: Choosing projects
modules.description: Use net present value to decide whether a project creates value, decide which cash flows belong in it, and know when IRR and payback mislead.

modules.title: The cost of capital
modules.description: Where the discount rate comes from: what investors require for risk, what debt and equity each cost, and how a firm's blended rate and a project's own rate differ.

modules.title: Financing and paying out
modules.description: Why firms borrow, when borrowing costs more than it saves, and how they decide between keeping cash, paying dividends and buying back shares, with Australia's franking credits.

modules.title: Uncertainty, deals and markets
modules.description: Which assumption an answer hinges on, whether an acquisition price can pay off, and what a share price does and does not tell a manager.

concepts.title: Time value of money
concepts.summary: Money in hand can be invested, so the same sum is worth more now than later.

concepts.title: Discount rate
concepts.summary: The return given up by waiting: what the same money would earn in the best alternative of the same risk.

concepts.title: Present value
concepts.summary: The value today of money due later, found by discounting it at the discount rate.

concepts.title: Break-even rate
concepts.summary: The rate at which waiting and not waiting are worth the same; below it waiting wins, above it taking the money now wins.

concepts.title: Annuity
concepts.summary: A series of equal payments at regular intervals.

concepts.title: Perpetuity
concepts.summary: Payments that continue forever; with a steady payment its value is the payment divided by the rate.

concepts.title: Terminal value
concepts.summary: The value placed on all cash flows after the years that are forecast in detail; often a large share of a valuation.

concepts.title: Rate sensitivity
concepts.summary: The further out a payment is, the more a change in the discount rate moves its present value.

concepts.title: Net present value
concepts.summary: The present value of a project's cash flows less its cost: the value it adds, in today's dollars, over what investors could earn elsewhere.

concepts.title: Required return (hurdle rate)
concepts.summary: The return investors could earn on other investments of the same risk; the discount rate in an NPV.

concepts.title: Independent projects
concepts.summary: Projects that can all be undertaken if each adds value and capital is not short; their NPVs add.

concepts.title: Zero NPV
concepts.summary: A project that earns exactly the required return: it neither adds nor loses value.

concepts.title: Incremental cash flow
concepts.summary: Cash that changes because the project goes ahead, compared with the firm without it.

concepts.title: Sunk cost
concepts.summary: Money already spent or committed that cannot be recovered whatever is decided; it stays out.

concepts.title: Opportunity cost
concepts.summary: The best use of an owned asset that the project gives up; it counts even though no cash is paid out.

concepts.title: Side effect
concepts.summary: A change to the firm's other products or costs caused by the project, including lost sales of existing products.

concepts.title: Working capital as a cash flow
concepts.summary: Stock, receivables and cash floats tie up cash at the start and release it at the end.

concepts.title: Internal rate of return
concepts.summary: The discount rate at which a project's NPV is zero: the return it earns.

concepts.title: Payback period
concepts.summary: The time taken for a project's cash flows to repay its cost; it ignores timing and what comes after.

concepts.title: Mutually exclusive projects
concepts.summary: Projects of which at most one can be undertaken, such as two designs for the same site.

concepts.title: Multiple IRRs
concepts.summary: A project whose cash flows change sign more than once can have more than one IRR, or none that make sense.

concepts.title: Risk-free rate
concepts.summary: The return on an investment assumed to meet every payment, usually a government bond in the same currency; the base of every required return.

concepts.title: Risk premium
concepts.summary: The extra return investors demand for cash flows that may not arrive.

concepts.title: Systematic and firm-specific risk
concepts.summary: Systematic risk is common to all shares and cannot be diversified away; firm-specific risk can, so the market does not pay for it.

concepts.title: Beta
concepts.summary: How much a share tends to move with the market as a whole; the average share has a beta of 1.

concepts.title: Cost of debt
concepts.summary: What lenders require on new borrowing today: the risk-free rate plus a premium for the chance of default, less the value of the interest deduction.

concepts.title: Cost of equity
concepts.summary: What shareholders require: the risk-free rate plus a premium for the risk they carry; no contract promises it, but it is a cost all the same.

concepts.title: Priority of claims
concepts.summary: Lenders are paid before shareholders, who receive what is left, which may be nothing.

concepts.title: Leverage raises the cost of equity
concepts.summary: More debt leaves shareholders with a riskier residual, so they require more.

concepts.title: Weighted average cost of capital
concepts.summary: The blend of what lenders and shareholders require, weighted by the market value of each and with interest taken after tax; set by the market, not by management.

concepts.title: Hurdle rate
concepts.summary: The return a project must beat; for a project like the rest of the firm it can be the WACC, otherwise it should match the project's own risk.

concepts.title: Project-specific rate
concepts.summary: A required return based on the systematic risk of the project, found from firms in the same line of business or by adjusting the WACC up or down.

concepts.title: WACC is an estimate
concepts.summary: Each input has several plausible proxies, so a fairly wide range of values can look defensible.

concepts.title: Financial leverage
concepts.summary: Borrowing to fund assets so that owners' return rises when the assets earn more than the debt costs, and falls further when they earn less.

concepts.title: Tax shield
concepts.summary: The tax saved because interest is deductible while dividends are not.

concepts.title: Modigliani-Miller without taxes
concepts.summary: In a perfect market with no taxes or distress costs, the mix of debt and equity does not change firm value.

concepts.title: Dividend imputation
concepts.summary: Company tax is passed to shareholders as a credit, so profit paid to eligible shareholders is taxed at their own rate.

concepts.title: Financial distress
concepts.summary: A condition in which promises to creditors are broken or honoured with difficulty; it has direct costs (fees) and indirect costs (higher interest, lost attention, lost projects).

concepts.title: Trade-off theory
concepts.summary: Firms balance the tax benefit of debt against the cost of bankruptcy and distress.

concepts.title: Interest cover
concepts.summary: Profit before interest divided by the interest bill: how many times the interest could be paid out of profit.

concepts.title: Debt overhang
concepts.summary: Existing debt so large that the firm cannot take on a good new investment because the gains would go to lenders.

concepts.title: Pecking order
concepts.summary: Firms prefer internal funds, then debt, and raise equity last, because outsiders read a share issue as bad news.

concepts.title: Payout ratio
concepts.summary: Dividends as a share of earnings (or of free cash flow); above 100% means paying out more than was earned.

concepts.title: Residual dividend policy
concepts.summary: Invest in every project that beats the required return, then pay out what is left.

concepts.title: Share buyback
concepts.summary: The company buys its own shares; earnings per share rise because there are fewer shares.

concepts.title: Franking credit
concepts.summary: A credit for company tax already paid, passed on with a dividend; usable by eligible Australian taxpayers, refundable to some.

concepts.title: Signalling
concepts.summary: A rise in the dividend, or a buyback, may tell the market that management is confident or thinks the shares are cheap.

concepts.title: Sensitivity analysis
concepts.summary: Changing one input at a time to see how far the answer moves; it shows which forecasts deserve effort.

concepts.title: Break-even input
concepts.summary: The value of an assumption at which NPV is zero.

concepts.title: Scenario analysis
concepts.summary: Changing linked inputs together, such as price and volume.

concepts.title: Outside view (reference class forecasting)
concepts.summary: Forecasting from the outcomes of similar past projects instead of from the details of this one.

concepts.title: Planning fallacy
concepts.summary: The tendency to underestimate time, cost and risk and overestimate benefits.

concepts.title: Control premium
concepts.summary: The amount a buyer pays over the market price to gain control of a listed company.

concepts.title: Synergy
concepts.summary: A benefit a buyer expects from combining the businesses; cost synergies are trusted more than revenue synergies.

concepts.title: Winner's curse
concepts.summary: In a contest where all bidders value the prize about the same, the winner is the one with the most optimistic estimate, and so tends to overpay.

concepts.title: Managerial overconfidence
concepts.summary: Managers overrate the synergies, and so overpay.

concepts.title: Efficient-market hypothesis
concepts.summary: Prices reflect all available information, so prices move only on new information and nobody can consistently beat the market on a risk-adjusted basis.

concepts.title: Surprise
concepts.summary: Only the part of news that differs from what was expected moves the price.

concepts.title: Weak, semi-strong and strong forms
concepts.summary: The information in question is past prices, all public information, or private information as well.

concepts.title: Event study
concepts.summary: Reading the effect of an event on a firm's value from its share price around the event.

lessons.title: Money now and money later

lead.text: Your answer to the opening question compared the two offers at the same date, a year from now. Taking the cash and putting it in the account leaves you with $105,000 then, and waiting for the customer leaves you with $108,000, so waiting is better by $3,000. The extra $8,000 is more than the $5,000 the cash would have earned in the meantime.

Behind that comparison is a fact about money itself, and Wikipedia states it in two sentences: "Money you have today can be invested to earn a positive rate of return, producing more money tomorrow. Therefore, a dollar today is worth more than a dollar in the future." We call this the **time value of money**, and it means that a payment can't be judged by its size alone, because it also matters *when* it arrives.

None of this depends on rising prices. In the same article's example, £100 invested for a year at 5% is worth £105, so £100 now and £105 in a year are worth the same to someone who expects 5%, even with [[inflation|A general rise in prices. Met in 'Compounding, inflation and time' in Personal Finance and Investing.]] at zero. Waiting costs whatever the money could have earned, whether or not prices move.

steps.headline: Bringing a payment back to today

lead.text: There is a second route to the same answer, and it is the one finance uses most. Instead of growing today's money forward to next year, we bring next year's money back to today. A sum that grows by 5% in a year is multiplied by 1.05, so to undo the growth we *divide* by 1.05: the customer's $108,000, due in a year, is worth $108,000 ÷ 1.05, which is about $102,900 today. Set beside the $100,000 on offer now, the later payment is worth about $2,900 more, the same verdict that growing the cash forward gave.

afterFigure.text: We call the $102,900 the **present value** of the $108,000, and the 5% used to bring it back the **discount rate**. The discount rate is what your firm could earn on the money elsewhere, at about the same risk, so it puts a price on each year of waiting.

diagram.alt: Two ways to compare $100,000 now with $108,000 in a year at 5%. Growing the cash forward gives $105,000 in a year against the customer's $108,000. Bringing the $108,000 back gives about $102,900 today against $100,000.
diagram.caption: Both routes give the same verdict at 5%. Use the buttons to switch between them.

lead.text: The offer stays the same this time, and only the return available elsewhere changes.

reveal.text: Only the divisor changed, from 1.05 to 1.10, and it was enough to reverse the verdict. Somewhere between the two rates the two offers must be worth the same.

lead.text: At 5% the later offer was worth more, and at 10% the cash was, so somewhere between those rates the verdict changes sides. The figure plots the present value of the $108,000 at every rate from 0% to 14%, with the $100,000 on offer now as a dashed line.

afterFigure.text: The curve falls as the rate rises, because each extra point of rate makes waiting dearer. While it sits above the dashed line, the customer's offer is worth more than the cash, and once it drops below, the *cash* is worth more. The rate at which the curve meets the line is the **break-even rate**, the rate at which waiting and not waiting are worth the same to you. It also tells you what the offer itself pays for waiting, which makes it the return that any rival use of the cash would have to beat.

diagram.alt: A falling curve of the present value of $108,000 due in a year, for discount rates from 0% to 14%, with a dashed horizontal line at the $100,000 offered now. The curve is above the line at 5% (about $102,900) and below it at 10% (about $98,200).
diagram.caption: Where the curve is above the dashed line, waiting is worth more than the cash. Where it falls below, the cash is worth more.

reveal.text: A return above the break-even makes the cash better, and one below it makes waiting better. In effect the customer is offering 8% for waiting, and your firm should accept only if it has nothing better than that.

lead.text: So far the wait has been one year. A *longer* wait puts more years of lost earnings against the payment, and Wikipedia's example makes the point with a lender who might offer 99 cents for the promise of $1.00 a month from now, but would pay much less today for the same dollar promised 20 years away, even if both were equally certain to arrive.

afterFigure.text: Each curve shows what $1 due in a given year is worth today. At 8% a dollar due in ten years is worth about 46 cents, and at 4% about 68 cents, so a higher rate shrinks a payment faster, and a longer wait gives that shrinking more years to build up. The same compounding that makes savings grow runs in reverse here, and it works hardest on the payments furthest away.

diagram.alt: Three falling curves showing what one dollar due in each of the next 20 years is worth today, at discount rates of 4%, 8% and 12%. A dollar due in ten years is worth about 68 cents at 4%, 46 cents at 8% and 32 cents at 12%.
diagram.caption: Each curve falls with the wait, and a higher rate makes it fall faster.

lead.text: A government bond is a loan: an investor pays $100, receives an interest payment each year, and gets the $100 back at the end of the bond's term. The RBA's explainer uses a bond that pays $2 a year and asks what investors would pay for it if they require a yield of 2%. They would pay $100, because $2 on $100 is exactly the **required yield** they are asking for.

A price like that is a present value. The bond is a set of promised payments, and what investors will pay for them today is those payments brought back at the rate they require, so the required yield plays the part of the discount rate. When the required yield changes, the price has to change *with* it, because the same payments are now being brought back at a different rate.

reveal.text: The bond's payments are the same as before, so the new price comes entirely from the lower rate used to bring them back to today. A rise in the required yield would push the price down by the same logic.

steps.headline: What the rate is made of

lead.text: The rate in all these examples has been a single number, but it pays for *two* different things. Wikipedia lists them as the time value of money, which compensates investors for the delay, and a **risk premium**, the extra return investors demand because the cash flow might not arrive after all. Together they make up the **required return**: what an investor needs before parting with money, and so the rate to discount at.

The RBA shows the two pulling apart. It calls the yield curve for government bonds the risk free curve, since a government isn't expected to default on debt in its own currency, and it notes that corporate bonds carry a higher yield as a rule, because investors see them as riskier. Choosing the rate is where much of the judgement in finance sits, and Wikipedia warns that using the wrong rate leaves the results meaningless. For the next few lessons the rate will be given, and lessons 6 to 8 return to the price of risk.

lessons.orientation: Compare a payment now with a larger payment later by asking what the money could earn elsewhere, and say which is worth more and at what rate the answer flips.
lessons.nextAction: You can now say which of two payments is worth more to a firm at a given rate, and find the rate at which the choice changes.

blocks.text: A customer owes your firm $100,000. It offers to pay the whole sum now, or to pay $108,000 in a year. The second sum is larger, which makes it look like the better deal, but the $100,000 could start earning for your firm at once, in a safe account that pays 5% for the year. (The customer and its offer are invented.)
You already know how money grows at a given rate, and that is enough to decide this offer.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say which of two payments is worth more to a firm, and at what rate the answer changes.
intro.whyItMatters: Every project, loan and valuation later in the course compares money at different dates, so this comes first.

recap.keyIdea: A payment due later is worth less today by what the money could have earned meanwhile, so the better of two offers depends on the rate, and the break-even rate is where they tie.

blocks.text: You saw $108,000 in a year beat $100,000 now at 5% and lose to it at 10%, with the flip at 8%, the return the later offer pays for waiting. The same idea explains why a bond's price rises when the yield investors require falls, and why a payment shrinks faster the further away it is and the higher the [[discount rate|The return given up by waiting. Met in 'Money now and money later'.]] is. Behind every rate sit two parts, one that pays for waiting and one that pays for risk.

recap.nextHook: Next we look at long streams of payments and ask where their value sits, in the near years or the far ones.

lessons.title: Value that arrives late

lead.text: A series of equal payments at regular intervals is called an **annuity**, and Wikipedia gives leases and rental payments as examples. To value one we bring each payment back to today *separately*, with the same step as before, and add the results. At 6% the first $50,000 is worth about $47,200, since it is a year away, and the thirtieth is worth about $8,700, since it is thirty years away. The figure draws every payment in between as a bar.

afterFigure.text: Each bar is one year's payment at what it is worth today, so the bars shrink steadily from left to right. Added up, the 30 payments are worth about $688,000, which is less than half of the $1.5 million they sum to. At 10% the bars start lower and fall faster, and the total comes to about $471,000, so four points on the rate take nearly a third off the lease's value.

diagram.caption: Each bar is one year's payment brought back to today. Use the buttons to compare 6% with 10%.

lead.text: The share carried by the first ten years moved when the rate did, and that movement shows something general about discounting. A payment due in year 2 is brought back by the rate's factor twice and one due in year 30 by it thirty times, so any change in the rate is applied again for *every* year of waiting. The figure takes two streams of equal yearly payments, one lasting 5 years and one lasting 30, and shows how the value of each changes with the discount rate, measured against its value at 6%.

afterFigure.text: Move from 6% to 10% and the 5-year stream loses about 10% of its value while the 30-year stream loses nearly a third. The 30-year stream has a higher **rate sensitivity**, because more of its value sits in distant years and a change in the rate takes the most off the distant years. A short project loses little to a rate rise, and a long one can lose a large part of its value to the same rise.

diagram.alt: Two falling curves showing how the present value of a stream of equal yearly payments changes with the discount rate, each as a share of its value at 6%. The 5-year stream falls to about 90% of its 6% value at 10%, and the 30-year stream falls to about 68%.
diagram.caption: Both streams are worth 100% at 6%. The 30-year curve is steeper, so a rise in the rate costs it more.

lead.text: A **perpetuity** is a payment of a set amount that continues for ever. It sounds as if it must be worth an infinite sum, but each payment is brought back by more than the one before it, so the present values shrink fast enough to add up to a *finite* total. For a steady payment that total is a simple division, the payment divided by the rate, which Wikipedia gives as the value of a perpetuity.

A lease paying $50,000 a year for ever is therefore worth $50,000 ÷ 0.10, or $500,000, at 10%, and $50,000 ÷ 0.06, or about $833,000, at 6%. Set these beside the 30-year lease, worth about $471,000 at 10% and $688,000 at 6%. Everything after year 30 adds only about $29,000 at 10% but about $145,000 at 6%, so the lower the rate, the further out the value reaches.

An analyst can forecast a business's cash for a handful of years and not for ever, so the usual way to finish the job is to forecast the early years in detail and then put *one* figure on everything after the last of them. That figure is the **terminal value**, and Wikipedia says it is frequently a large part of the total and reacts strongly to the growth and discount rate chosen. One way to estimate it is to treat everything after the forecast as a growing perpetuity: the cash in the first year after the forecast, divided by the discount rate less the growth rate.

The sensitivity shows in the arithmetic. With $50,000 in the first year and a 10% rate, growth of 2% a year gives $50,000 ÷ 0.08, or $625,000, and growth of 4% gives $50,000 ÷ 0.06, or about $833,000, a third more from a two-point change in an assumption. The formula also needs growth to stay below the rate, which Wikipedia writes as g < i. If growth equalled the rate, each year's present value would be as large as the last, and if it exceeded the rate each would be larger, so the total would never settle.

Woolworths has to test whether each of its businesses is still worth the amount recorded for it in the books, and the test is a discounted cash flow of the kind we have been building. Its 2026 annual report says the forecast cash flows are extrapolated to a terminal value, with a long-term growth rate of 2.5% a year, and each business is discounted at a rate of its own, stated after tax, which runs from 8.6% for New Zealand Food to 11.2% for Quantium. The amount recorded in the books is the carrying value, and the recoverable value is what the future cash flows are worth *today*.

For every unit tested the recoverable value was above the carrying value, so no impairment was recorded, but for some the report adds a warning about how much of the cushion would survive a change in the assumptions. The note for New Zealand Food gives two changes made together.

lessons.orientation: Judge how much of a long cash stream's value arrives in the early years and how much far out, and say which streams a change in the discount rate hurts most.
lessons.nextAction: You can now say how much of a long stream's value lies in its early years, and which streams and assumptions a change in the rate or in growth moves most.

blocks.text: A landlord has signed a lease that pays $50,000 a year for 30 years. Added up, the 30 payments come to $1.5 million. A buyer who wanted to purchase the right to receive them would pay less than that, because each payment arrives a year later than the one before it, and 'Money now and money later' showed what each year of waiting costs. (The lease is invented.)
The question is how much less, and where in the 30 years most of the value lies.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say how much of a long stream's value lies in its early years, and which streams a change in the rate hurts most.
intro.whyItMatters: Most projects and businesses are valued as long streams of cash, so where the value sits decides how much a rate or forecast can move the answer.

recap.keyIdea: The early years of a long stream carry about half its value, and a change in the discount rate cuts the distant payments most, which is why terminal values are large and sensitive.

blocks.text: You saw the first ten of 30 yearly payments carry about half of a lease's value at 6% and about two thirds at 10%, and a rise from 6% to 10% take about a tenth off a 5-year stream and nearly a third off a 30-year one. A [[perpetuity|A payment of a set amount that continues for ever, worth the payment divided by the rate. Met in 'Value that arrives late'.]] has a finite value, a growing one needs growth below the rate, and a terminal value rests on exactly those two assumptions. Woolworths's New Zealand Food note shows how close a real valuation can sit to the edge of its cushion.

recap.nextHook: Next we put a project's cost beside the present value of its cash and ask whether it creates value.

lessons.title: Net present value

lead.text: To find out what the firm gains, we bring each year's cash back to today at the required return and add the results. For fit-out A the five payments of $300,000 are worth about $277,800, $257,200, $238,100, $220,500 and $204,200 today, and together they come to about $1,197,800. Against a cost of $1,000,000, A returns about $197,800 *more*, in today's money, than the firm puts in.

afterFigure.text: That difference, the present value of what a project brings in less what it costs, is the **net present value**, or NPV. Wikipedia describes it as the amount by which the cash flows, measured in today's money, exceed or fall short of the cost of funds. The 8% is the firm's [[required return|The return investors could earn on other investments of the same risk. Met in 'Money now and money later'.]], so A's NPV of $197,800 is the amount by which it beats what investors could have earned elsewhere. Switch to B and C in the figure: B's cash is worth about $998,200 against its cost, and C's about $798,500.

reveal.text: A project that only returns its cost has a return of zero, and investors could earn 8% elsewhere. Getting the cost back is the minimum, and the required return is the test.

lead.text: Fit-out B's cash is worth about $998,200 against a cost of $1,000,000, which leaves an NPV close to zero. A **zero NPV** means a project earns *exactly* the required return: the firm gets what investors could have earned elsewhere and no more, so taking the project or leaving it changes the firm's value by about nothing.

Wikipedia adds a point that is easy to miss. A project with a negative NPV won't necessarily make a net loss, because the negative figure means only that the project's return falls below the required return. Fit-out C returns every dollar it cost and still destroys about $200,000 of value, which is why the sign of the NPV decides the matter, even when the whole cost is repaid.

reveal.text: A near-zero NPV is also where the forecasts matter most, since a small error in the cash flows can tip the answer either way.

lead.text: A firm usually has more than one project to judge, and Wikipedia notes that NPV has the benefit of being additive: the NPVs of different projects can be added up. Projects that can *all* go ahead together, because taking one doesn't rule out another or change the cash from it, are called **independent projects**.

Wikipedia's rule is that, unless capital is constrained or projects depend on each other, a firm aiming to maximise the value it adds would accept all projects with a positive NPV. So the NPVs of independent projects simply add when the projects are taken together, and a project doesn't have to be the best of the group to be worth doing. The goal behind the rule, in the same article's words, is to raise what the firm is worth to its shareholders.

reveal.text: Money does run out in practice, and then the firm can't take every positive-NPV project and has to choose among them. The last question in this lesson looks at that case.

lead.text: An NPV is a sum of forecast cash flows brought back at a chosen rate, and it holds up only as well as *both*. Wikipedia says an NPV depends heavily on how well we know the future cash flows and when they fall, how long the project lasts, the initial investment and the discount rate. The figure draws fit-out A's NPV at every rate from 0% to 20%.

afterFigure.text: At 0% the five payments are simply added, and A returns $500,000 more than it cost. As the rate rises the NPV falls, and a little above 15% it crosses zero, so the same cash flows are worth doing at 8% and not at 20%. Wikipedia gives one more caution: NPV is purely financial, so it leaves out non-financial considerations, such as a safety benefit that earns no cash, which a decision may still need to weigh.

diagram.alt: A falling curve of fit-out A's net present value for discount rates from 0% to 20%, in thousands of dollars. It starts at +500 at 0%, is +198 at 8%, crosses zero a little above 15% and is about -103 at 20%.
diagram.caption: The same cash flows give a different NPV at every rate.

lessons.orientation: Decide whether a project creates value by comparing its cost with the present value of what it returns at the rate investors require, and read the answer as value added today.
lessons.nextAction: You can now judge whether a project adds value by comparing the present value of its cash with its cost, and say what a zero or negative NPV means.

blocks.text: A firm is choosing among three shop fit-outs. Each costs $1 million and brings in the same cash every year for five years: $300,000 from the first fit-out, A, $250,000 from the second, B, and $200,000 from the third, C. Added up, they bring in $1.5 million, $1.25 million and $1 million. Investors could earn 8% elsewhere, so every year of waiting for the cash has a price. (The fit-outs are invented.)
Two of the three look like they get their money back with room to spare, and the third only just gets it back. Whether that is enough depends on what the cash is worth by the time it arrives.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say whether a project creates value, and why a project that returns its whole cost can still lose value.
intro.whyItMatters: Net present value is the test most of the course applies to a project, a borrowing or a deal.

recap.keyIdea: A project's net present value is what its cash is worth today less what it costs, so it measures the value added over the required return, and a project that only returns its cost has a negative one.

blocks.text: You saw fit-out A add about $198,000, B land near zero and C destroy about $200,000 although it returns every dollar of its cost. A negative NPV marks a return below the required return and can occur even when a project returns more cash than it cost. The NPVs of independent projects add, and the answer depends on the forecasts and the rate and leaves out benefits that earn no cash. When capital is short, the aim becomes the largest total NPV the money can buy.

recap.nextHook: Next we ask which of a proposal's cash flows belong in an NPV and which don't.

lessons.title: Which cash flows count

lead.text: The test for any item on the roaster's list is a comparison of two futures: the firm *with* the café, and the firm *without* it. Only the cash that differs between them belongs in the [[net present value|The present value of a project's cash flows less its cost. Met in 'Net present value'.]], which is why the cash that counts is called the **incremental cash flow**. The survey fee is the same in both futures, because it is paid either way. A cost that is already incurred and can't be recovered is a **sunk cost**, and Wikipedia says that a rational decision looks only at prospective, or future, costs.

The test looks forward from the decision and ignores the project's history. A cost already paid in the project's name isn't part of what the decision changes, and cash that the project causes elsewhere in the firm is, even when it never appears on the project's own books.

The shop is the roaster's own, so the café needs no purchase and no rent. It still has a cost, because the $60,000 a year that a tenant pays now would stop. Using an asset the firm already owns costs the best alternative use of it, here the rent, and that is called an **opportunity cost**. It is cash the project loses, even though no cash *leaves* the firm to pay it.

A project can also change the cash from the firm's other activities. A café that sells the roaster's own beans will take some sales from its wholesale customers, and the contribution lost there counts against the café. A change of this kind is a **side effect**, and it can help as well as harm: a volume discount the café brings to the roaster's bean purchases would count in its favour. UQ's finance text gives a streaming service that reduces DVD rentals as its example.

The roaster expects to pay its bank $15,000 a year in interest on the fit-out loan, and it is natural to subtract that from the café's cash flows. It doesn't belong there. The discount rate is the return investors could earn elsewhere on money put into a project of this risk, so the price of the funds is already inside it, and counting interest as well would charge for the same money *twice*. The same goes for dividends, which are payments to owners for their money.
A project's cash flows are meant to show what the project does for the firm before anyone is paid for the funds behind it. The discount rate then asks whether that is enough to pay for them.

A project also ties up cash that never shows as a cost. The café needs $25,000 of extra stock before it can sell anything, and a business that sells on credit waits for its customers to pay. Stock, money owed by customers and cash kept in a till are **working capital**, and the project pays for them at the *start* and gets the money back when it *ends*, as the stock is sold or the customers settle.

UQ's finance text counts tax on the extra profit as well, because it is cash that leaves the firm only if the café goes ahead, and it falls in the years the profit does. The figure sets out the café's cash flows in time.

afterFigure.text: The two things the figure leaves out are the ones this lesson has already ruled out, the survey fee and the loan interest.

lead.text: Leaving sunk costs out is easy to say and hard to do when the sums are large. Wikipedia reports evidence from De Bondt and Makhija (1988) that managers of many US utility companies were too reluctant to end nuclear plant projects that could no longer pay their way, and it says the Concorde fallacy takes its name from the British and French governments that kept funding the Concorde once the economic case for the aircraft had gone.

Long-term investments can't be undone without losing a good deal of the capital put into them, which is what makes the pull to carry on so strong. The loss is real, but it is the same whichever way the decision goes, so the only question that remains is whether the money still to be spent earns more than it costs.

lessons.orientation: Sort the items in a project proposal into the cash flows that belong in its NPV and those that do not: sunk costs, opportunity costs, side effects, working capital, tax and financing costs.
lessons.nextAction: You can now sort a proposal's items into the cash flows that belong in its NPV and those that don't, and say when each one falls.

blocks.text: A coffee roaster wants to open a café in a shop it owns, which a tenant rents from it for $60,000 a year. The roaster has already paid $30,000 for a survey of the site, and the survey said the café would work. It would borrow most of the fit-out money from a bank at $15,000 a year in interest. The café would sell the roaster's own beans, some of which are now sold wholesale, and it needs $25,000 of extra stock before it opens. (The roaster and its figures are invented.)
Each of these items could go into the café's net present value, and most proposals contain a mixture of items that should and items that shouldn't.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to sort the items in a proposal into the cash flows that belong in its NPV and the ones that don't.
intro.whyItMatters: A correct discount rate can't rescue an NPV built from the wrong cash flows.

recap.keyIdea: A cash flow belongs in a project's NPV when it changes because the project goes ahead: sunk costs and financing stay out, while lost rent, lost sales elsewhere, working capital and tax stay in.

blocks.text: You applied one test to a roaster's café, a phone maker's new model, a bicycle maker's workshop and a gift shop's branch: compare the firm with the project against the firm without it. A survey fee already paid is sunk and stays out, loan interest stays out because the discount rate already prices the money, and the rent an owned shop could earn, the sales a new product takes from an old one, working capital and tax all stay in. Managers who keep funding a failing plant because of what is already spent are making the mistake the Concorde fallacy is named for.

recap.nextHook: Next we compare three ways of ranking projects, NPV, IRR and payback, and see where the last two mislead.

lessons.title: IRR and payback: where they mislead

lead.text: The 36% and 22% in the opening question are each project's **internal rate of return**, or IRR: the discount rate at which its NPV falls to zero. Wikipedia defines it as the "annualized effective compounded return rate" that sets the net present value of all the cash flows, both positive and negative, equal to zero. At 8% S has an NPV of about $54,600, and as the rate rises that NPV shrinks until it reaches zero at 36%, which is the return S earns on the money tied up in it.

For a single project judged against a required return, and in isolation from any other project, Wikipedia says the IRR comparison is equivalent to the NPV method. For an ordinary project, an IRR above the required return goes with a positive NPV, so the two rules agree. The trouble starts when the choice is between projects, because a rate of return and a dollar of value are different measures.

Projects of which *at most one* can be undertaken, such as two designs for the same site, are **mutually exclusive**. For these Wikipedia says IRR should not be used to choose. When one project needs a higher initial investment than the other, it may have a lower IRR and a higher NPV, and it should then be accepted if capital is not constrained. The figure shows how this happens with a different pair: a small project X and a large project Y, each drawn as its NPV at every discount rate.

afterFigure.text: Each line meets zero at the project's IRR, 30% for X and about 18% for Y, so IRR ranks X first. Below the crossing rate of about 15%, Y has the higher NPV, so at any required return under 15% the large project is the better choice, and only above it does X come out ahead. IRR measures the return on the money invested, and NPV measures the dollars added, so when the project with the higher rate also uses far less money, the two measures answer different questions, and the owners are paid in dollars.

diagram.alt: Two falling lines showing the net present value of a small project X, which costs $100,000, and a large project Y, which costs $400,000, at discount rates from 0% to 35%. Y is higher at low rates, the lines cross at about 15%, and X is higher above that. X meets zero at 30% and Y at about 18%.
diagram.caption: Each line meets zero at the project's IRR. Y's line is above X's at any rate below the crossing.

lead.text: A third rule is simpler. The **payback period** is the time a project takes to recoup the funds spent on it, so the only question the rule asks is *how soon*. A firm using it sets a limit and accepts the projects that repay within it. It is quick to work out, but Wikipedia names its faults: it takes no account of the time value of money, and it ignores any cash that arrives after the payback period. UQ's finance text adds that the cut-off year is arbitrary and that the rule favours quick projects, so it can reject long-term ones such as research.

Wikipedia also says that, used carefully or to compare similar investments, payback can be quite useful, and the UQ text notes that it suits small businesses short of cash. What it can't do is show which project is worth the most.

IRR can fail in a different way. When the cash flows change sign *more than once*, for example when a large outflow comes at the end of a project, Wikipedia says the IRR may have multiple real values, and it names strip mines and nuclear power plants as examples. The figure takes an invented wind farm that costs $900,000 to build, earns $2,800,000 over its working life and costs $2,000,000 to take down.

afterFigure.text: The wind farm's NPV is below zero at low rates, above zero between about 11% and 100%, and below zero again beyond that, so there are two rates at which it equals zero and neither can fairly be called the project's return. A single sign change gives a curve that crosses zero once, and a second change can bend it back. That is why the IRR rule, which asks only whether a rate clears the hurdle, can say yes where NPV says no.

diagram.alt: A hump-shaped curve of a wind farm's net present value, in thousands of dollars, for discount rates from 0% to 120%. The wind farm costs $900,000 to build, earns $2,800,000, and costs $2,000,000 to take down. NPV is below zero at 0%, crosses zero at about 11%, peaks near +80 at about 43%, and crosses zero again at 100%.
diagram.caption: The curve is above zero only between 11% and 100%, so the project has two IRRs.

lead.text: Of the three, only NPV measures what the owners care about, the value added in today's dollars. IRR agrees with it for a single project against its required return, and it can disagree when mutually exclusive projects differ in size, as the figure showed, or in duration, since Wikipedia says IRR is not a sound way to compare projects of different durations, or when the cash flows change sign more than once. Payback agrees with NPV only by luck, because it ignores timing and everything after its cut-off.

A sensible order is to work out NPV first at a rate that matches the projects' risk, and to treat IRR and payback as summaries that help a reader, never as the deciding rule. The sources add that surveys find executives preferring IRR even though academics strongly favour NPV, and they don't say why.

lessons.orientation: Compare projects by NPV, IRR and payback, say which rule to trust when they disagree, and spot the cases where IRR or payback gives the wrong answer.
lessons.reviewLabel: IRR and payback: where they mislead
lessons.nextAction: You can now compare projects by NPV, IRR and payback, say which to trust when they disagree, and spot the cases where IRR or payback misleads.

blocks.text: A firm has one site and two proposals for it, and only one can be built. Proposal S is small: it costs $100,000 and returns $60,000 a year for three years. Proposal L is large: it costs $1,000,000 and returns $400,000 a year for four years. Both clear the firm's required return of 8%, and each has a rate of return that a manager could quote in a single number, 36% for S and 22% for L. (The proposals are invented.)
A rate of return is easy to compare, and S has the higher one. Whether that is enough to choose it is the question.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say which of NPV, IRR and payback to trust when they disagree, and spot the cases where IRR or payback gives the wrong answer.
intro.whyItMatters: Managers quote IRR and payback every day, so knowing where they mislead protects a firm from funding the wrong project.

recap.keyIdea: IRR and payback are useful summaries, but NPV is the rule that measures value, because IRR ignores size and duration and can have several values, and payback ignores timing and later cash.

blocks.text: You saw the smaller project with the higher IRR lose to the larger one on NPV, a project that is repaid in 2 years destroy value while one repaid in 3.75 years added about $675,000, and a quarry with two IRRs above the hurdle that still had a negative NPV. A single project against its required return gives the same answer on IRR and NPV, and the sources report that executives prefer IRR without saying that this makes it right. Work out NPV first at a rate that matches the risk, and use the other two as a check.

recap.nextHook: Next we turn to the rate itself, and ask what makes one project's required return higher than another's.

lessons.title: Risk and required return

lead.text: The Reserve Bank of Australia answers the opening question directly. It says that companies and other bond issuers usually have to offer investors a higher yield than the government does, because investors see them as the riskier borrower. The government's own yield curve is the one it calls the 'risk free yield curve', since a government is not expected to default on what it borrows in its own currency.

That gives every required return a starting point. Wikipedia draws the consequence: because the risk-free rate is available without taking any risk, an investment that carries some risk has to promise a *higher* return than that to attract any holder.

A [[required return|The return investors could earn on other investments of the same risk; the discount rate in an NPV. Met in 'Money now and money later'.]] therefore has two parts, a payment for waiting and a payment for risk. The payment for waiting is the **risk-free rate**, the yield on a government bond of the same term, and whatever is added on top for the chance that the cash never arrives is the **risk premium**.

diagram.alt: Three stacked bars for bonds of the same term. A government bond is only the risk-free base. A company bond has a small risk premium on top of the same base. A riskier company has a larger premium. The sizes are for illustration, not real yields.

reveal.text: That is the base. The premium on top of it depends on which kinds of risk the market pays for, and the next screen separates them.

lead.text: Now take a share, whose cash flows are less certain than any bond's. The University of Queensland's textbook makes a point about it with two Australian listed companies, one whose profits depend on the price of iron ore and one whose profits don't. Hold both, and a bad year for iron ore can hurt only one of them, so you have taken away some of your risk. You have not taken away the risk that the whole economy turns down, because that reaches both.

Wikipedia gives the two kinds names. **Systematic risk** is the risk common to all securities, which is why it is also called market risk, and *no amount* of spreading removes it. What is left is unsystematic risk, also known as idiosyncratic or diversifiable risk, and we'll call it **firm-specific risk** because it belongs to one company. (Personal Finance used market risk and diversifiable risk for the same two.)

Why should this split change what a required return contains? Wikipedia's account of the standard pricing model is direct: a rational investor has no reason to carry risk that could be diversified, because the model pays only for risk that cannot be. The reasoning is that anyone can remove firm-specific risk by holding many shares, so a market that paid extra for carrying it would be paying for something investors can drop for free, and the payment goes to the risk nobody can remove.

diagram.alt: Three stacked bars showing the risk of an investor's holdings. With one share the bar is tall, with a large firm-specific block above the systematic block. With many shares the firm-specific block is small. With every share in the market it is gone, and only the systematic block is left. Sizes are illustrative.

reveal.text: So the market pays for one kind of risk and not the other. The next screen gives a way to measure how much of the first kind a share carries.

lead.text: If only systematic risk is paid, we need a way to say how much of it a particular share carries. The usual measure is **beta**, which Wikipedia describes as a statistic for how far an individual share's price is expected to rise or fall when the whole market moves, *in proportion* to the market's move. The average share has a beta of 1 by definition, so a share with a beta of 1.5 is expected to move about one and a half times as far as the market, and a share with a beta of 0.5 about half as far.

What makes a beta high or low? Wikipedia says each firm has a beta of its own, which depends on its management, its business and the way it is funded. Its standard low-beta example is the utility. The article gives no reason, so this one is our own reasoning: people keep using power and water through a downturn, so a utility's cash flows follow the economy less closely than most.

afterFigure.text: A high beta says that a business's cash flows rise and fall with the economy, and it says nothing about whether the business is run well.

reveal.text: Woolworths shows a real company putting this into practice, with a different rate for each of its businesses.

lead.text: Woolworths shows the same idea *inside* one company. Its annual report for the year to 28 June 2026 includes a test of whether its business units are still worth what the books say. For the test it discounts each unit's forecast cash flows at a rate of its own, which the company says reflects the market's current view of the time value of money and of the risk specific to that unit. The note calls each unit a CGU, short for cash-generating unit. Those are our two parts again, a payment for waiting and a payment for the risk of that unit.

Each rate is stated after tax. In 2026 they run from 8.6% for New Zealand Food to 11.2% for Quantium, so the Group does not treat all its businesses as equally risky, which **a single rate for the whole Group could not show**. The note does not split any rate into a base and a premium, so we can see the pattern in the rates and nothing finer.

reveal.text: Rates like these are estimates, and the last screen says how far to trust the model behind them.

lead.text: The model behind these ideas is the capital asset pricing model, or **CAPM**. Wikipedia says it was developed in the 1960s by Jack Treynor, William Sharpe, John Lintner and Jan Mossin, and that Sharpe shared the 1990 Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences for his part in it. Within the model, the premium on a share comes from the systematic risk it carries, which beta measures.

It is worth knowing how far to trust it. Economists Eugene Fama and Kenneth French concluded in a 2004 review that, because the model fails in empirical tests, most applications of it are invalid. So treat a beta as one *estimate* and as a useful way of asking how much a business moves with the economy. The same caution applies to every rate built on it in the lessons that follow.

reveal.text: That is the chain of the lesson: a base, a premium, and a premium that pays only for the risk that cannot be spread away.

lessons.orientation: Explain why riskier cash flows are discounted at higher rates, separate the risk investors are paid for from the risk they can remove by holding many shares, and rank businesses by how much they move with the economy.
lessons.nextAction: Say why a firm's debt costs less than its equity, and why that does not make borrowing cheap overall.

blocks.text: Until now the discount rate has been given to us, 5% in one example and 10% in the next, and we have only asked what it does to a present value. A firm can't wait to be told, because the rate it uses decides which projects pass the test, so where does the rate come from? We can start with the simplest cash flows there are, those of a bond.
Suppose the Australian government and a company each sell a bond with the same term, so that both pay on the same dates. An investor has to choose one.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to build a required return from a risk-free rate and a premium, say which risks the market pays for, and read what a beta tells you.
intro.whyItMatters: Every project test in this course needs a rate, and a rate that ignores risk would treat a safe cash flow and a doubtful one alike.

recap.keyIdea: A required return is a risk-free rate plus a premium, and the premium pays only for systematic risk, the part that holding many shares cannot remove.

blocks.text: You built the rate from the yield on a government bond, which the Reserve Bank calls risk free since governments are not expected to default on borrowing in their own currency, and a premium that grows with the chance the cash does not arrive. You then split risk into the part an investor can spread away and the part nobody can, and saw that only the second is paid for.

[[Beta|How much a share tends to move with the market as a whole; the average share has a beta of 1. Met in 'Risk and required return'.]] says how much of that second kind a share carries. Woolworths' five discount rates, from 8.6% to 11.2%, show one company using a different rate for each of its businesses, and the doubts Fama and French raise about CAPM are a reason to treat any rate built on a beta as an estimate.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson asks what lenders and shareholders each require from a firm, and why its debt costs less than its equity.

lessons.title: What debt and equity cost

lead.text: When a project's cash comes in, it does not go to everyone at once. The lenders, who were promised interest on set dates, are paid *first*, and the shareholders receive whatever is left. The University of Queensland's textbook gives the order: interest is paid before dividends, and if the firm fails the lenders have the first claim on its assets. We call this ranking the **priority of claims**.

The ranking changes what each side can gain and lose. A lender's gain is capped at the agreed interest, so a very good year doesn't pay it more, while a shareholder's upside has no cap and the whole investment can be lost. CLEM7 in the opener showed the lost end of that range.

The Cross City Tunnel in Sydney shows how much of one real project sat on each side. Wikipedia lists its funding as A$220 million of equity from three companies and A$580 million from a syndicate of banks, so about seven dollars in every ten were borrowed. The article puts the tunnel's cost at A$680 million, which doesn't match those two figures, so we use them only for the rough proportion. In December 2006 the tunnel became insolvent and the banks appointed receivers, and the article doesn't say what the shareholders received.

diagram.alt: Bars showing how a project's cash is shared. lead.text: Because lenders come first and hold a fixed claim, they carry less risk than shareholders, and what they require reflects it. Wikipedia builds the **cost of debt** from the yield on a risk-free bond with the same term as the firm's debt, with a default premium added. It is the two-part [[required return|The return investors could earn on other investments of the same risk; the discount rate in an NPV. Met in 'Money now and money later'.]] built in 'Risk and required return', and here the premium pays for the chance that this borrower does not repay.

This is what lenders require *now*, and the Reserve Bank's bond example shows why that differs from the coupon on a bond already issued. A bond paying $2 a year was worth $100 to investors who required a yield of 2%, and worth $109.50 once they required only 1%, so the price moved while the $2 stayed fixed. A firm's cost of debt is the yield lenders require today, and the coupon on its old bonds records only what it promised then.
Interest can also be deducted from a company's taxable profit, which lowers what debt costs after tax, and 'Why firms borrow' takes that up.

reveal.text: Lenders, then, require the risk-free rate plus a premium for default. Shareholders are paid after them, and the next screen asks what that does to what they require.

lead.text: A firm's debt has a contract behind it and its shares do not. Nobody promises shareholders a dividend, so is equity free? It is not, and the reason is the one behind the cost of debt. Wikipedia says the cost of equity is worked out from comparable investments with a similar level of risk, and it writes the result as the risk-free rate plus a premium expected for risk. Shareholders could put their money into those comparable investments, so a firm that wants it has to offer *what they could earn there*.

That makes the **cost of equity** a real cost even though no contract states it, and it explains why the cost of equity is higher than the cost of debt. Shareholders are paid after the lenders and hold no fixed claim, so the premium they need for the risk is larger than the default premium lenders need.

reveal.text: Equity costs more than debt, and the next question is what happens when a firm swaps some of one for the other.
The next screen explains why the shareholders who remain ask for more, and what Modigliani and Miller made of it.

steps.headline: Why more debt makes equity dearer

lead.text: Lenders must be paid before shareholders, so the more a firm borrows, the larger the fixed claim that stands *ahead* of them. The same operating profit is divided with a bigger slice going to the lenders first, which leaves the shareholders' share more uncertain. Modigliani and Miller proposed their theorem in 1958. Wikipedia sums up its second proposition this way: the more debt a firm has relative to its equity, the more return its shareholders require, since holding shares in an indebted company is riskier.

So a swap of equity for debt does two things. The debt costs less than the equity it replaces, which lowers the average, and **the equity that remains costs more**, which raises it. The second effect cancels part of the first.

There is a further limit. Wikipedia says debt is cheaper than new equity, though only for profitable firms, because tax breaks go only to them, and that past some point raising new debt costs more than raising new equity. The saving from replacing equity with debt therefore shrinks as a firm borrows more, and it can turn into a cost.

lessons.orientation: Say why a firm's debt costs less than its equity, why that does not make borrowing cheap overall, and where each cost comes from.

blocks.text: Brisbane's Clem Jones Tunnel, known as CLEM7, was completed on time and on budget, and its operator still went into receivership. Wikipedia says that the operator, RiverCity Motorway, collected too little in tolls to cover the interest on its $1.3 billion of debt, and that its shares are now worthless because there is no prospect of a profit or a dividend.

Two groups had put money into that tunnel, lenders who were promised interest and shareholders who were promised nothing, and when the tolls fell short they did not share the loss equally. What does each group require before it will take its place in the queue, and why are the two requirements different?

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say why a firm's debt costs less than its equity, why that doesn't make borrowing cheap overall, and where each cost comes from.
intro.whyItMatters: Treating debt as the cheap way to fund a project, or shares as free, leads a firm to accept projects that don't earn what its funders require.

recap.keyIdea: Debt costs less than equity because lenders are paid first, but swapping equity for debt makes the equity that remains dearer, so cheaper debt does not make a cheaper firm.

blocks.text: You saw lenders and shareholders queue for a project's cash, with CLEM7's shares left worthless once the tolls could not cover $1.3 billion of debt. Each side requires a risk-free rate plus a premium for its own risk: a default premium from lenders, who hold a fixed claim and come first, and a larger premium from shareholders, who take what is left.

A firm's cost of debt is what lenders require now, whatever the coupon on its old bonds says, and its cost of equity is a real cost though no contract states it. More debt raises the cost of the equity beside it, and past some point new debt costs more than new equity.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson blends the two costs into one rate for the whole firm, and asks which rate a single project should be judged at.

lessons.title: WACC and hurdle rates

lead.text: The opening question has a weighted answer: each source of funds counts *in proportion* to how much of the funding it supplies. Wikipedia defines the **WACC**, the weighted average cost of capital, as the average rate a company is expected to pay everyone who holds its securities in return for funding its assets. For Sorrel Group the blend is 0.7 × 10% + 0.3 × 5%, which is 8.5%, nearer the cost of equity because equity supplies most of the funds.

Three details decide whether the number means anything. UQ's textbook says the weights use the market values of the firm's debt and equity, which can differ from the book figures, and that the debt term is reduced by the tax rate because interest is tax-deductible. Wikipedia adds that the market, and not management, dictates the rate, a point we return to at the end of the lesson.

A firm's funders pay for all its businesses at once, so the firm's single rate is an average across its businesses as well. Juniper is an invented firm whose steady business is worth 80% of the whole and carries a [[required return|The return investors could earn on other investments of the same risk; the discount rate in an NPV. Met in 'Money now and money later'.]] of 7%, and whose cyclical business is worth the other 20% and carries 11%. The next screen works out its blend.

steps.headline: Find Juniper's blended rate, when 80% of its value is a steady business at 7% and 20% is a cyclical business at 11%.

workedSteps.text: Each business counts in proportion to its share of the firm's value, so multiply each rate by its weight.
Add the two parts to get the rate for the firm as a whole.
A weighted average always lies between the rates it blends, so Juniper's 7.8% is above the steady rate and below the cyclical one.

lead.text: WACC blends what lenders and shareholders require, so anything that changes those requirements changes it. The risk-free rate is the base of both, which means that when yields on government bonds rise across the economy every required return rises with them. [[Beta|How much a share tends to move with the market as a whole; the average share has a beta of 1. Met in 'Risk and required return'.]] is the second input: if a firm's shares become more sensitive to the economy, shareholders require more. Lenders respond to the firm's credit standing, so an upgrade lowers the default premium on its debt and a doubt about its safety raises it.

The fourth influence is the mix of debt and equity, and it **can pull either way**. Replacing equity with debt swaps a dearer source for a cheaper one, which *lowers* the blend, but it also *raises* the cost of the equity that remains and, past some point, the cost of new debt. Touro's textbook describes the traditional view as a U: the average cost falls to a low point as cheap debt replaces equity and then rises again as lenders see more default risk and charge more. It gives no formula for where the low point lies, and says it depends on the industry and on the firm's risk.

reveal.text: WACC follows the market's view of the firm, and so far we have treated it as the rate for the firm as a whole. The next screen asks whether one rate can be right for every project inside it.

lead.text: A project is judged against a rate it has to beat, called its **hurdle rate**. For a project that looks like the rest of the firm, the firm's WACC can serve: Wikipedia says that when the aim is only to find out whether a project adds value, the firm's own WACC may be a suitable rate. It also notes that many people argue for a higher rate to reflect risk, opportunity cost or other factors.

The trouble starts when the project does not look like the rest of the firm. UQ's textbook gives the reason: a project's required return follows the [[systematic risk|Risk common to all shares that holding many shares cannot remove. Met in 'Risk and required return'.]] of that project *itself*, whatever the company's average happens to be. A firm made of a steady business and a cyclical one has a single WACC that suits neither, so using it rejects safe projects that earn more than the market requires for their risk and accepts risky ones that earn less.
For Juniper the rates fall as the figure shows. The rate that fits a project is its **project-specific rate**, the one that matches the project's own risk.

steps.headline: Juniper's steady business plans an expansion expected to earn 7.5%. Should it go ahead?

workedSteps.text: Juniper's blended rate is 7.8%, so a test against the average would reject an expansion that earns 7.5%.
But the expansion is a steady project, so the average is the wrong test. Choose the rate that matches its own risk.
The expansion clears the rate for its own risk by half a point, so it adds value and should go ahead.

reveal.text: The firm's average passed the cyclical project and blocked the steady one. The next screen asks how a firm finds the rate that does fit.

steps.headline: Finding the rate for a project

lead.text: How does a firm find the rate for a business it has little data on? UQ's textbook gives two ways. One is to borrow the WACC of companies that do *only* that kind of business, which it calls the **pure-play approach**. The other is to sort projects into risk classes and add a margin to the firm's rate or subtract one, with plus or minus two percentage points as its example.

Woolworths also uses a different rate for each part of itself. In the impairment test met in 'Risk and required return' it applies a different post-tax rate to each of its five business units. Four of the five rose between 2025 and 2026, by 0.5 to 0.6 percentage points, and New Zealand Food stayed at 8.6%. The report does not say why they rose.

reveal.text: Rates move because the market's requirements move, and the next screen asks who controls them.

steps.headline: Set by the market, and loose

lead.text: Who sets a firm's WACC? Wikipedia is direct: the market sets it, and management does not. A board chooses how its firm is funded, and it **can't choose what lenders and shareholders require** for supplying the money.

It is not a precise number either. Each input has several plausible proxies, so Wikipedia notes that *quite different* values for the WACC of one firm in one year can all look defensible. Two careful analysts can therefore reach different figures for the same firm, and a project that passes at one rate and fails at another is close to the line. That is a reason to test a project across a range of rates.

reveal.text: The market sets the cost of capital, and the project's own risk sets the rate it has to beat. The last question puts both to work on a purchase.
A firm's WACC is a good test only for projects that look like the firm, and for the rest it is the project's own risk that counts.

lessons.orientation: Say what WACC measures, what raises or lowers it, and why a project should be judged at a rate that matches its own risk rather than the company's average.
lessons.nextAction: Judge what borrowing does to the return and the risk of a firm's owners, and say how tax changes the case for debt.

blocks.text: Woolworths states its aim for its funding in one phrase. The annual report says the Group manages how it funds itself with the aim of raising long-term value for shareholders, and that it seeks its own 'optimised weighted average cost of capital'. 'What debt and equity cost' gave us the two costs that phrase blends, what lenders require and what shareholders require, and it left open how the two are combined.
Take an invented firm, Sorrel Group, to see the idea before we name it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say what WACC measures, what moves it, and why a project should be judged at a rate that matches its own risk.
intro.whyItMatters: A firm's average rate can pass a risky project that earns too little and block a safe one that earns enough, so the choice of rate decides the choice of project.

recap.keyIdea: WACC blends what lenders and shareholders require, the market sets it, and a project should be judged at the rate that matches its own risk, which can sit well away from the firm's average.

blocks.text: You blended required returns by weight, first for Sorrel's funding and then for Juniper's two businesses, and saw that the risk-free rate, the firm's sensitivity to the economy, its credit standing and its mix of debt and equity move the result, the last of them in either direction. Juniper's 7.8% would have rejected a steady expansion that cleared its own 7% and passed a cyclical one that fell short of its own 11%.

Borrowing the rate of firms that do only a project's kind of business, or adjusting the firm's rate for the project's risk class, gives a better hurdle, and Woolworths' five rates, from 8.6% to 11.2%, show the same thinking in practice. A fairly wide range of WACC values can look defensible, so test a project across a range of rates.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson asks why firms borrow at all, and what borrowing does to the return and the risk of their owners.

lessons.title: Why firms borrow

lead.text: The opener gave one year. To see the whole pattern, give both firms three years, a good one, a normal one and a bad one, in which their assets earn $16 million, $10 million and $2 million before interest. The assets are the *same*, so the operating profit is the same however they are funded and only the split of it differs. U's owners keep all of it. L's owners keep what is left after $3 million of interest, and that $3 million is owed in the good year and the bad year alike.

This is **financial leverage**: borrowing so that a smaller amount of the owners' money controls the same assets. Wikipedia says leverage boosts profit when the asset earns more than borrowing costs, and can boost losses as well. Touro's textbook adds the condition: borrowing lifts the return on equity above the return on assets only when profit before interest is above a crossover point. What the owners care about is the [[return on equity|Profit after interest and tax as a share of the owners' money in the business. Met in 'Return on equity and return on capital' in Accounting.]] in each year, the profit left for them divided by the money they put in.

diagram.alt: Two stacked bars of funding for assets of $100 million. Firm U is funded entirely by owners. Firm L is funded by $50 million of owners' money and a $50 million loan at 6%. A table gives profit before interest in three years: $16 million, $10 million and $2 million. Firm L owes $3 million of interest every year.

steps.headline: L's owners put in $50m and the firm borrows $50m at 6%. What return do they earn in a normal year, and in a bad year?

workedSteps.text: In a normal year the assets earn $10m before interest. Take off the $3m of interest to find what is left for the owners.
Divide by the owners' $50m and compare with U, whose owners keep all $10m on $100m.
In the bad year the assets earn only $2m, while the interest bill is still $3m.
The $1m gap comes out of the owners' pockets, so their return is below zero while U's owners still earn 2%.

reveal.text: So leverage widens the spread of the owners' returns. The next screen asks whether it makes the firm worth more.

lead.text: L's owners earn more in good and normal years and less in bad ones, so is L worth more than U? Look at who receives the profit. In every year the firm's operating profit is the same $16 million, $10 million or $2 million however the firm is funded, and borrowing changes only how that profit is divided between lenders and owners. Modigliani and Miller's first proposition says that when there are no taxes and no chance of bankruptcy, a firm that borrows can never be worth more than the same firm without debt, so **the two values must match**.

If that were all there is to say, the choice between debt and equity would never matter. Wikipedia's reply is that the mix matters exactly because at least one of the theorem's assumptions fails in practice, and the *first* assumption to check is that there are no taxes.

Interest is a deductible expense and dividends are not, which Wikipedia gives as the reason that a firm gains from being levered. A **tax shield** is the tax a firm saves by taking a deduction that the rules allow, and Wikipedia's own example is the interest on debt.

Put numbers on it with the normal year and a company tax rate of 30%. U earns $10 million and pays $3.0 million of tax. L earns the same $10 million, deducts its $3 million of interest, and pays tax on $7 million, which is $2.1 million. L pays $0.9 million less, which is the interest of $3 million multiplied by the 30% rate, and that $0.9 million is shared between its lenders and owners. The ATO lists company tax rates for 2025-26 of 25% for base rate entities and 30% otherwise.

Wikipedia states what follows for value: with deductible interest, and setting other frictions aside, a company's value rises in step with the amount of debt it uses. The saving needs *taxable profit*, though, and Wikipedia notes that only profitable firms can use the tax breaks.
