reveal.text: Taxes make debt cheaper for a company, and Australia adds a second tax rule that bears on how much.

lead.text: Wikipedia says Australia and New Zealand run a **dividend imputation** system, in which a company may attach franking credits to its dividends, and that Australia introduced it in 1987. The ATO describes the effect for the shareholder: the amount taxed is the whole of the profit behind the dividend, including the franking credits attached to it, and the shareholder gets credit for the tax the company has already paid. So company profit paid out to eligible shareholders is taxed in its entirety at the shareholder's rate, while profit retained by the company, or paid to ineligible shareholders, stays taxed at the company rate. Wikipedia sums it up by saying that imputation makes company tax largely irrelevant, with exceptions.

What does that do to the tax shield? The sources do not say, so this is *our own* reasoning. The shield works by cutting the company tax a firm pays. When profit goes to eligible shareholders that company tax comes back to them as a credit, so a deduction that cuts the tax also cuts the credit, and the saving at company level is worth less to them than the plain tax-shield picture suggests. On retained profit, and on profit paid to ineligible shareholders, the company rate still applies and the shield still works.

Woolworths says it is committed to holding solid investment-grade credit ratings, which stand at BBB with Standard & Poor's and Baa2 with Moody's. It reports net debt of 2.5 times EBITDA before significant items for 2026, down from 2.8 times, and its net debt includes lease liabilities.

Lovisa describes its policy as **a balance**. The report says its Board aims to balance the higher returns that more borrowing might bring against the advantages and security of a sound capital position. At the end of the year it had $87 million drawn on a facility with a limit of $120 million. Set beside the table at the start of the lesson, the first half of that sentence is the extra return that debt can bring and the second half is the security that a bad year puts at risk.

reveal.text: Debt is a choice about return and risk, and tax rules change the price of that choice. The next lesson sets the tax benefit against the cost of getting into trouble.

lessons.orientation: Judge what borrowing does to the return and risk of a firm's owners, and say how the tax treatment of interest, and of dividends in Australia, changes the case for debt.
lessons.nextAction: Weigh the tax benefit of debt against the cost of financial distress, and judge how much a firm can safely borrow.

blocks.text: Two firms each hold $100 million of assets. Firm U is funded by its owners alone. Firm L is funded half by its owners and half by a $50 million loan at 6%, so it pays $3 million of interest a year. In a good year each firm's assets earn $16 million before interest.
The assets and their profit are identical, so the only difference is the way the profit is shared between lenders and owners.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to read what borrowing does to owners' returns in good and bad years, say why debt creates no value without taxes, and say how tax on interest and on dividends changes the case for it.
intro.whyItMatters: A loan can lift owners' returns in most years and turn them negative in a bad one, and the tax rules decide how much of the lift is real.

recap.keyIdea: Borrowing raises the owners' return in years when the assets earn more than the debt costs and lowers it in years when they earn less, and the tax treatment of interest and dividends decides whether it adds value.

blocks.text: L's owners earned 26% in the good year, 14% in the normal year and a loss of 2% in the bad year, against 16%, 10% and 2% for U's, because $3 million of interest was owed in every year. With no taxes and a perfect market Modigliani and Miller say the mix makes no difference to value, since debt only divides the same profit. With interest deductible at 30%, L paid $0.9 million less tax in the normal year, which is the interest times the rate.

Australia's imputation system credits eligible shareholders with the company tax paid on the profit they receive, which by our own reasoning makes the company-level saving from interest worth less to them. Woolworths and Lovisa both describe their borrowing as a balance, and the point about utilities and technology firms is that a debt ratio alone does not say how risky a firm is.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson sets the tax benefit of debt against the cost of getting into trouble, and asks how much a firm can safely borrow.

lessons.title: Distress and the trade-off

lead.text: The [[interest cover|Operating profit divided by finance costs. Met in 'Liquidity and gearing' in Accounting.]] from Accounting puts numbers on the answer. Divide each year's profit before interest by the $40 million owed. The steady firm covers its interest 2.25, 2.5 and 2.75 times, and the cyclical firm 0.5, 2.5 and 4.5 times. The two average the same cover, but the lender is owed the full $40 million in *every* year, and in the cyclical firm's bad year the profit pays only half of it.

Where does the other half come from? It can come from cash the firm saved earlier, from new borrowing or from its owners, each of which has a cost, and if none of them is available the interest goes unpaid. So **the worst year decides how much debt a firm can carry**, and the average does not. The passage on utilities and technology firms in 'Why firms borrow' made the same point from the other side: how much a firm owes says little until you know how steady its cash flows are.

reveal.text: The tunnel opened on 28 August 2005 and was averaging about 30,000 trips a day in early 2006. In November 2006 it was reported that 60,000 to 90,000 a day were needed to meet the interest payments, and by December it was insolvent, with debts of over A$500 million. The next screen names what that kind of trouble costs a firm.

lead.text: A firm whose profit cannot pay its interest, like the cyclical firm in its bad year, is in **financial distress**. The Cross City Tunnel in the figure was a real firm in that position. Wikipedia describes it as a condition in which a firm breaks its promises to creditors, or keeps them only with difficulty, and says that unrelieved distress can end in bankruptcy. Distress usually has costs of its *own*.

Wikipedia separates them. The **direct costs** are the ones bankruptcy itself brings: the fees of auditors, lawyers and managers, and other payments. The **indirect costs** arise even when bankruptcy is avoided, and Wikipedia's example is a higher cost of capital, since banks usually raise interest rates when a firm is in distress. Wikipedia adds that distress draws management's attention away from running the business. One more cost follows from the same logic, though Wikipedia does not describe it and we offer it as reasoning: a firm short of cash may drop a sound project.

reveal.text: Both kinds of cost count against borrowing. The next screen sets them beside the tax saving from 'Why firms borrow'.

lead.text: Put this lesson beside 'Why firms borrow'. Borrowing brings a tax shield, and it also brings the chance of distress. **Trade-off theory** says a firm chooses how much to borrow by *balancing* the two: Wikipedia describes it as setting the cost of bankruptcy against the tax benefit of debt. Touro's textbook draws the same balance as a U-shaped curve. As cheap debt replaces equity the average cost of capital falls to a low point, and then it rises again because lenders see more default risk and charge more. It gives no formula for where the low point lies and says the best level depends on the industry and the firm's risk.

The theory has a rival. Pecking order theory, which Wikipedia links to the costs of asymmetric information, holds that firms prefer to use profit they have kept, then debt, and to raise new shares last, because outsiders read a share issue as bad news. This lesson works with the first theory.

diagram.alt: A U-shaped curve of the average cost of capital against the share of debt in a firm's funding. The cost falls as cheap debt replaces equity, reaches a lowest point, and rises again as lenders see more default risk and charge more. The shape is a sketch, with no numbers.

reveal.text: Heavy debt also changes what owners and managers want, and the next screen names two ways.

lead.text: Heavy debt changes what a firm's owners and managers want, as well as what it costs. Wikipedia names one effect: as debt rises relative to equity, managers acquire an incentive to take on risky projects, even ones whose net present value is negative. This is the **asset substitution effect**. Wikipedia gives the reason: if a risky project succeeds the shareholders earn the benefit, and if it fails the lenders bear the downside.

The *opposite* problem is **debt overhang**. Wikipedia defines it as a debt load so heavy that the firm struggles to borrow any more, even for an investment worth more than it costs. A firm in that position may have to pass up a good project, which is a cost of debt that no bankruptcy fee records.

reveal.text: Debt can push a firm towards bad projects and block good ones. The last question asks what that means for judging a project funded with it.
A firm can borrow only as much as its cash flows can carry in a bad year, and a project's cash flows are only as good as the forecast behind them.

lessons.orientation: Judge whether a firm should borrow more by weighing the tax benefit of debt against the costs of financial distress, given how steady its cash flows are.
lessons.nextAction: Judge whether a firm should pay out cash or keep it, and what a franked dividend is worth to different shareholders.

blocks.text: Two firms each owe $40 million of interest a year. The first earns $90 million, $100 million or $110 million before interest, depending on the year. The second earns $20 million, $100 million or $180 million. Over the three years each averages $100 million.
A lender has to decide which of the two it can trust with that much debt, and the averages do not separate them.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to judge whether a firm can carry its debt, name the costs of distress, and say why a firm should not simply borrow as much as the tax rules allow.
intro.whyItMatters: The tax saving from debt is easy to see, and the cost of getting into trouble is easy to leave out until a bad year arrives.

recap.keyIdea: A firm can carry as much debt as its worst year allows, and the right amount balances the tax saved against the costs of getting into trouble, which include fees, dearer borrowing and the poor choices that heavy debt invites.

blocks.text: You compared a steady firm and a cyclical one with the same interest bill and the same average profit, and saw that the bad year, with cover of only 0.5, is the test of debt capacity. The Cross City Tunnel showed it in practice: about 30,000 trips a day against the 60,000 to 90,000 reported as needed to meet interest, then insolvency and receivers by the end of 2006.

Distress has direct costs, such as legal and auditors' fees, and indirect costs, such as lenders raising the interest rate, and trade-off theory sets them against the tax shield. Heavy debt can also push owners towards risky projects and block good ones, so the amount of debt matters beyond the tax it saves.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns to the cash a firm gives back to its owners, through dividends and buybacks, and asks what a franking credit is worth.

lessons.title: Dividends, buybacks and franking credits

lead.text: A dividend is a distribution of profit to shareholders, and whatever is distributed has left the company. That is why the share in the opening question lost about the dividend: the company's value dropped by the cash it paid, and the owner now holds that cash instead. The argument of Modigliani and Miller, which you met in 'Why firms borrow', says the same about payouts in general. In a perfect market, the way a company splits its cash between paying it out and keeping it does not change what the company is worth.

So the useful question is who can put the cash to better use, the company or its owners. If the company has a project that earns more than owners could earn elsewhere at the same risk, they are better off when it keeps the cash and invests it. If its best project earns less, the cash is worth more in their hands. A company that follows this rule invests in every project that beats its [[required return|The return investors could earn on other investments of the same risk; the discount rate in an NPV. Met in 'Money now and money later'.]] and pays out what is left, which is called a **residual dividend policy**. The leftover cash can be returned in more than one way, which a later screen compares.
Apply the rule to a company with cash it has no immediate need for.

reveal.text: A company gains nothing by keeping cash that its owners could use better. Had the same project earned 14%, the answer would reverse, so the comparison decides it.

lead.text: A company's **payout ratio** is the dividends it pays divided by what it earned, so a ratio of 60% means 60 cents of every dollar of profit went out as dividends. Above 100% the company paid out more than it earned, and the extra has to come from somewhere, such as cash it already held or borrowing. Wikipedia adds a caution: earnings are an accounting measure and do not necessarily match cash flow, so the safer check replaces earnings with [[free cash flow|The operating cash flow left after the spending a business must make to carry on. Met in 'What a business is worth' in Accounting.]].

afterFigure.text: In four of the five years Lovisa paid out more than it earned, by between 1% and 19%, and in 2026 it paid out about 93% of its profit. The same report shows $87 million drawn on a $120 million borrowing facility at the end of 2026, up from $77 million a year earlier. A ratio above 100% marks where to look, and the cash and the borrowing show whether the dividend can be kept up.

lead.text: A **share buyback** is the other way to return cash: the company buys some of its own shares from the people who hold them. Cash leaves the company either way, and the difference is what the owners are left holding. After a dividend there are as many shares as before, each worth less. After a buyback there are fewer shares, each worth the same.

afterFigure.text: The owner of 1,000 shares ends with $10,000 in all three columns, so before tax a dividend and a buyback leave the owner equally well off. Earnings per share does differ: the same $10 million of profit spread across 9 million shares is $1.11 a share, against $1.00 across 10 million. Wikipedia makes the same point, that earnings per share rises after a repurchase even if profits stay the same. A higher figure after a buyback reflects a smaller number of shares, and it is no sign that the business improved.

The owner of 1,000 shares holds $9,000 of shares and $1,000 in cash after either, a total of $10,000 in all three columns.

lead.text: Australian company profit is taxed at the company, and shareholders are then taxed on the dividends they receive. Imputation stops that from taxing the same profit twice: the company passes on the tax it has paid as a **franking credit** attached to the dividend, and the ATO calls such a dividend franked. Take a company that earns $100 and pays $30 tax at the 30% company rate. It has $70 left to pay as a dividend, and it can attach $30 of credit to it.

The shareholder includes the cash and the credit in income, so $100 here, and works out tax on that at their own rate. The credit is then taken off the tax bill, which the ATO describes as the gross-up and credit approach. Why include the credit in income at all? Because the $100 of profit before company tax is what the shareholder is treated as having earned, and the credit then returns the $30 already paid on it. Because the credit stands for tax the company has already paid, what a franked dividend is worth depends on the shareholder's own tax rate, and the figure shows three shareholders who each receive the same $70.

afterFigure.text: Holder A pays no tax, so the whole $30 comes back as a refund. Credits have been refundable since 1 July 2000, and before that an unused credit was lost. Holder B's credit matches the tax exactly, and holder C pays the $15 by which tax on the grossed-up amount exceeds the credit, which the ATO says is sometimes called top-up tax. In each case the $100 of profit ends up taxed at the shareholder's own rate, as if the company had been a conduit.

diagram.alt: A company earns $100, pays $30 tax and pays a $70 dividend with $30 of credit. Three shareholders include $100 in income. Holder A owes tax of $0, so the $30 credit is refunded and A keeps $100. Holder B owes $30, so nothing more is owed and B keeps $70. Holder C owes $45, so $15 more is paid and C keeps $55.

lead.text: The ATO's own worked example applies the same steps to a real figure.

reveal.text: A credit larger than the tax owed is paid back to a resident individual, so Rodney keeps the $700 in cash and receives a $100 refund as well. The dividend came with $300 of tax the company had already paid, and he could use all of it.

lead.text: The ATO sorts shareholders by what they can do with a credit. Australian resident individuals use it against their tax and receive a refund for any excess, and so do complying superannuation funds and endorsed charities. A company that receives a franked dividend can use the credit to bring its own tax down to nil but is not refunded any excess. Only Australian resident taxpayers can claim a credit at all, and Wikipedia adds that foreign shareholders cannot use them.

A company also chooses how much franking to attach. A dividend can be fully franked, partly franked or unfranked, and an unfranked dividend is ordinary income to the holder with no credit. Woolworths says all its dividends are fully franked, with credits at the 30% company rate, and its total for 2026 was 97 cents a share. Lovisa paid a final dividend of 27.0 cents, unfranked, in October 2025 and an interim dividend of 53.0 cents, 50% franked, in March 2026. Woolworths ended 2026 with $1,746 million of credits available for later dividends and Lovisa with $2.1 million. The reports do not say why the two companies differ.

afterFigure.text: To a holder who can use the whole credit, a fully franked dollar is worth about $1.43, a half-franked dollar about $1.21 and an unfranked dollar $1.00. Wikipedia suggests valuing a franked dividend by treating the credit as part of the income received. To a holder who cannot use a credit, all three are worth the dollar in cash.

diagram.alt: Bars for each $1 of dividend at a 30% company tax rate. A fully franked dollar carries 42.9 cents of credit, as with all of Woolworths' dividends. A 50% franked dollar carries 21.4 cents, as with Lovisa's 2026 interim dividend and proposed final dividend. An unfranked dollar carries none, as with Lovisa's final dividend paid in October 2025.
diagram.caption: At a 30% company tax rate the credit is 30/70 of the franked part of a dividend, which is how $70 of cash carried $30 of credit.

lead.text: Place each holder in the group the ATO's rules put it in.

reveal.text: The same franked dividend gives its full benefit to the holders in the first group, a smaller one to the company and none to the overseas fund.

lead.text: Managers know more about the company than outsiders do, so a payout can carry information. The dividend signalling hypothesis says that a rise in the dividend tells the market the firm is doing better than average, though Wikipedia notes that the idea has been contested. A buyback can say something similar: a manager who thinks the shares trade below their value may buy them back, which is a bet that the market has it wrong.

A buyback is a looser promise than a dividend. Wikipedia reports that the market treats a cut in a dividend more harshly than a cut in buybacks, so buybacks are seen as the more flexible tool and tend to carry out cash that may not last. Pay can also be tied to earnings per share or to the share price, which a buyback pushes up, so a buyback can serve managers as well as owners. When a company announces a payout, three questions cover most of what matters: whether cash and borrowing can support it, whether a project would earn more than the owners could earn elsewhere, and who receives it and what the credit is worth to them.
Read two announcements together, as an investor would.

reveal.text: A signal is a reason to look, and the payout itself should be judged on cash, alternative uses and who receives it.

lessons.orientation: Judge whether a firm should pay cash out or keep it, whether to use a dividend or a buyback, and what a franked dividend is worth to different shareholders.
lessons.nextAction: Find which assumption a project's value hinges on, and how far it can move before the answer flips.

blocks.text: Woolworths paid $1,100 million in cash dividends in the year to June 2026, against a profit of $1,138 million for its shareholders. Lovisa paid out $88.6 million against a profit of $95.6 million. A dividend can look like a bonus that arrives on top of what a company is worth, but the cash that reaches shareholders is cash that leaves the company.
So when should a company hand cash back, in what form, and what does a shareholder in Australia actually receive when it does?

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to judge whether a company should pay cash out or keep it, and say what a franked dividend is worth to a given shareholder.
intro.whyItMatters: A payout is a choice about where cash does more good, and in Australia it carries a tax credit that different holders can use in different ways.

recap.keyIdea: A company should pay out cash when it cannot earn more on it than its owners could elsewhere, and a franked dividend is worth more to a holder who can use the credit.

blocks.text: You saw that a dividend moves value from the company to its owners, and that a buyback does the same while lifting earnings per share by shrinking the share count. Lovisa paid out more than its profit in four of five years, which is a reason to check its cash. In the ATO's example Rodney's $300 credit was larger than his $200 tax, so $100 came back as a refund, while Woolworths's fully franked dividends and Lovisa's unfranked and half-franked ones show that the credit depends on what a company chooses to attach.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns from what a company gives out to what it assumes in the first place: which forecast a project's value hinges on.

lessons.title: Forecasts and sensitivity

steps.headline: A base case and its inputs

lead.text: Here is a project invented for this lesson. A company spends $2.0 million on equipment that will last 8 years. It expects to sell 12,000 units a year at $100 each, each unit costs $55 to make, and fixed costs are $120,000 a year. That leaves $420,000 of cash a year, which discounted at 9% is worth about $2.32 million today, so the NPV is about +$325,000. Tax and working capital are left out to keep the numbers readable.

That one figure rests on seven assumptions at once, and Wikipedia notes that an NPV depends heavily on the forecast cash flows, when they arrive, how long the project lasts, what it costs to start and the discount rate. A **sensitivity analysis** changes one assumption at a time and shows how far the NPV moves, which tells you which forecasts deserve the effort of checking. Each assumption is moved by an amount that is plausible for it. A price that could easily be 10% out matters more than a cost that is almost certain, so the size of each move reflects how far that input could really miss.

lead.text: A table of bad cases says how far the answer falls. A second question is how far an input can move before the answer changes sign, and the value of an input at which the NPV is exactly zero is called its **break-even** value. Take units sold in the same project. Each extra unit adds the same $45 of cash a year for eight years, so the NPV rises in a straight line with volume: about −$273,000 at 9,600 units, +$325,000 at 12,000 and +$922,000 at 14,400. Where that line crosses zero is the break-even volume.

afterFigure.text: It crosses at about 10,700 units, some 11% below the plan. The project can lose about a ninth of its volume before it stops earning the 9% required return, and any shortfall beyond that destroys value. Price, volume and the two costs all move the NPV in a straight line, so two calculated points are enough to find the crossing. Whether 11% is comfortable depends on how far volume could plausibly miss, and a break-even close to the plan says the value is thin.

reveal.text: A cushion of 5% on price is small beside the 10% miss the firm already thought plausible, which is what makes this project's value thin.

lead.text: One-at-a-time tests treat the inputs as unrelated, and in practice they are not. UQ's textbook points out that raising a price often reduces demand, so looking at price separately from units sold makes little sense. **Scenario analysis** changes linked inputs together, such as a lower price with a lower volume in a weak market, and shows what the NPV would be if that situation really occurred.

afterFigure.text: A price 10% lower on its own leaves the NPV at about −$340,000, and volume 20% lower on its own leaves it at about −$273,000. A weak market that brings both leaves it at about −$804,000. The combined case is a worse answer than either test gave, and it describes a bad year better than either one does. Which scenarios to run depends on what could really happen together, and a best case and a worst case around the base case are the usual pair.

lead.text: Sensitivity and scenarios test a forecast without asking where it came from. Wikipedia's account of Kahneman and Tversky's work says that human judgement about plans is generally optimistic: people tend to understate what a planned action will cost, how long it will take and how risky it is, and to overstate what it will deliver, a tendency now called the **planning fallacy**. The cause is the **inside view**, which looks at the parts of this particular project and ignores how similar ventures ended. The **outside view** does the reverse and starts from how they ended.

Reference class forecasting makes the outside view a method with three steps: pick out a group of similar projects that have already finished, work out how their results were spread, and place the project at hand within that spread to find its most likely outcome. The two tunnels in this lesson are a small reference class. The Cross City Tunnel's operators expected about 35,000 vehicles a day at first, and between 20,000 and 25,000 were reported a month in. CLEM7's forecast was about 60,000, and around 20,000 used it once the reduced toll applied. Two projects prove little, yet a board looking at a third tunnel forecast would begin from the fact that both of these fell well short.
One famous project shows the pattern on a larger scale.

reveal.text: A single project is only a warning. The outside view asks how often estimates run low in the reference class and by how much.

lead.text: Companies run this arithmetic on themselves. Woolworths tests whether each business unit's recoverable value still exceeds its [[carrying value|The amount a business is recorded at in the accounts. Met in 'Value that arrives late'.]], and for two units its 2026 report says how far the assumptions could move before that headroom disappears. For New Zealand Food, a 1.0 point rise in the post-tax discount rate together with a 10% cut to EBIT in the year the [[terminal value|The one figure that stands for everything after the last forecast year. Met in 'Value that arrives late'.]] is built on would bring the recoverable value down to the carrying value. For Petstock the figures are 0.2 points and 4%. Each note is a break-even for two inputs moved together.

afterFigure.text: The notes also say what each valuation rests on. New Zealand Food's value depends on management's forecasts being met, and those assume a steady but difficult market, efficiency gains and a recovery in earnings. Petstock's value depends on its growth continuing and on synergies with the Group, because it was acquired recently.

lead.text: Apply the outside view to a forecast for a project the lesson has not used.

reveal.text: A careful forecast and a careless one can both be optimistic in the same way, so the check that helps most is one that looks at other projects.

lessons.orientation: Find which assumption a project's value hinges on, work out how far it can move before the answer flips, and judge a forecast against what happened to similar projects.
lessons.nextAction: Judge whether an acquisition price can pay off by comparing the premium with the synergies a buyer can realistically deliver.

blocks.text: Before Sydney's Cross City Tunnel opened in 2005, its operators indicated that they expected about 35,000 vehicles a day at first, rising over the first year to a projected 90,000. About a month after it opened, media reports put daily use at only 20,000 vehicles, though the government and the toll operators maintained that the average since opening was about 25,000.
A financial model built on figures like these produces one answer, the base case. What should a board ask of a forecast like that, and of the project value that rests on it?

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say which assumptions a project's value hinges on, how far they can move before the answer flips, and how a forecast compares with what happened to similar projects.
intro.whyItMatters: An NPV is one guess about many things, and this is how you find out which of them you most need to check.

recap.keyIdea: A project's NPV rests on a few assumptions, so find the ones where a plausible miss would change the answer, how far each can move before it does, and what similar projects actually did.

blocks.text: In the invented project a price 10% lower, or volume 20% lower, turned an NPV of +$325,000 negative, and the break-even showed that a fall of about 11% in volume would erase the value. CLEM7's traffic fell with its toll, so price and volume belong in a scenario together. The Opera House and the two tunnels showed estimates running low, which is the reason to add an outside view to the inside one, and Woolworths's notes on New Zealand Food and Petstock showed a company reporting break-evens on its own valuations.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns to the price a buyer pays for a whole business, where the forecasts behind the deal are the buyer's own.

lessons.title: Acquisitions and the price paid

lead.text: To gain control of a listed company a buyer has to persuade many shareholders to sell, and the market price alone does not usually do that. Wikipedia describes the **control premium** as a payment above a listed company's current market price that a buyer will sometimes make to gain a controlling stake. Take an invented bid: a company whose shares are worth $1,000 million on the market is offered $1,350 million, a premium of 35%, or $350 million. Its shareholders receive that $350 million.

What could a buyer justify paying? Wikipedia gives the ceiling as the sum of three things: the target's intrinsic value, which is what the cash it can produce is worth today, the synergies it expects from combining the two firms, and what it would lose if a rival bought the target instead. A **synergy** is a financial benefit a firm expects to realise by merging with or acquiring another, such as savings from removing duplicate departments. In this bid the buyer believes the combination is worth $120 million more than the two firms apart. That puts the ceiling at $1,120 million before counting any rival, and Wikipedia says an offer above the future benefit of the acquisition is not a prudent investment decision.
Compare the price with the ceiling before you decide who gains.

reveal.text: A premium moves value to the seller's shareholders at once and for certain. What the buyer gets back is whatever synergy it manages to deliver, which the next screen takes up.

lead.text: The premium is paid on the day the deal is done, and the synergies arrive later, if at all. Only the part that is delivered comes back to the buyer, so its gain is the value of the synergies delivered less the premium it paid. The sellers' shareholders keep the premium whatever happens. The figure uses a second invented bid with a smaller target: Rowan Paper is worth $600 million on the market, and a buyer offers a premium of 15%, or $90 million, for $100 million of expected synergies.

afterFigure.text: The share of the synergies that must arrive for the buyer to break even is the premium divided by the synergies, which is 90% here. A buyer who pays almost all the expected synergy away to the sellers has nothing left to absorb a shortfall. A bid has to be judged on how much of the synergy is likely to arrive and how much of it has already gone to the sellers.

diagram.alt: Bars compare the invented Rowan Paper bid's $90 million premium with the synergy delivered. If every synergy arrives ($100 million) the buyer gains $10 million. If two thirds arrive (about $67 million) it loses about $23 million. If half arrive ($50 million) it loses $40 million. The sellers' shareholders gain $90 million in every case.

lead.text: Try a lower premium on a larger target.

reveal.text: A premium of 10% looks modest, yet it takes most of a synergy forecast of 12% of the target's value. The comparison that counts is the premium against the synergies.

lead.text: Decide which list deserves more doubt before you read what the sources say.

reveal.text: Wikipedia says that bankers take potential revenue synergies less seriously than cost synergies because of the uncertainty markets introduce, and it reports a McKinsey finding that about 70% of the revenue synergies forecast for mergers did not appear. That figure is the article's report of the study, which this course has not seen.

lead.text: Suppose five bidders compete for a block of a company that is worth the same to each of them, but none knows what it is worth, so each makes an estimate. In the figure the block is worth $100 million and the estimates are $70 million, $85 million, $100 million, $115 million and $130 million, which average $100 million. Wikipedia describes the **winner's curse** as what follows in a contest like this: the winner is whoever values the prize most optimistically, and so tends to overestimate and overpay. Our own reading is that a takeover contest can work this way when the target is worth about the same to every bidder. The article's account is of auctions in general, and it adds that the curse does not arise where bidders value the prize for private reasons of their own.

afterFigure.text: If each bidder bids its own estimate, bidder E wins and pays $30 million more than the block is worth. Bidder E's method was no worse than anyone else's, and the contest selected its estimate for being the highest. Winning is bad news about the value, because it tells the winner that every rival thought the block worth less. Wikipedia says the winner's curse was first addressed in 1971 by three petroleum engineers at Atlantic Richfield, who claimed that oil companies were earning unexpectedly low returns on early offshore lease auctions.

lead.text: Apply the contest to a new case with seven bidders.

reveal.text: A winner that takes its own estimate at face value pays for the estimate's errors as well as for the prize. The next screen looks at other reasons a buyer's price can end up above what it can deliver.

lead.text: Wikipedia reports that the commonly studied measures show no improvement, on average, in an acquirer's financial performance after it makes acquisitions, and that outcomes often disappoint against what was predicted. It cites up to 70% of such activity failing, which is the article's claim, and this course has not checked the studies behind it.

Some motives for a deal do not add value for the buyer's owners even when the deal goes through. Diversification is one. It can protect a company from a slump in one industry, yet shareholders can get the same protection by spreading their own holdings, at far lower cost than a merger. Managerial overconfidence is another, and it works through the price: a manager's overconfidence about the synergies leads to overpayment for the target. A deal adds value for owners when it does something they could not do for themselves, such as cutting duplicated costs, and the buyer pays less than that is worth.

Company reports show where a value leans on synergies. Woolworths's 2026 annual report says that, because Petstock was acquired recently, its value depends on growth continuing and on synergies with the Group. It also says that the carrying values of BIG W, MyDeal and Healthylife were fully impaired in the prior period. The pages quoted here do not say what was paid for any of them.
Read the extract and decide how much it can show.

reveal.text: The article stops at the price and says nothing about how the deal turned out. Whether a price was too high is settled later, by the cash flows the business delivers against it.

lead.text: Use what winning tells a bidder to decide how it should bid.

reveal.text: Bid shading is the answer Wikipedia gives to the curse: a savvy bidder revises its estimate down to allow for the news that winning brings, so it overpays only if it ignores that.

lessons.orientation: Judge whether an acquisition price can pay off by comparing the premium with the synergies the buyer can realistically deliver, and say how competition and overconfidence push buyers to overpay.
lessons.nextAction: Judge from a piece of news whether a share price should move, and say what a price can and cannot tell a manager.

blocks.text: In April 2011 Rio Tinto gained a majority stake in Riversdale Mining, an Australian coal miner with significant interests in Mozambique, in what Wikipedia describes as a $2.9 billion all-cash deal. Two years later it wrote the value of the assets down by $3 billion, and it later sold them for $50 million.
Nobody sets out to pay more for a business than it is worth, so how does a price end up so far above what the assets later fetched? And what would a price need to look like to pay off?

intro.whyItMatters: A takeover price is a bet that the synergies will cover the premium, and this is how you tell which side of the bet you are looking at.

recap.keyIdea: A takeover pays off for the buyer only if the synergies it delivers exceed the premium it paid, and competition and overconfidence push buyers to pay more than they can deliver.

blocks.text: The premium goes to the sellers on the day of the deal, while the buyer's gain depends on how much synergy it delivers: a premium of $350 million could not be covered by $120 million of synergies, and a premium of $100 million needed more than four fifths of them. In a contest the winner is the bidder whose estimate is highest, so winning is bad news about the value, and a savvy bidder shades its bid. Rio Tinto's price for Riversdale and its later sale for $50 million show how far a price can end above the value delivered, while the extract on its bid for Alcan shows a hostile rival bid and says nothing about whether the price was too high.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson asks what a share price, the number every bid starts from, can and cannot tell you.

lessons.title: What a share price tells you

lead.text: The **efficient-market hypothesis** says that an asset's price already contains whatever information is available. The mechanism is a simple one. If a share's price does not yet reflect some piece of information, investors can trade on it, and their trading pushes the price along until the information has no more trading value. A direct implication, as Wikipedia puts it, is that nobody can consistently beat the market on a risk-adjusted basis, since prices should react only to new information. That is why the reading you chose in the opening question holds: a price reflects what is known and expected now.

Two common readings of the idea go further than it does. The first is that prices are always right. New information can lower a price as readily as it can raise one, and a price built on information that later proves incomplete can look wrong afterwards. The second is that analysis is pointless, yet analysis is how information reaches prices: investors who work out what news means and trade on it are the ones who move the price.
Pick the statement that matches what the idea claims.

reveal.text: The claim is about information and trading, and it is a weaker claim than the two readings above. It leaves room for prices to fall, and for analysts to matter.

lead.text: If prices already reflect what is known, the only news that moves a price is news that was not expected. UQ's textbook puts it in terms of forecasts: an announcement moves the price by changing what investors expect of a company's future cash flows or their risk. One of its examples is from the ASX. In June 2019 shares in AfterPay Touch fell as much as 15% in an afternoon on news that Visa planned to start offering buy now, pay later credit, an unexpected large competitor that gave analysts reason to cut their forecasts.

The size of news is measured against what was expected. Suppose analysts forecast a profit rise of 4%. A reported rise of 4% leaves forecasts unchanged, so the price should stay about where it was. A rise of 7% lifts forecasts and a rise of 1% lowers them, even though profit rose both times.

diagram.alt: Bars comparing analysts' forecast of a 4% profit rise with three reported results. A reported rise of 4% matches the forecast, so the price should stay about the same. A rise of 7% beats it, so the price should rise. A rise of 1% misses it, so the price should fall.

lead.text: Measure each announcement against what was expected before you place it.

reveal.text: An announcement is judged against the forecast the price was built on, and the direction of profit is not the test. That is why profit can rise on the day a price falls.

lead.text: A price that reflects information lets you measure what a piece of news was worth. An **event study** assesses the impact of an event on an outcome, and in finance it reads the effect of an event on a firm's value from its share price. In MacKinlay's account, as Wikipedia quotes it, if the marketplace is rational the effects of an event are reflected in security prices at once, so a short window of prices around the event gives a measure of its economic impact. Event studies are used for corporate events such as earnings announcements and mergers and acquisitions.

Short windows are the point. A price reacts to many things, so a day or a few days around the event isolates it, while a long window collects everything else that happened meanwhile. Wikipedia adds that studies over a few days are more dependable than studies over many months or years, which run into many limitations.
Read the extract as an event study would, with the release of the figures as the event.

reveal.text: The shares later declined to nothing, as the article records. The fall of one fifth on the day is the price taking in that day's news, and the later decline followed from what came after it.

lead.text: The claim comes in three strengths, which Eugene Fama named in his influential 1970 review according to what "all available information" covers. The **weak form** concerns historical prices. The **semi-strong form** covers all publicly available information beyond past prices, and the **strong form** covers private information as well, so each form widens the information that is said to be in the price.

The evidence is mixed. Wikipedia says it has mostly failed to back the stronger forms of the hypothesis, and that investors including Warren Buffett and George Soros, along with researchers, have disputed the idea both empirically and theoretically. The lesson therefore treats the hypothesis as a claim under dispute.
Name the form that fits what the researcher found.

reveal.text: Each form is a claim about which information is already in the price, and a study can test one level of it without testing the next.

lead.text: A manager can treat the price as information: it is the market's combined forecast of the firm's cash flows and risk, updated by everyone who trades. A fall after an announcement shows how investors read it, and a price well below the manager's own estimate is a disagreement that needs an explanation.

A manager can also act on a disagreement. Wikipedia notes that a manager who believes the firm's stock is trading below its intrinsic value may consider repurchasing shares, which makes a buyback a bet that the price is too low. On the efficient-market reading that bet needs the manager to know something the price does not. It is also worth asking what else the buyback does, since Wikipedia reports that executive pay is often affected by buybacks.
Decide what a premium over the market price shows about the price.

reveal.text: Wikipedia says that to gain control a buyer may have to offer more than the market price so that existing shareholders agree to sell. The market price is set by small trades, and the premium pays for control and for the gains the buyer expects from it.

lead.text: Respond to a director who believes the market has the price wrong.

reveal.text: A price is a view that the manager is free to disagree with. The efficient-market idea asks the manager to say why the disagreement is likely to pay.

lessons.orientation: Judge from a piece of news whether a share price should move, say what the efficient-market idea does and does not claim, and decide what a manager can and cannot read from the market's price.
lessons.reviewLabel: What a share price tells you
lessons.nextAction: You can now judge whether a project, a borrowing, a payout or an acquisition makes sense, and say what a share price can and cannot tell the managers who decide.

blocks.text: Lovisa's annual report gives its earnings per share and its share price for five years. Earnings per share rose every year, from 54.3 cents in 2022 to 86.3 cents in 2026. The share price rose until 2024 and then fell, and at $23.25 in 2026 it was about a quarter below the $30.91 of a year earlier.
In Accounting you turned this table into price-to-earnings ratios. Here the question is what a price is made of, if it can fall in a year when earnings rise.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say whether a piece of news should move a share price, what the efficient-market idea does and does not claim, and what a manager can read from a price.
intro.whyItMatters: Every decision in this course ends up in a share price, and this is how to read what that price can and cannot tell you.

recap.keyIdea: A share price reflects what is known and expected about a firm, so only news that differs from expectations moves it, and a manager can read the price as information without treating it as a verdict.

blocks.text: You saw Lovisa's price fall while its earnings per share rose, which fits a price that looks at expected future earnings and risk. News moves a price by its surprise, and an event study reads the effect of an event from prices in a short window around it, as with the one-fifth fall in the CLEM7 operator's shares on the poor traffic figures. The three forms of the hypothesis name how much information is already in the price, with the evidence mixed. A bid above the market price pays for control, and a buyback is a bet that the price is too low.

questions.prompt: Your firm can put $100,000 in a safe account at 5% for the year. Which offer is worth more to the firm?
hints: Work out what $100,000 would become in the account by the time the customer pays.
Compare that figure with what the customer offers for the same date.

acceptedIdeas: The $108,000 in a year, because $100,000 would grow to only $105,000
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The $108,000 in a year, because $100,000 would grow to only $105,000

choices.label: The $100,000 now, because money in hand beats a promise of more
The $108,000 in a year, because $100,000 would grow to only $105,000
They are worth the same, because the extra $8,000 only covers rising prices

questions.onCorrect: Kept in the account, the $100,000 reaches $105,000 in a year, so the customer's $108,000 is $3,000 better. Any comparison of money at different dates works this way.

misconceptions.feedback: Money in hand can be put to work, and the 5% account already counts that: $100,000 would be $105,000 a year from now, which is $3,000 less than the customer pays.
Nothing in the offer mentions prices. The comparison is with what $100,000 would earn, which is $5,000 at 5%, and the extra $8,000 is more than that.

questions.prompt: A colleague says the time value of money is only inflation in disguise. In an economy where prices have been flat for a year, a firm is offered $200 now or $204 in a year, and it can earn 5% on spare cash. What should it take, and what does that show?
hints: What would $200 become in a year at 5%?
Does that comparison need prices to change at all?

acceptedIdeas: The $200 now, since it grows to $210 and waiting has a price even without inflation
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The $200 now, since it grows to $210 and waiting has a price even without inflation

choices.label: The $204 in a year, since flat prices make the extra $4 a pure gain
The $204 in a year, since banks pay interest only to make up for rising prices
The $200 now, since it grows to $210 and waiting has a price even without inflation
Either one, since with flat prices a dollar now and a dollar later are worth the same

questions.onCorrect: The $200 reaches $210 in the year, which beats $204 with prices unchanged. The return on money in hand is what gives it a time value.

misconceptions.feedback: Flat prices don't make the $4 a pure gain. The firm could earn $10 on $200 in the year, so the later $204 gives up $6 of earnings.
Interest pays for more than rising prices. Flat prices and a 5% return are both in the question, so the 5% is the price of waiting itself.
A dollar now can be invested and a dollar later can't, whatever prices do. That is the difference the 5% measures.

questions.prompt: Your firm's best alternative now earns 10% a year at the same risk. Which is worth more today: $100,000 now, or the customer's $108,000 in a year?
hints: Bring the $108,000 back a year at 10% by dividing by 1.10.
Compare the result with the $100,000 on offer now.

acceptedIdeas: The $100,000 now, because waiting gives up more than the later payment adds
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The $100,000 now, because waiting gives up more than the later payment adds

choices.label: The $100,000 now, because waiting gives up more than the later payment adds
The $108,000, because it is the larger sum whatever rate you could earn elsewhere
Both are worth the same, because both amounts are fixed in dollars today
The $108,000, because the offer hasn't changed since the 5% case

questions.onCorrect: $108,000 ÷ 1.10 is about $98,200, which is $1,800 under the cash. The same offer is worth waiting for at 5% and not at 10%.

misconceptions.feedback: A larger sum later isn't automatically worth more. At 10% the $108,000 shrinks to about $98,200 today, which is less than $100,000.
Both amounts are fixed, but they fall on different dates. The $108,000 arrives a year later, and bringing it back at 10% shrinks it below $100,000.
The offer is the same, but its worth depends on what the cash could earn, and that has changed. At 10% waiting costs more than the later payment adds.

questions.prompt: At roughly what return on your alternative would your firm be indifferent between $100,000 now and the customer's $108,000 in a year?
hints: Look at where the curve crosses the dashed line, between the 5% case and the 10% case.
The offer pays $8,000 extra on $100,000 over one year. What rate is that?

acceptedIdeas: About 8%, where the extra amount just matches the return given up
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 8%, where the extra amount just matches the return given up

choices.label: About 5%, the rate the safe account paid in the opening example
About 0%, because the extra $8,000 is a gain whatever the rate
About 10%, the rate at which taking the cash won in the last question
About 8%, where the extra amount just matches the return given up

questions.onCorrect: $8,000 on $100,000 is 8% for the year, and $108,000 ÷ 1.08 is exactly $100,000. At any alternative return above 8%, the cash wins.

misconceptions.feedback: At 5% the later offer is still worth about $102,900 today, above the $100,000, so the verdict hasn't flipped yet.
At a rate of 0% waiting costs nothing, so the $108,000 wins easily. The rate that matters is the one where the $8,000 stops being enough.
At 10% the cash is already ahead, so the rate at which the two tie has to be lower than that.

questions.prompt: The bond in the extract keeps paying $2 a year. Suppose the yield investors require falls from 2% to 1%. What happens to the price they will pay for it?
hints: At a required yield of 1%, how much interest does $100 need to pay?
Compare that with the $2 this bond pays, and ask what buyers would do about the difference.

acceptedIdeas: It rises above $100, because $2 a year is now more than investors require
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It rises above $100, because $2 a year is now more than investors require

choices.label: It falls, because a lower required yield means the bond pays investors less
It rises above $100, because $2 a year is now more than investors require
It stays at $100, because the bond's payments of $2 a year haven't changed
It doubles to $200, because the required yield has halved

questions.onCorrect: The bond pays $1 more than investors now need on $100, so they bid the price up. The RBA puts the new price at $109.50.

misconceptions.feedback: The bond's payments are the same, so a lower required yield makes them worth more, not less, because they are brought back at a smaller discount.
The $2 is the same, but investors now need only $1 a year on $100, so they will pay more than $100 for a bond that pays $2.
The price rises only until the bond offers the 1% investors now require, which stops well short of $200.

extracts.text: Imagine that investors require a yield of 2 per cent to invest in a government bond. They will be willing to pay $100 to invest in a government bond that offers an annual interest payment of $2, because this will provide them with their required yield.
