questions.prompt: These changes each affect the present value of a payment of $80,000 due in six years. Which raise it and which lower it?
hints: Ask of each change whether waiting now costs more or less.
Two things are at work: the rate used, and the number of years until the payment.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Raises: a fall in the rate from 8% to 5%, payment moved to year 4, a smaller risk premium. Lowers: a rise in the rate from 6% to 9%, payment delayed to year 9, a less certain payment.

items.label: The return your firm can earn elsewhere falls from 8% to 5%
items.explanation: A lower rate is a smaller price for waiting, so the payment is brought back by less and is worth more today.

items.label: The customer agrees to pay in year 4 instead of year 6
items.explanation: Two fewer years of waiting means two fewer years of lost earnings set against the payment.

items.label: Investors become more confident the payment will arrive, so they ask for a smaller risk premium
items.explanation: A smaller risk premium lowers the required return, so the discount rate falls and the present value rises.

items.label: The return your firm can earn elsewhere rises from 6% to 9%
items.explanation: A higher rate is a bigger price for waiting, so the payment is brought back by more and is worth less today.

items.label: The customer delays the payment from year 6 to year 9
items.explanation: Three more years of waiting adds three more years of lost earnings against the payment.

items.label: The payment becomes less certain, so investors demand a higher return
items.explanation: A bigger risk premium raises the required return, so the discount rate rises and the present value falls.

questions.onCorrect: A smaller price for waiting or a shorter wait raises the present value, and a larger price or a longer wait lowers it. Risk works through the rate.

questions.prompt: Another customer offers $100,000 now or $150,000 in five years. Brought back to today, the $150,000 is worth about $112,100 if your firm's alternative earns 6%, and about $97,500 if it earns 9%. Which reading is best?
hints: Compare each present value with the $100,000 on offer now.
If waiting wins at one rate and loses at the other, where must the break-even rate sit?

acceptedIdeas: Waiting wins at 6% and the cash wins at 9%, so the break-even rate lies between them
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Waiting wins at 6% and the cash wins at 9%, so the break-even rate lies between them

choices.label: Waiting wins at both rates, since $150,000 is half as much again as $100,000
The cash wins at 6% and waiting wins at 9%, since a higher rate rewards patience
Waiting wins at 6% and the cash wins at 9%, so the break-even rate lies between them
The cash wins at both rates, since five years is too long to wait for any sum

questions.onCorrect: The break-even rate is about 8.4%, where the $150,000 is worth exactly $100,000. A firm earning less than that elsewhere should wait, and one earning more should take the cash.

misconceptions.feedback: At 9% the $150,000 is worth about $97,500 today, which is less than the $100,000. The extra $50,000 is spread over five years, and that isn't enough at 9%.
A higher rate means waiting costs more, which lowers what the later payment is worth today. That is why the $150,000 is worth less at 9% than at 6%.
At 6% the $150,000 is worth about $112,100 today, more than the $100,000, so five years isn't too long at that rate.

questions.prompt: At 8%, $1 due in 1, 5 and 15 years is worth about 93 cents, 68 cents and 32 cents today. Put these four payments in order of what they are worth today, largest first.
hints: Multiply each amount by the cents-per-dollar figure for its date.
The payment made now needs no discounting.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The $120 due in a year is worth about $111 today, the $100 now is worth $100, the $130 due in five years about $88 and the $200 due in 15 years about $63.

items: $120 due in 1 year
$100 paid now
$130 due in 5 years
$200 due in 15 years

questions.onCorrect: A larger payment can lose to a smaller one that comes sooner: the $200 is the biggest sum and the least valuable today.

questions.prompt: A different government bond pays $3 a year, and investors currently require 3%, so they pay $100 for it. Suppose the yield they require rises to 4%. What happens to the price they will pay?
hints: At a required yield of 4%, how much interest does $100 need to pay?
Compare that with the $3 this bond pays.

acceptedIdeas: It falls below $100, because $3 a year is now less than investors require
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It falls below $100, because $3 a year is now less than investors require

choices.label: It rises above $100, because a higher yield means a better bond
It stays at $100, because the bond still pays $3 a year as before
It rises to $133, because the required yield has gone up by a third
It falls below $100, because $3 a year is now less than investors require

questions.onCorrect: The bond pays $1 less on $100 than investors now require, so buyers pay less than $100 for it. The required yield and the price move in opposite directions.

misconceptions.feedback: A higher required yield is a higher bar for the bond to clear. The $3 stays the same, so it falls short of what buyers now need.
The payments are the same, but investors want $4 on every $100 now, so they will pay less than $100 for $3.
A higher required yield lowers what investors will pay for fixed payments, because the payments are brought back at a larger discount.

questions.prompt: At a discount rate of 6%, roughly what would a buyer pay today for the right to all 30 payments of the lease?
hints: A payment due in year 15 is worth roughly 42 cents on the dollar at 6%. What does that suggest about a typical payment?
The first payments are worth nearly their face value and the last ones much less. Where would the total settle?

acceptedIdeas: About $690,000, a little under half the sum
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About $690,000, a little under half the sum

choices.label: About $1.5 million, the sum of the payments
About $1.1 million, roughly three quarters of the sum
About $690,000, a little under half the sum
About $300,000, about a fifth of the sum

questions.onCorrect: The 30 payments are worth about $688,000 at 6%, a little under half of the $1.5 million they add up to.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the payments as if each arrived today. A payment due in year 30 is worth far less than one due next year, so the total today is well under $1.5 million.
Discounting takes off more than that. At 6% a payment 15 years away is worth only about 42 cents on the dollar, and the later payments are worth less still.
That takes off too much. The early payments are worth nearly their face value, and at 6% the first ten alone are worth about $370,000.

questions.prompt: At 6%, the first ten of the lease's 30 payments are the highlighted bars. Roughly what share of the lease's total present value do they carry?
hints: Compare the area of the first ten bars with the area of the other twenty.
The later bars are shorter than the early ones, but there are twice as many of them.

acceptedIdeas: About one half of it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About one half of it

choices.label: About one fifth of it
About one half of it
About three quarters of it
Nearly all of it

questions.onCorrect: At 6% the first ten payments carry about 53% of the value, though they are only a third of the payments.

misconceptions.feedback: The first ten payments are a third of the payments, and they are worth far more than a fifth of the value because they are the least discounted.
That would leave only a quarter of the value for the last 20 payments. At 6% those payments still carry nearly half of it.
The later bars are shorter, but there are twenty of them, and at 6% together they carry nearly half of the value.

questions.prompt: Two leases each pay $50,000 a year, one for 10 years and one for 20. The discount rate rises from 6% to 10%. Which lease loses the larger share of its value?
hints: Which lease has more of its value in the later years?
A change in the rate cuts a distant payment by more than a near one.

acceptedIdeas: The 20-year lease, because more of its value sits in distant years
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The 20-year lease, because more of its value sits in distant years

choices.label: The 10-year lease, because it has less time to make up the loss
Both lose the same share, because every payment is discounted at one rate
Neither, because the payments themselves haven't changed
The 20-year lease, because more of its value sits in distant years

questions.onCorrect: The 10-year lease loses about 17% of its value and the 20-year lease about 26%, because the longer lease has more of its value in the years a higher rate cuts hardest.

misconceptions.feedback: A shorter lease has less of its value in the distant years, and those are the payments a rise in the rate cuts hardest, so it holds up better.
One rate is used, but it is applied once for each year of waiting, so the tenth payment is cut by more than the first and the twentieth by more still.
The payments are the same, but their present values aren't: a higher rate brings each payment back to a smaller amount today.

questions.prompt: A valuation assumes that a business's cash flow grows by 8% a year for ever and discounts it at 6%. What is wrong with it?
hints: In the growing-perpetuity formula, what is the bottom line when growth is 8% and the rate is 6%?
What happens to each year's present value if the cash grows faster than the rate that discounts it?

acceptedIdeas: Growth above the discount rate gives no sensible value, so it cannot last
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Growth above the discount rate gives no sensible value, so it cannot last

choices.label: Nothing is wrong, since faster growth simply means a higher value for the business
The discount rate should always be set equal to the growth rate
Growth above the discount rate gives no sensible value, so it cannot last
A perpetuity cannot have growth in it, so the cash flow must be flat

questions.onCorrect: With growth above the rate, each year's present value would be larger than the last and the total would never settle. A steady growth rate has to be below the discount rate.

misconceptions.feedback: Faster growth does raise the value, but once growth reaches the discount rate the total never settles, and the formula stops giving a sensible figure.
Setting the two equal makes the formula divide by zero, so no value comes out at all.
A perpetuity can grow. The formula for one with steady growth is the one in the lesson, and it needs growth to stay below the rate.

questions.prompt: Woolworths's note on its New Zealand Food business says this. What does it show about how that business's value is built?
hints: Which two assumptions does the note change?
Which year's profit does it cut, and what part of a valuation does that year stand for?

acceptedIdeas: Much of it rests on far-off profit and on the rate used to discount it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Much of it rests on far-off profit and on the rate used to discount it

choices.label: Much of it rests on far-off profit and on the rate used to discount it
It rests only on this year's cash flow, which the note then discounts to today
The business is about to be sold, so its book value is being tested
A one-point change in a rate is too small to matter to a valuation

questions.onCorrect: The two assumptions that would remove the cushion are the discount rate and the profit in the terminal year, which is the year a terminal value is built on.

misconceptions.feedback: The note speaks of a terminal year and a long-term growth rate, so the valuation reaches well past this year's cash flow.
The note belongs to an annual test of the business's recorded value, and it says nothing about a sale.
The note says the reverse: a change of one point in the rate, together with a cut to terminal-year profit, would bring the value down to the book figure.

extracts.text: As a result, a 1.0% increase in the post-tax discount rate, and a 10.0% reduction in EBIT within the terminal year, would result in the recoverable value approximating its carrying value.
extracts.who: Woolworths Group Limited, Annual Report 2026, note 3.9 on impairment testing, New Zealand Food
extracts.kind: A company's note to its financial statements, written for shareholders

questions.prompt: Each of these is valued by discounting its cash flows. Which rest mainly on distant years, and which mainly on the next few?
hints: Ask when most of each one's cash arrives.
A project with no cash for years, or one whose cash builds up late, has its value far out.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Mainly distant years: the drug developer, the toll road and the mine. Mainly the next few years: the supply contract, the shop fit-out and the two-year loan.

items.label: A drug developer with no revenue for the next eight years
items.explanation: Nothing arrives for eight years, so all of the value is discounted for at least that long.

items.label: A toll road whose traffic is expected to build slowly over forty years
items.explanation: The biggest payments come last, where a rate rise cuts hardest.

items.label: A mine that will not start producing until its twelfth year
items.explanation: Every dollar of its value is at least eleven years away.

items.label: A supply contract paying a fixed fee for three years
items.explanation: All three payments are close, so the rate hardly matters.

items.label: A shop fit-out recovered over a five-year lease
items.explanation: The whole return arrives within five years.

items.label: A loan that the borrower will repay in full within two years
items.explanation: Every payment falls within two years, so little of the value is far out.

questions.onCorrect: A value rests on distant years when cash is slow to start or builds late, and those are the values a change in the rate or in growth moves most.

questions.prompt: A firm's discount rate rises by three points, from 6% to 9%. Put these four assets in order of the share of their value that the rise takes off, the largest loss first.
hints: The further out a payment is, the more a change in the rate takes off it.
Which asset has the largest share of its value in distant years?

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The asset that pays for ever loses about a third of its value, the 25-year concession about 23%, the 5-year contract about 8% and the one-year loan under 3%.

items: An asset that pays a level amount every year for ever
A concession that pays a level amount every year for 25 years
A contract that pays a level amount every year for 5 years
A loan repaid in one payment after a year

questions.onCorrect: The longer the payments run, the more of the value sits where a rise in the rate cuts hardest, and a perpetuity runs longest of all.

questions.prompt: An analyst values a business as a growing perpetuity: cash of $60 million in the first year, growth of 3% a year and a discount rate of 10%. She then lowers the rate to 9% because she feels more hopeful. By roughly how much does her value change?
hints: The value is the first year's cash divided by the rate less the growth. What is that bottom line at 10%, and at 9%?
Compare the two bottom lines as a share of the first.

acceptedIdeas: By about a sixth, since the gap between rate and growth narrows from 7 points to 6
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: By about a sixth, since the gap between rate and growth narrows from 7 points to 6

choices.label: By about 1%, since a one point change is a small change to any valuation
By about a sixth, since the gap between rate and growth narrows from 7 points to 6
By about a half, since the cut makes every future year's cash much more valuable
By nothing, since growth drives the value and the growth rate hasn't changed

questions.onCorrect: The value rises from about $857 million to $1,000 million, an increase of about a sixth, from a change of one point in the rate.

misconceptions.feedback: In a growing perpetuity a small change in the rate acts on a small gap. The gap between rate and growth narrows from 7 points to 6, which moves the value by about a sixth.
A one point cut does raise the value, but not by that much. The gap between the rate and growth narrows from 7 points to 6, which is a sixth.
The value divides the first year's cash by the rate less the growth, so a change in the rate moves it even when growth stays put.

questions.prompt: An analyst values an invented software firm, and 85% of her figure comes from the terminal value. A colleague says that makes the valuation worthless. What is the best reply?
hints: Which two assumptions does a terminal value rest on?
If a figure is mostly one component, which of its assumptions most needs checking?

acceptedIdeas: It makes the value depend on the growth and rate assumed after the forecast, so check those
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It makes the value depend on the growth and rate assumed after the forecast, so check those

choices.label: He is right, since any valuation that relies on a large terminal value must be rejected
He is wrong, since the terminal value is only a small tail added on for completeness
He is wrong, since the terminal value is a fact about the firm and not an assumption at all
It makes the value depend on the growth and rate assumed after the forecast, so check those

questions.onCorrect: Wikipedia says terminal value is highly sensitive to the growth and discount rate assumptions, and here it is 85% of the figure, so those two assumptions carry the valuation.

misconceptions.feedback: A large terminal value is common, and Wikipedia says it is frequently a large part of the total. It doesn't make a valuation worthless, but it does make it depend on a few assumptions.
Here the terminal value carries most of the figure, and Wikipedia says it is frequently a large part of the total, so it is far from a small tail.
A terminal value is an estimate built from an assumed growth rate and discount rate, and nothing in the firm fixes either of them.

questions.prompt: At 8%, a dollar paid over the next five years is worth about 80 cents today on average. With that in mind, which description of the three fit-outs is best?
hints: Multiply each fit-out's total cash by about 0.8 to put it into today's money.
Compare the result with the $1 million that each one costs.

acceptedIdeas: Only A creates value, B roughly breaks even, and C destroys value
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Only A creates value, B roughly breaks even, and C destroys value

choices.label: All three create value, since each one returns at least what it cost
Only A creates value, B roughly breaks even, and C destroys value
A and B create value, and C is the only one that loses
Only A is worth considering, since B and C earn nothing

questions.onCorrect: At about 80 cents on the dollar, A's $1.5 million is worth about $1.2 million, B's $1.25 million about $1.0 million and C's $1.0 million about $0.8 million, against a cost of $1 million each.

misconceptions.feedback: C returns exactly its cost, spread over five years. At about 80 cents on the dollar those later dollars are worth well under the $1 million it cost.
B's five payments total $1.25 million, which at about 80 cents on the dollar is roughly $1 million today, the same as its cost, so B adds almost nothing.
B and C do pay cash back. B's cash is worth about what it cost today, so it adds almost nothing, and C's is worth less than its cost.

questions.prompt: Fit-out C's five payments of $200,000 add up to exactly its $1,000,000 cost. Why is its NPV still about $200,000 below zero?
hints: C's payments arrive over five years. What is each year's $200,000 worth today at 8%?
Compare the total of those present values with the $1 million spent at the start.

acceptedIdeas: The money returns too slowly, while investors could earn 8% elsewhere
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The money returns too slowly, while investors could earn 8% elsewhere

choices.label: The money returns too slowly, while investors could earn 8% elsewhere
The payments must have been forecast too low for this kind of project
Fit-outs lose value in their first year, whatever the cash flows are
NPV subtracts the interest on the loan that paid for the fit-out

questions.onCorrect: C spends $1 million now and gets it back over five years. Those later dollars are worth about $800,000 today, so C returns nothing for the wait.

misconceptions.feedback: The forecast is taken as given. The shortfall comes from timing, because the $1 million is spread over five years.
Nothing in NPV depends on a fit-out losing value. It compares the cash coming back, in today's money, with the cost.
NPV doesn't deduct loan interest. The 8% already stands for what the money could earn elsewhere, whoever supplied it.

questions.prompt: A firm's required return is 10%. Project M costs $400,000, and the present value of its cash flows is about $401,000. An analyst says its NPV is about zero, so the project fails. What is the best reply?
hints: What return does a project with an NPV of zero earn?
Compare that return with the 10% investors can earn elsewhere.

acceptedIdeas: It earns about the required return, so accepting or rejecting changes little
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It earns about the required return, so accepting or rejecting changes little

choices.label: It should be rejected, since a zero is not positive enough to bother with
The forecasts must be wrong, since real projects never earn exactly zero
It pays out no cash at all, so it cannot create anything for the firm
It earns about the required return, so accepting or rejecting changes little

questions.onCorrect: M's cash, in today's money, is within $1,000 of what it cost, so it earns about the 10% investors could get elsewhere. The firm is no better or worse off either way.

misconceptions.feedback: A zero NPV doesn't hurt the firm. The project still earns the required return, so rejecting it costs nothing and accepting it gains nothing.
Real projects do land close to zero, and M's cash is worth within $1,000 of its cost. That is an ordinary result and says the return is about 10%.
M's cash flows are worth about $401,000 today. Its NPV is near zero because that cash is worth about what it cost, not because there is none.

questions.prompt: Capital is not short. Fit-out A (NPV +$198,000) and a separate project D (NPV +$40,000) don't affect each other. What should the firm do?
hints: Does taking D change the cash that A brings in?
What does an NPV of +$40,000 say about D's return compared with the required return?

acceptedIdeas: Accept both, because the NPVs of independent projects add
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Accept both, because the NPVs of independent projects add

choices.label: Accept only A, since a firm should take the single best project
Reject D, because an NPV of $40,000 is too small to matter
Accept both, because the NPVs of independent projects add
Accept neither until a project with a much larger NPV turns up

questions.onCorrect: Each project is judged on its own NPV, and independent ones add, so taking both adds about $238,000 to the firm's value.

misconceptions.feedback: With capital not short, nothing makes the firm choose. D adds $40,000 on top of A's value without taking anything from it.
Any positive NPV is value above what investors could earn elsewhere. $40,000 of it is worth having, however small it looks beside A's.
Waiting for a larger NPV gives up the value these two would add now. Nothing in the rule asks for a minimum size.

questions.prompt: The same project has an NPV of about $120,000 below zero at a 10% rate and about $60,000 above zero at 6%. What is the best reading?
hints: What changes between the two calculations, the cash flows or the rate?
Which of the two rates should reflect what investors require for a project with this much risk?

acceptedIdeas: Its value depends on the rate, so the rate must match the project's risk
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Its value depends on the rate, so the rate must match the project's risk

choices.label: One of the two calculations must contain an arithmetic error somewhere
NPV cannot be used on a project whose result changes with the rate
Its value depends on the rate, so the rate must match the project's risk
The project is worth about the average of the two results, a loss of $30,000

questions.onCorrect: The cash flows are the same and the rate differs, so the choice of rate decides the sign. Using a rate that matches the project's risk is part of getting NPV right.

misconceptions.feedback: Both can be right. The cash flows are the same, but a higher rate shrinks the later cash more, so the NPV is lower at 10% than at 6%.
NPV is built for this: the result depends on the rate, so the rate has to be chosen with care. Wikipedia says an incorrect rate will make the results meaningless.
The two results come from two different rates, and the project can't be worth both. What matters is which rate fits the project's risk.

questions.prompt: A firm has $2.0 million to invest and three independent proposals, all with positive NPVs. X costs $1.5 million and has an NPV of +$150,000, Y costs $1.0 million with +$100,000, and Z costs $1.0 million with +$90,000. Which choice adds the most value?
hints: Which combinations of these projects cost no more than $2.0 million?
Add up the NPVs of each combination that fits.

acceptedIdeas: Fund Y and Z, since together they add more value than X alone
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Fund Y and Z, since together they add more value than X alone

choices.label: Fund X alone, since it has the largest NPV of the three
Fund Y and Z, since together they add more value than X alone
Fund all three, since every positive NPV is worth taking
Fund Y alone, since it adds more than Z and costs less than X

questions.onCorrect: Y and Z fit within $2.0 million and add about $190,000, against $150,000 for X alone. When capital is short, the aim becomes the largest total NPV the money can buy.

misconceptions.feedback: X has the largest NPV on its own, but it uses $1.5 million to add $150,000. Y and Z together use $2.0 million and add $190,000.
The rule accepts every positive-NPV project only when capital is not short. Here the three cost $3.5 million and the firm has $2.0 million.
Y alone adds $100,000 and leaves $1.0 million unused. Adding Z puts that money to work and brings another $90,000.

questions.prompt: A board is told that a proposal's NPV is positive. For each of these, say whether NPV already builds it in or whether it is left out or only as good as the figures put into it.
hints: Ask whether the item is part of how NPV is worked out, or something an analyst must supply or judge.
NPV is purely financial, and it depends on the cash flows, their timing, the project's length and the rate.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Built in: the timing of the cash, the dollar size of the gain and the cost of waiting. Left out or only as good as the inputs: a reputation benefit that earns no cash, the sales forecast and the choice of rate.

bins.label: Left out, or only as good as its inputs

items.label: When each cash flow arrives
items.explanation: Discounting gives each cash flow its own date, so timing is part of the calculation.

items.label: How many dollars of value the project adds
items.explanation: NPV is a dollar figure, so it shows how much value is added as well as whether any is.

items.label: What waiting for later cash costs
items.explanation: The discount rate is the price of waiting, and every later cash flow is brought back at it.

items.label: A boost to the firm's reputation that earns no cash
items.explanation: Wikipedia says NPV is purely financial and leaves out non-financial considerations.

items.label: Whether the sales forecast turns out right
items.explanation: NPV depends heavily on knowing the future cash flows, and it can't check them.

items.label: Whether the chosen rate suits the project's risk
items.explanation: An incorrect rate makes the result meaningless, and NPV can't tell you whether the rate is right.

questions.onCorrect: NPV handles timing, size and the cost of waiting, and it relies on the forecasts and the rate being right and on the benefits being cash.

questions.prompt: A firm's required return is 9%. Project H costs $600,000 and returns $160,000 a year for four years, $640,000 in all. Its inflows are worth about $518,000 in today's money. Which statement fits?
hints: Compare the present value of H's inflows with its cost.
Is the $640,000 in today's money?

acceptedIdeas: H destroys about $80,000 of value, even though it returns more cash than it costs
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: H destroys about $80,000 of value, even though it returns more cash than it costs

choices.label: H adds about $40,000 of value, the gap between the cash it returns and its cost
H neither adds nor destroys value, since it returns more cash than it costs
H destroys about $80,000 of value, even though it returns more cash than it costs
H loses $80,000 of cash, since its NPV is negative

questions.onCorrect: H returns $640,000 in cash on a $600,000 outlay, but at 9% that cash is worth about $518,000 today. A negative NPV means a return below the required return, and it isn't a cash loss.

misconceptions.feedback: That subtracts the cost from cash received on different dates. In today's money the inflows are worth about $518,000, which is less than the $600,000 spent.
Returning more cash than it cost isn't the test. The cash arrives over four years, and at 9% it is worth about $518,000 today against $600,000 spent.
H does return $640,000 on a $600,000 outlay, so it doesn't lose cash. A negative NPV means the return falls short of the required return.

questions.prompt: A division head proposes a package of two independent projects. K has an NPV of +$150,000 and L has an NPV of $30,000 below zero. She says the package's total of +$120,000 makes it worth approving. What is the best reply?
hints: If the projects are independent, can the firm take K without L?
What does each choice add to the firm's value: K alone, L alone, and both together?

acceptedIdeas: Approve K and reject L, since NPVs add and L only subtracts value
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Approve K and reject L, since NPVs add and L only subtracts value

choices.label: Approve the package, since the NPV of the two together is positive
Approve K and reject L, since NPVs add and L only subtracts value
Reject both, since a package that contains a loser is a bad package
Approve the package only if the firm's capital is not short

questions.onCorrect: K alone adds $150,000, and the package adds $120,000, so L costs the firm $30,000 of value. Judging each independent project on its own NPV stops a loser hiding inside a total.

misconceptions.feedback: The total hides the fact that L subtracts $30,000. Because the projects are independent, the firm can take K alone and be $30,000 better off than with the package.
K is worth taking on its own, and rejecting it throws away $150,000 of value. Only L needs to be turned down.
Plentiful capital wouldn't make L worth taking. A project is taken only if its own NPV is positive.

questions.prompt: The roaster's survey cost $30,000 and said the café would work. Should the $30,000 count as a cost of the café when the roaster works out its NPV?
hints: Would the roaster still have paid the $30,000 if it decided against the café?
Which costs change because of the decision?

acceptedIdeas: No, because it is spent whether or not the café goes ahead
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, because it is spent whether or not the café goes ahead

choices.label: Yes, because the café should earn back what was spent on it
Yes, but only if the survey turns out to have been wrong
Only half, because the survey also informs other decisions
No, because it is spent whether or not the café goes ahead

questions.onCorrect: The $30,000 is spent whether or not the café opens, so it can't affect the choice. Only cash that changes with the decision belongs in the NPV.

misconceptions.feedback: The fee is spent already, and declining the café won't get it back. Only costs that depend on the decision belong in the comparison.
Whether the survey turned out right doesn't change what it cost. The $30,000 is gone either way.
The roaster pays the $30,000 whether or not it builds the café, so no share of it depends on the decision.

questions.prompt: A bakery plans a coffee corner in a spare room it owns, which is let to a dentist for $12,000 a year. The owner says the room costs the coffee corner nothing, because the bakery already owns it. What is wrong with that?
hints: What happens to the dentist's rent if the coffee corner opens in the room?
Would the bakery's cash be different without the coffee corner?

acceptedIdeas: The room could earn $12,000 a year in rent, which the coffee corner gives up
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The room could earn $12,000 a year in rent, which the coffee corner gives up

choices.label: The room could earn $12,000 a year in rent, which the coffee corner gives up
Nothing is wrong, because rooms the bakery already owns cost nothing to use
The room should be charged at what the bakery paid for it
Rent is a financing cost, so it stays out of the cash flows

questions.onCorrect: The coffee corner takes over a room that earns $12,000 a year, so the bakery's cash falls by that amount if the project goes ahead. The lost rent is an opportunity cost, and it counts.

misconceptions.feedback: An owned room has other uses. Using it for the coffee corner means no dentist, and the lost rent is cash the bakery would otherwise receive.
What the bakery paid in the past is sunk. The cost to charge is what the room could earn now in its best alternative use.
Rent paid by a tenant is income from using the room, and it has nothing to do with the cost of raising money. Giving it up is a cash flow lost to the coffee corner.

questions.prompt: A phone maker expects its new model to sell $300 million in a year, but about a third of those buyers would otherwise have bought its older model. Which approach to the new model's cash flows is right?
hints: Compare the firm's total cash with the new model and without it.
Which sales would the firm have made even if it never launched the new model?

acceptedIdeas: Count the new model's cash less the cash the older model no longer brings in
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Count the new model's cash less the cash the older model no longer brings in

choices.label: Count all of the new model's cash, since every sale is a sale of the new model
Count the new model's cash less the cash the older model no longer brings in
Leave the older model out, since it is a different product from the new one
Count none of the new model's cash, since a third of it comes from the firm itself

questions.onCorrect: The test compares the firm with and without the new model, so cash taken from the older model is subtracted. Only the net change in cash counts.

misconceptions.feedback: A third of those buyers would have bought the older model anyway, so the firm's cash from them doesn't all arrive because of the new model.
The older model's lost sales are a side effect of the new one, and the test asks what changes in the firm's cash. They belong in the NPV as a reduction.
Two thirds of the sales are new to the firm, and their cash counts in full. Only the part taken from the older model is offset.

questions.prompt: A trucking firm is judging a new depot. The manager subtracts $200,000 a year of interest on the loan that will build it from the depot's cash flows. She also discounts them at the firm's required return, which already reflects what its lenders and owners ask for. What is the error?
hints: Where else does the cost of the money that funds the project appear?
What does the discount rate already stand for?

acceptedIdeas: The cost of funding is charged twice, in the cash flows and in the rate
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The cost of funding is charged twice, in the cash flows and in the rate

choices.label: The cost of funding is charged twice, in the cash flows and in the rate
None, because a project should always carry the interest on its own loan
Interest should be added back to the cash flows instead of being subtracted
The rate should leave out the cost of debt so that the interest can stay in

questions.onCorrect: The discount rate already prices the money that funds the project, so interest in the cash flows would charge for it a second time.

misconceptions.feedback: A project's cash flows show what it does for the firm before anyone is paid for the money. Charging its interest there as well counts the funding cost a second time.
The interest isn't a cash flow of the project to begin with. It is the price of the money, and the discount rate already carries that price.
The required return is meant to include what the firm's funds cost. Taking it out of the rate and leaving it in the cash flows would only move the error.

questions.prompt: A bakery's new shop needs $40,000 of flour and packaging on its shelves at opening, and no more after that. The shop will run for six years. How should the $40,000 appear in its cash flows?
hints: When does the shop pay for the stock?
What becomes of the stock when the shop closes?

acceptedIdeas: As an outflow at the start, returned when the shop closes
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: As an outflow at the start, returned when the shop closes

choices.label: As an expense in each of the six years of the shop
As an outflow at the start, returned when the shop closes
It doesn't appear, since stock is an asset and not a cash flow
As an outflow in the final year only, when the stock is sold

questions.onCorrect: Stock is paid for at the start and the cash is released when the shop closes, so it appears as an outflow at the start and an inflow at the end.

misconceptions.feedback: The $40,000 is spent once, to fill the shelves, and the stock is still there afterwards. It doesn't recur each year.
Stock has to be bought with cash, so the project pays $40,000 at the start. The fact that stock is also an asset is why the cash comes back later.
The cash is paid when the shelves are filled, at the start. Only the recovery of the stock happens at the end.

questions.prompt: A bicycle maker is judging a second workshop. Which of these belong in the NPV of the workshop, and which stay out?
hints: For each item, ask whether the firm's cash would be different with the workshop than without it.
Items that pay for the money behind a project, or that were spent already, don't change with the decision.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Counts: the fit-out, the land's sale value, the lost sales of existing frames, the tax and the parts held in stock. Left out: the design fees already paid, the loan interest and the dividends.

items.label: Fitting out the new workshop
items.explanation: It is cash that goes out only if the workshop goes ahead.

items.label: The $400,000 the firm could get by selling the land that the workshop would use
items.explanation: The firm owns the land, and the sale it gives up is an opportunity cost of the workshop.

items.label: Sales the workshop's new frames take from the firm's existing frames
items.explanation: A side effect on other products changes the firm's cash, so it counts as a reduction.

items.label: Tax on the workshop's extra profit
items.explanation: It is cash that leaves the firm because the workshop goes ahead.

items.label: Parts held on the shelves, bought at the start and recovered at the end
items.explanation: Working capital is paid for at the start and released at the end, and both are cash flows.

items.label: Design fees paid last year, which can't be recovered whatever is decided
items.explanation: They are a sunk cost, the same in either future.

items.label: Interest on the bank loan that will pay for the equipment
items.explanation: The cost of the funds is already in the discount rate, so counting it here charges for it twice.

items.label: Dividends the firm will pay its owners out of the workshop's profit
items.explanation: Dividends are a payment for the owners' funds, which the discount rate covers.

questions.onCorrect: An item counts when the firm's cash differs with the project, and it stays out when it is the same either way or is a payment for the money that funds the project.

questions.prompt: An invented utility has spent $2 billion on a plant that now looks unviable. Another $500 million would finish it, and the present value of what the finished plant would earn is below $500 million. What does the finance rule say?
hints: Which of the two sums depends on the decision?
What does the $500 million buy, and is it worth more than it costs?

acceptedIdeas: Ignore the $2 billion and stop, since finishing earns less than it costs
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Ignore the $2 billion and stop, since finishing earns less than it costs

choices.label: Finish it, so that the $2 billion already spent does not go to waste
Finish it, because stopping now would mean admitting a $2 billion mistake
Ignore the $2 billion and stop, since finishing earns less than it costs
Stop only if the plant's original backers agree to write off the loss

questions.onCorrect: Only the $500 million still to be spent depends on the choice, and finishing earns back less than that. The $2 billion is the same either way.

misconceptions.feedback: The $2 billion is gone whether the plant is finished or not, and finishing doesn't recover it. It adds a further $500 million that the plant won't earn back.
Admitting a mistake doesn't change the cash. The $2 billion is spent either way, and finishing would add another loss.
Who agrees to the loss doesn't change which choice earns more. The test is whether the $500 million still to be spent is earned back.

questions.prompt: A gift shop is judging a second branch. When does each of these cash flows fall in the branch's life?
hints: Ask when the cash leaves or arrives: before trading, while trading, or when the project ends.
Working capital is paid for at the start and released at the end.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: At the start: the fit-out and the stock to fill the shelves. Each year: the extra profit and the tax on it. At the end: the stock sold off or returned and the money collected from customers.

items.label: Fitting out the new branch
items.explanation: The fit-out is paid for before the branch can trade.

items.label: Gifts bought to fill the shelves
items.explanation: Stock is paid for at the start, when the shelves are filled.

items.label: Extra profit from the branch's sales
items.explanation: Profit arrives as the branch trades, year after year.

items.label: Tax on that extra profit
items.explanation: Tax falls in the years the profit does.

items.label: Gifts still on the shelves when the branch closes, sold off or sent back
items.explanation: The cash tied up in stock is released when the project ends.

items.label: Money owed by business customers when the branch closes, collected at the end
items.explanation: Receivables are paid for at the start of a project and come back when it ends.

questions.onCorrect: Fit-out and stock go out at the start, profit and tax follow the years of trading, and the cash tied up in stock and customers' debts comes back at the end.

questions.prompt: A furniture retailer plans to use a warehouse it owns for a new online store. The warehouse cost $1.2 million years ago and could be sold for $2 million today. What should the online store's NPV charge for using it?
hints: What would the retailer do with the warehouse if the store didn't go ahead?
Which figure reflects the choice open today: what it cost, or what it could fetch?

acceptedIdeas: Its best alternative use, here the $2 million the retailer could get by selling it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Its best alternative use, here the $2 million the retailer could get by selling it

choices.label: Nothing, since the retailer already owns it and the warehouse is paid for
The $1.2 million that the retailer paid for it years ago
A charge of $0.8 million, the gain the retailer would make by selling it
Its best alternative use, here the $2 million the retailer could get by selling it

questions.onCorrect: The warehouse's best alternative use is a sale for $2 million, and that is what the store gives up. What the retailer paid for it long ago is sunk.

misconceptions.feedback: Using the warehouse for the store means not selling it. The $2 million the retailer gives up is a cost of the store, even though no cash is paid out.
What the retailer paid years ago is sunk. What matters is what the warehouse could fetch or earn today if it weren't used for the store.
Selling would bring in $2 million, and the whole sum is what the store gives up. Taking off the old purchase price brings a sunk cost back in.

questions.prompt: A new product line will sell about $1 million a year to businesses that pay 60 days after delivery. Which adjustment follows in the project's cash flows?
hints: When does the project actually receive its cash?
Is the money tied up in unpaid invoices lost, or only delayed?

acceptedIdeas: Cash tied up in unpaid invoices counts, put up at the start and recovered at the end
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Cash tied up in unpaid invoices counts, put up at the start and recovered at the end

choices.label: Late payment is the customers' financing of the line, so it stays out of the cash flows
Cash tied up in unpaid invoices counts, put up at the start and recovered at the end
Nothing changes, since a sale is a cash flow on the day the invoice goes out
The unpaid invoices are a cost to the project and are never recovered

questions.onCorrect: Money owed by customers is working capital: the project pays for it at the start and gets it back when the line ends, so it shows up as an outflow and later an inflow.

misconceptions.feedback: The project pays for the invoices, and lenders don't. The money tied up in them is working capital, and it is a cash flow of the project.
Cash arrives only when the customers pay. Until then the money is tied up in unpaid invoices, which the project has to fund.
The money tied up in invoices comes back when customers pay, so it is an outflow at first and an inflow later, and it isn't a lasting cost.

questions.prompt: The site has room for only one. S earns about 36% a year on the money put into it, and L about 22%. At the firm's required return of 8%, S has an NPV of about $55,000 and L about $325,000. Which should the firm build?
hints: Only one project can be built. What does the firm want the chosen project to do for its owners?
Which of the two figures measures the value added, in dollars?

acceptedIdeas: L, because it adds more value and a rate of return ignores size
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: L, because it adds more value and a rate of return ignores size

choices.label: S, because its return is higher than L's on every dollar put in
Neither, because the two figures disagree and no choice is possible
Both, since each earns more than the 8% required return
L, because it adds more value and a rate of return ignores size

questions.onCorrect: L's NPV of about $325,000 is six times S's NPV of about $55,000, so L adds far more value. A higher return on a much smaller sum doesn't make up for the size.

misconceptions.feedback: S does earn more on each dollar, but only $100,000 goes into it. L puts ten times as much money to work at a return well above 8%, and it adds more value in total.
The two figures disagree on the ranking, but the aim is value for the owners and NPV measures that directly, so there is a clear choice.
Only one project can be built on the site, so the firm can't take both. That is why it has to pick the one that adds more.

questions.prompt: Two alternative uses of one site cost $1,000,000 each. P returns $500,000 in each of two years, so it is repaid in 2 years, and its NPV at 8% is about $108,000 below zero. Q returns $200,000, $200,000, $300,000, $400,000, $600,000 and $600,000 over six years, so it is repaid in 3.75 years, and its NPV is about $675,000 above zero. What do payback and NPV each say?
hints: Payback asks how soon the cost is repaid. Which project is repaid first?
NPV counts all the cash at today's value. Which project has a positive NPV?

acceptedIdeas: Payback prefers P, but NPV says to reject P and build Q instead
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Payback prefers P, but NPV says to reject P and build Q instead

choices.label: Both rules prefer P, since it is the one that is repaid first
Payback prefers P, but NPV says to reject P and build Q instead
Payback prefers Q and NPV prefers P, since Q is slower to repay
Both rules prefer Q, since Q returns more cash in total

questions.onCorrect: P is repaid in 2 years, so payback favours it, yet its cash is worth less than its cost and its NPV is negative. Q is repaid in 3.75 years and adds about $675,000.

misconceptions.feedback: NPV doesn't favour P. Its two payments total $1,000,000, which at 8% is worth less than the $1,000,000 it cost, so its NPV is negative.
Payback prefers the project that is repaid sooner, which is P at 2 years against 3.75. NPV points the other way, to Q.
Q does return more cash in total and has the better NPV, but payback looks only at how soon the cost is repaid, and P does that in 2 years against Q's 3.75.

questions.prompt: A quarry project has cash flows of -$1,000,000 now, +$3,000,000 in year 1 and -$2,200,000 in year 2, because the land must be restored. Its IRRs are about 28% and 72%, and the firm's required return is 10%. Its NPV at 10% is about $91,000 below zero. What should the firm conclude?
hints: What is the project's NPV at the firm's required return?
When the cash flows change sign twice, which of the two rules should the firm trust?

acceptedIdeas: Reject it: IRR misleads here, and the NPV at 10% is negative
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Reject it: IRR misleads here, and the NPV at 10% is negative

choices.label: Accept it, because both of its IRRs are above the 10% required return
Accept it, taking the higher IRR of 72% as the project's return
Keep recomputing the IRR until a single, clearer answer turns up
Reject it: IRR misleads here, and the NPV at 10% is negative

questions.onCorrect: At 10% the NPV is negative, so the quarry destroys value whatever its IRRs say. With two sign changes, IRR can point the wrong way, and NPV is the safer test.

misconceptions.feedback: Both IRRs are above 10%, yet the NPV at 10% is negative. With two sign changes the IRR rule can disagree with NPV, and NPV is the measure of value.
Picking the higher of two IRRs has no basis. The NPV at the required return shows whether the project adds value, and here it is negative.
Recomputing gives the same two rates, because both are real solutions. The cash flows change sign twice, so NPV is the test to use.

questions.prompt: Wikipedia reports this about how the rules are used. What does it show?
hints: Does a survey of what executives prefer say which rule picks the most valuable project?
What does the extract say academics prefer?

acceptedIdeas: It shows what managers prefer, not that IRR picks the most value
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It shows what managers prefer, not that IRR picks the most value

choices.label: IRR is the better rule, since the people who run companies choose it
Academics don't use NPV when they study real projects
It shows what managers prefer, not that IRR picks the most value
NPV cannot be used to compare projects of different sizes at all

questions.onCorrect: The extract reports what executives prefer. Which rule picks the most valuable project is a separate question, and NPV is the one that measures value.

misconceptions.feedback: What people prefer doesn't show which rule picks the project with the most value. The extract reports the preference beside an academic preference for NPV, and doesn't say IRR is better.
The extract says academics have a strong preference for NPV, so it points the other way.
NPV compares projects of any size by the dollars of value each adds, which is why it copes with size differences that IRR can't.

extracts.text: Despite a strong academic preference for NPV, surveys indicate that executives prefer IRR over NPV.
extracts.who: Wikipedia, article "Internal rate of return" (CC BY-SA 4.0)
extracts.kind: An encyclopedia article written by volunteer editors

questions.prompt: A firm can take one of two contracts for the same $100,000 outlay. A two-year contract returns $75,000 a year, with an IRR of about 32% and an NPV at 8% of about $34,000. A ten-year contract returns $30,000 a year, with an IRR of about 27% and an NPV at 8% of about $101,000. Which should it take?
hints: The firm can take only one contract. Which measure says how much value each adds?
What does Wikipedia say about using IRR to compare projects of different duration?

acceptedIdeas: The ten-year contract, since its NPV is higher and IRR misleads across durations
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The ten-year contract, since its NPV is higher and IRR misleads across durations

choices.label: The ten-year contract, since its NPV is higher and IRR misleads across durations
The two-year contract, since its IRR is higher than the ten-year contract's
Either one, since both IRRs are far above the 8% required return and both add value
The two-year contract, since it repays the $100,000 sooner than the other one does

questions.onCorrect: The ten-year contract has an NPV of about $101,000 against about $34,000, and IRR isn't a reliable guide when durations differ.

misconceptions.feedback: A higher IRR doesn't mean more value when the projects run for different lengths of time. The ten-year contract has the larger NPV.
Both clear the required return, but only one can be taken, and the firm should take the one that adds more value.
Payback looks only at how soon the cost is repaid and ignores what comes after. The ten-year contract keeps paying for eight more years and adds far more value.

questions.prompt: Each project has its own pattern of cash flows. Which change sign only once, so that a single IRR is the usual result, and which change sign more than once, so that IRR may have several values?
hints: Write each pattern as a run of plus and minus signs, with plus for cash in and minus for cash out.
Count how many times the run switches from one sign to the other.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: One sign change: the $500,000 purchase with eight years of receipts, the two payments followed by five years of receipts, and the software product. More than one: the nuclear plant, the strip mine and the film.

items.label: Pay $500,000 now, then receive $120,000 a year for eight years
items.explanation: Cash goes out once and then comes in, so the sign changes only once.

items.label: Pay $100,000 now and $50,000 next year, then receive $80,000 a year for five years
items.explanation: Two outflows in a row are still one stretch of outflow, and the sign changes once when the inflows begin.

items.label: Pay for a software product's development in years 0 and 1, then earn from sales
items.explanation: Costs first and receipts after make a single change.

items.label: A nuclear power plant: pay to build it, sell power for decades, then pay to decommission it
items.explanation: The final outflow adds a second change of sign, as Wikipedia notes for plants of this kind.

items.label: A strip mine: pay to open it, mine it for ten years, then pay to restore the land
items.explanation: Out, then in, then out again is two changes of sign.

items.label: A film company receives an advance, pays for production, then collects box office takings
items.explanation: In, then out, then in again is two changes of sign.

questions.onCorrect: A project with a large outflow at the end, or any pattern that switches sign twice or more, can have several IRRs, which is when NPV is the rule to trust.

questions.prompt: An owner with little cash and several small, similar equipment purchases screens them by payback. What do the sources say about using payback this way?
hints: What do the sources list as payback's weaknesses?
Do they say it has any use at all?

acceptedIdeas: It is quick and can suit similar investments, but it ignores later cash
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is quick and can suit similar investments, but it ignores later cash

choices.label: It is never acceptable, because it ignores the time value of money altogether
It always agrees with NPV when the purchases are small ones
It is acceptable only when the discount rate happens to be zero
It is quick and can suit similar investments, but it ignores later cash

questions.onCorrect: Payback is a quick screen for similar investments, and a business short of cash may care how soon its money comes back. It still ignores what comes after the payback period.

misconceptions.feedback: Payback does ignore the time value of money, but Wikipedia says it has real uses, and with care it can screen similar investments quickly.
Payback doesn't agree with NPV just because the purchases are small. It still ignores timing within the payback period and the cash after it.
Nothing in the sources limits payback to a zero rate. It ignores the rate altogether, and it can still be a quick screen for similar investments.

questions.prompt: A firm judges a single project on its own, with no alternative. It costs $500,000 now and returns $180,000 a year for four years. Its IRR is about 16% and the firm's required return is 10%. What does its NPV at 10% say?
hints: At what rate is the project's NPV zero, and is the required return above or below it?
What does Wikipedia say about IRR and NPV for a single project judged on its own?

acceptedIdeas: It is positive, since an IRR above the required return means a positive NPV here
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is positive, since an IRR above the required return means a positive NPV here

choices.label: It is positive, since an IRR above the required return means a positive NPV here
It is negative, since IRR and NPV always give different answers about a project
It is zero, since the project's IRR is the rate at which its NPV is zero
It can't be known unless the other projects on offer are also considered

questions.onCorrect: The NPV at 10% is about +$71,000. For a single ordinary project the IRR test and the NPV test agree, and the trouble starts only when projects compete or cash flows change sign more than once.

misconceptions.feedback: For a single project judged against the required return, Wikipedia says the IRR comparison is equivalent to the NPV method, so they give the same answer.
The NPV is zero at the IRR, which is 16%. At the required return of 10% the NPV is above zero, because the project earns more than that.
A single project judged in isolation needs no comparison with others. Its IRR against the required return gives the same answer as its NPV.

questions.prompt: Which bond will investors require the higher yield on, and why?
hints: Both bonds promise payments on the same dates, so the difference has to lie in how likely each promise is to be kept.
A yield is what an investor requires for taking the bond on. Which of the two promises would an investor trust less?
questions.onCorrect: Investors treat the company as the greater risk, so they require a higher yield from its bond, which is the reason the Reserve Bank gives.

acceptedIdeas: The company's, because the company might not repay on time
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The company's, because the company might not repay on time

choices.label: The government's, because it is much the larger borrower
Neither, because two bonds of the same term must pay the same yield
The company's, because the company might not repay on time
The company's, because companies earn more profit than governments do

misconceptions.feedback: Size doesn't set a yield. The chance of not being repaid does, and a larger borrower isn't a riskier one.
The term fixes when the payments fall due. It says nothing about how likely they are to arrive, and investors ask for more where a missed payment is likelier.
The direction is right but the reason isn't. Profit doesn't set the yield. The yield is higher because the company is likelier than the government not to repay.

questions.prompt: An analyst says a government bond yield is risk-free, so it can serve as the base of a required return with no further thought. What does this sentence add to that claim?
hints: Default is one way of losing money on a bond. The sentence lists others.
Ask what the label risk-free is promising, and what it leaves out.
questions.onCorrect: The Reserve Bank's own bond example shows one of the other risks: a bond paying $2 a year was worth $100 at a 2% required yield and $109.50 at 1%.

extracts.text: Default risk is not the only risk. Other risks include interest rate risk, currency risk, and inflation risk.
extracts.kind: An encyclopedia article written by volunteer editors

acceptedIdeas: It is free of default risk, but interest rate, currency and inflation risk remain
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is free of default risk, but interest rate, currency and inflation risk remain

choices.label: It is free of default risk, but interest rate, currency and inflation risk remain
It is exactly free of risk, so the base needs no adjustment
It is as risky as a share, so the yield cannot serve as a base
The label is wrong, because governments often fail to repay their own-currency debt

misconceptions.feedback: The sentence names three other risks. Risk-free describes default only, and the base still has to be read with those in mind.
Naming other risks doesn't make the bond as risky as a share. The sentence says default isn't the only risk, and the yield stays the benchmark for the base.
The Reserve Bank says governments are not expected to fail to repay borrowing in their own currency. The sentence adds that default isn't the only risk to consider.

questions.prompt: Mia owns shares in a single regional airline and nothing else, so she carries a great deal of firm-specific risk. Does the market pay her a higher return for carrying it?
hints: Ask whether Mia could have got rid of this risk herself, and what it would have cost her to do so.
The market pays for risk that investors cannot remove, so first decide which kind of risk the airline's troubles belong to.
questions.onCorrect: Mia can still lose a great deal if the airline fails, but she cannot expect the market to pay her for a risk she could have spread.

acceptedIdeas: No, because she could have diversified it away, so the market doesn't pay for it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, because she could have diversified it away, so the market doesn't pay for it

choices.label: Yes, because more risk always earns a higher return, whatever its kind
Yes, but only if the airline is a small company with few other owners
No, because the market pays for no kind of risk, systematic or otherwise
No, because she could have diversified it away, so the market doesn't pay for it

misconceptions.feedback: The model pays only for risk that can't be removed. Mia's is the removable kind, so the extra risk earns her nothing extra.
Size doesn't change the logic. Firm-specific risk can be spread away however large or small the company is.
The market does pay for one kind, which is systematic risk, because holding many shares can't remove it.

questions.prompt: Two invented companies have the same total profit this year. Harbour Grocers sells food and household basics, and its sales barely change whether the economy is strong or weak. Coastline Towers builds apartment towers for sale, and its sales climb in good years and collapse in bad ones. Which is more likely to have the higher beta, and why?
hints: Beta says how closely a business moves with the economy. Which company's sales follow the economy up and down?
The average share has a beta of 1. Would a business that ignores the economy sit above or below that average?
questions.onCorrect: A high beta is no verdict on the business, and Coastline may be run very well. It says that the cash flows swing with the economy, and that is the risk the market pays for.

acceptedIdeas: Coastline Towers, because its cash flows follow the economy closely
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Coastline Towers, because its cash flows follow the economy closely

choices.label: Harbour Grocers, because steady sales mean it has more profit at stake
Coastline Towers, because its cash flows follow the economy closely
Neither, because beta depends only on how large a company is
Harbour Grocers, because a firm with many customers has the most to lose

misconceptions.feedback: Steady sales are what a low beta looks like. How much profit is at stake doesn't set beta, which measures how closely cash flows follow the economy.
Size isn't what beta measures. Two companies of the same size can have very different betas, depending on how their cash flows move with the economy.
The number of customers doesn't enter. Beta measures how far a business moves with the economy, and the grocer's sales barely move.

questions.prompt: Suppose Woolworths had discounted Quantium's forecast cash flows at the Australian Food rate, 8.7%, instead of Quantium's own 11.2%. What would that have done to the value the test finds for Quantium?
hints: A present value falls as the discount rate rises. Which way does it move when the rate falls?
Compare 8.7 with 11.2, and ask what a lower rate does to the same stream of cash flows.
questions.onCorrect: A single rate for the whole Group would price Quantium as if it were as safe as Australian Food. 'WACC and hurdle rates' uses this idea to choose the rate for one project.

acceptedIdeas: It would have raised it, because a lower rate hides the extra risk in the cash flows
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It would have raised it, because a lower rate hides the extra risk in the cash flows

choices.label: It would have lowered it, because 8.7 is the smaller number and smaller means less
It would have left it unchanged, because the forecast cash flows are the same ones
It would have raised it, because a lower rate hides the extra risk in the cash flows
Nothing can be said, because the table gives no betas for either of the two units

misconceptions.feedback: A lower discount rate makes each future dollar worth more today, so the present value rises.
The cash flows are the same, but the rate decides how much each one is worth today, so the value changes.
The direction needs no betas. A lower rate always raises a present value, and the table gives both rates.

questions.prompt: Wattle Pharma is an invented company with one drug in its final trial. If the trial succeeds its shares will multiply in value, and if it fails they will be nearly worthless, and the result has nothing to do with how the economy is doing. By this lesson's model, what premium should a well-diversified investor require for holding Wattle?
hints: Ask whether the trial's result depends on the economy, or on Wattle alone.
Only systematic risk is paid for. Which kind of risk is a single drug trial?
questions.onCorrect: Wattle's owners carry a large risk, but an investor who holds many companies carries little of it, and the required return follows the investor's risk.

acceptedIdeas: Little above the risk-free rate, because the trial's risk can be diversified away
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Little above the risk-free rate, because the trial's risk can be diversified away

choices.label: A very large one, because a share that could lose nearly everything carries the most risk
Little above the risk-free rate, because the trial's risk can be diversified away
The same as an average share, because every share carries the risk of its own company

misconceptions.feedback: Most of Wattle's risk belongs to one trial. A diversified investor can spread it away, and the market doesn't pay for risk that can be removed.
The premium follows systematic risk. The average share moves with the economy, and Wattle's outcome doesn't, so its beta would be low.

questions.prompt: A fund manager lists six events that moved share prices. Which kind of risk is each one?
hints: Ask whether holding shares in many other companies would blunt the event or leave it untouched.
An event that reaches nearly every company is systematic. One that belongs to a single company is firm-specific.
questions.onCorrect: Spreading across companies shrinks the second kind of event and leaves the first, which is why only the first earns a premium.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The rate cut, the recession and the jump in inflation are systematic, because they reach every share. The flooded shaft, the resignation and the new rival are firm-specific, because each belongs to one company.

items.label: The RBA lowers the cash rate
items.explanation: It reaches almost every company, so holding more shares does not remove it.

items.label: A mine's main shaft floods
items.explanation: It hurts one mining company, and other holdings are untouched.

items.label: A recession cuts household spending
items.explanation: It touches the whole economy, so it reaches every share.

items.label: A chief executive resigns
items.explanation: It is one company's event, which a spread of holdings dilutes.

items.label: Inflation jumps
items.explanation: It is common to all securities, which is what makes it systematic.

items.label: A new rival opens beside one chain's stores
items.explanation: It threatens one chain's sales and leaves other companies alone.

questions.prompt: A colleague says that a share's beta settles the return investors require from it exactly. What does this sentence suggest about that claim?
hints: The sentence is a judgement on how the model has fared when tested against real prices.
Ask what a careful analyst would do with a number that comes from a model the authors doubt.
questions.onCorrect: A beta-based rate is one estimate, and a sensible analyst checks it against other ways of judging how risky a business is.

extracts.text: In their 2004 review, economists Eugene Fama and Kenneth French argue that "the failure of the CAPM in empirical tests implies that most applications of the model are invalid".
extracts.who: Wikipedia, article "Capital asset pricing model" (CC BY-SA 4.0)
extracts.kind: An encyclopedia article written by volunteer editors

acceptedIdeas: It overstates things, because two economists found the model fails in tests
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It overstates things, because two economists found the model fails in tests

choices.label: It is right, because the model has been tested and has held up
It is right for utilities, since their betas are low and so easy to measure
It shows that systematic risk is not paid for, since beta can be wrong
It overstates things, because two economists found the model fails in tests

misconceptions.feedback: The sentence says the opposite. Fama and French wrote that the model's failure in empirical tests makes most applications of it invalid.
Nothing in the sentence is about utilities or about how easy a beta is to measure. It is a judgement on the model's tests.

A risk-free government yield for the same term, plus a premium for the chance of default on it
A share of Lovisa's profit, since lenders take part in what the business earns each year
Lovisa's dividend yield, since lenders are paid in the same way that owners are paid

questions.prompt: Ignore tax. A firm funded entirely by equity costing 11% borrows at 5% and replaces half its equity with debt. If the equity that remains still cost 11%, its blended cost of funds would fall from 11% to 8%, a fall of 3 points. Will the real fall be larger, the same or smaller?

Smaller, because the equity that is left has become riskier and costs more
Larger, because with lenders in the firm the shareholders' share is safer

misconceptions.feedback: That holds only if the remaining equity keeps its 11% cost. After the swap lenders rank ahead of a larger fixed claim, so shareholders ask for more.

questions.prompt: Bracken Ltd, an invented company, issued a bond some years ago with a 9% coupon, when lenders required about 9% from it. Lenders now require about 6% from a firm like Bracken. Its finance team says its cost of debt is 9%, the rate on the bond. What is Bracken's cost of debt today?

questions.prompt: Sorrel Group is funded 70% by shares that cost it 10% and 30% by debt that costs it 5%. Roughly where does its blended cost of funds lie?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About $2.5m, which is the tax rate applied to the interest bill

choices.label: About $2.5m, which is the tax rate applied to the interest bill
About $10m, because the whole interest bill comes off the tax
About $7.5m, which is what is left of the interest after tax
Nothing, because debt and equity cost the firm the same after tax

misconceptions.feedback: The deduction cuts taxable profit by $10m, and the tax saved is the tax rate applied to that $10m.
That is what the interest costs after tax. The saving is the part the tax office no longer takes.
Interest is deductible and dividends are not, so debt costs the firm less after tax by the amount of the deduction.

questions.prompt: What does this passage tell you about judging how risky a firm's borrowing is?
hints: Compare what the passage says about utilities and technology firms. What differs between them besides debt?
The passage says borrowing always adds risk, yet an indebted firm is not always riskier than a debt-free one. What else decides which is riskier?
questions.onCorrect: The same debt is safe for a firm whose cash flows are steady and dangerous for one whose cash flows are not.

extracts.text: So while adding leverage to a given asset always adds risk, it is not the case that a levered company or investment is always riskier than an unlevered one. In fact, many highly levered hedge funds have less return volatility than unlevered bond funds, and normally heavily indebted low-risk public utilities are usually less risky stocks than unlevered high-risk technology companies.
extracts.kind: An encyclopedia article written by volunteer editors

acceptedIdeas: Look at how steady its cash flows are as well as how much it owes
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Look at how steady its cash flows are as well as how much it owes

choices.label: A utility can never fail, however much it borrows against its income
A technology firm should borrow more than a utility, since it is riskier already
Debt adds no risk once a firm is large and well known to its lenders
Look at how steady its cash flows are as well as how much it owes

misconceptions.feedback: The passage says indebted utilities tend to be safer shares than debt-free technology firms. It does not say they cannot fail.
Borrowing always adds risk to a given asset, so a risky technology firm has less room to borrow, not more.
The passage says borrowing against an asset always adds some risk. Size does not remove it.

questions.prompt: Six statements are made about a firm that swaps equity for debt. Which are true in a world with no taxes and a perfect market, and which need interest to be tax-deductible?
hints: Ask whether each statement depends on there being a tax bill to reduce.
If the total profit is the same however the firm is funded, only the division of it can change.
questions.onCorrect: Taxes are the first of the frictions that make the mix of debt and equity matter.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: With no taxes, firm value is the same either way, debt only divides the profit, and a levered firm can never be worth more. Once interest is deductible, borrowing lowers the tax bill, value rises with debt ignoring other frictions, and a firm with no taxable profit gets nothing.

items.label: Firm value is the same however the firm is funded
items.explanation: This is Modigliani and Miller's result: the levered and unlevered firm must be worth the same.

items.label: Debt only divides the same operating profit between lenders and owners
items.explanation: With no taxes the total profit does not change, only who receives it.

items.label: A firm that borrows can never be worth more than the same firm without debt
items.explanation: With no taxes the two values must be equal.

items.label: Borrowing lowers the firm's tax bill
items.explanation: The deduction on interest is what lowers the bill.

items.label: A firm's value rises with the amount of debt it uses, ignoring other frictions
items.explanation: Each dollar of interest saves tax, so more debt saves more.

items.label: A firm that makes no taxable profit gets no benefit from borrowing
items.explanation: The tax saving exists only when there is taxable profit to deduct from.

questions.prompt: A firm's assets earn 4% a year before interest. It borrows at 6% to fund more of the same assets. What happens to the return its owners earn for each dollar they have invested?
hints: Compare what a borrowed dollar earns with what it costs.
In the lesson's table the borrowing helped in years when the assets earned more than 6%. What happens when they earn less?
questions.onCorrect: The crossover is the cost of the debt: above it borrowing lifts the owners' return, below it borrowing cuts it.

acceptedIdeas: It falls, because each borrowed dollar earns 4% and costs 6%
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It falls, because each borrowed dollar earns 4% and costs 6%

choices.label: It rises, because borrowing always lifts the return to the owners
It falls, because each borrowed dollar earns 4% and costs 6%
It stays the same, because the assets earn 4% however they are funded
It rises, because the firm now controls more assets with the same money

misconceptions.feedback: That is true only when the assets earn more than the debt costs. Here they earn less, so each borrowed dollar loses 2 cents.
The assets do earn 4% whichever way they are funded, but the interest comes off before the owners are paid, so the owners' return falls.
More assets don't help when each earns less than the borrowed money costs. Each added dollar takes a little from the owners.

questions.prompt: A company earns a profit and keeps it in the business instead of paying a dividend. According to this passage, at what rate is that retained profit taxed?
hints: The passage separates profit that is distributed from profit that is not.
Ask whose rate applies when profit is distributed to eligible shareholders, and whose when it is kept.
questions.onCorrect: Imputation affects profit that is paid out to eligible shareholders. Profit kept in the firm stays at the company rate.

extracts.text: Thus company profits distributed to eligible shareholders are taxed in their entirety at the shareholder's rate. Profits retained by the company or distributed to ineligible shareholders remain taxed at the corporate rate.
extracts.kind: An encyclopedia article written by volunteer editors

acceptedIdeas: The company rate, since retained profit stays taxed at the corporate rate
