answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The company rate, since retained profit stays taxed at the corporate rate

choices.label: The shareholders' rate, because all company profit passes through to them
Not at all until it is paid out, because imputation defers company tax
At both rates, because imputation taxes company profit twice
The company rate, since retained profit stays taxed at the corporate rate

misconceptions.feedback: Only profit distributed to eligible shareholders is taxed at their rate. Retained profit stays taxed at the corporate rate.
The passage says retained profit remains taxed at the corporate rate. It doesn't say the tax is deferred.
Imputation exists to avoid taxing distributed profit twice, as it was before 1987. Retained profit meets the company rate only.

questions.prompt: Which firm can carry that debt, and why?
hints: The $40m of interest has to be paid in every year, including the worst one.
Compare each firm's worst year with the $40m it owes.
questions.onCorrect: The steady firm's profit covers its interest at least 2.25 times in every year, while the cyclical firm's worst year covers only half of it.

acceptedIdeas: The steady firm, because even its worst year covers the interest twice over
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The steady firm, because even its worst year covers the interest twice over

choices.label: The steady firm, because even its worst year covers the interest twice over
The cyclical firm, because its best year is by far the strongest of the six
Both, because their profit before interest averages the same $100m a year
Neither, because $40m of interest is a large share of profit in any year

misconceptions.feedback: A strong best year can't pay the interest in the worst year. The cyclical firm's worst year brings in $20m against $40m of interest.
An average doesn't pay the interest in any particular year. The $40m falls due every year, whatever the average is.
A large share of profit can be carried if profit is steady. The test is whether the worst year still covers the interest.

questions.prompt: Sydney's Cross City Tunnel was funded with A$220 million of equity and A$580 million borrowed from banks. These five things happened to it in its first two years. In what order did they happen?
hints: A tunnel has to open before its traffic can be counted, and a sale comes after a failure.
Ask what has to happen before the banks will appoint receivers.
questions.onCorrect: Traffic fell short of what the interest needed, and insolvency followed, so the order follows the way the shortfall built.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The tunnel opened on 28 August 2005, averaged about 30,000 trips a day in early 2006, was reported in November 2006 to need 60,000 to 90,000 a day to meet its interest, became insolvent in December 2006 and had receivers appointed on 27 December, and had preferred purchasers chosen on 20 June 2007.

items: The tunnel opens to traffic
Traffic is reported at about 30,000 trips a day
It is reported that investors must add equity and that 60,000 to 90,000 trips a day are needed to meet interest
The tunnel becomes insolvent and the banks appoint receivers
Preferred purchasers are chosen to buy the tunnel for $700 million

questions.prompt: A finance director says, "Interest is tax-deductible, so we should borrow as much as we can." What does trade-off theory say about that?
hints: Trade-off theory names two things a firm balances. The tax saving is one of them. What is the other?
Ask what happens to the chance of distress as the debt grows.
questions.onCorrect: The theory has the firm borrow up to the point where more debt costs more in distress than it saves in tax.

acceptedIdeas: More debt also raises the chance of distress, so the saving has to be weighed against it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: More debt also raises the chance of distress, so the saving has to be weighed against it

choices.label: She is right, because the tax saving grows with the debt and nothing sets a limit on it
She is right, provided the firm is profitable enough to make full use of the deduction
More debt also raises the chance of distress, so the saving has to be weighed against it
She is wrong, because the tax saving disappears as soon as a firm borrows anything

misconceptions.feedback: Something does offset it. Each extra dollar of debt raises the chance of distress, and the theory sets that cost against the tax saving.
Profit is needed for the saving, but it doesn't remove the cost of distress, which grows as the debt does.
The saving exists for every dollar of interest paid by a firm with taxable profit. The theory weighs it against distress costs and doesn't say it vanishes.

questions.prompt: A mining company's existing debt is so large that no lender will advance it any more, although a new shaft is worth more than it would cost. What does this lesson call that condition?
hints: Think of the two problems named on the last screen. Which one is about a good project being blocked?
The firm has a project that would pay for itself and still cannot raise the money. What stands in the way?
questions.onCorrect: Existing debt blocks the new money even though the project would pay for itself, so the firm loses value it could have had.

acceptedIdeas: debt overhang
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Debt overhang: a debt load so heavy that the firm struggles to borrow any more, even for an investment worth more than it costs.

misconceptions.feedback: Asset substitution is the incentive to take risky projects. This firm has the opposite trouble: it cannot fund a good one.
Financial distress describes promises to lenders being broken or honoured with difficulty. Here the problem is that existing debt blocks a good new investment, and that has its own name.
The pecking order is the order in which firms prefer to raise money. It does not name a firm that is blocked from borrowing.
Trade-off theory is about balancing the tax saving against distress costs. It does not name a firm blocked from borrowing for a good project.

questions.prompt: CLEM7's operator built the tunnel to plan and budget and still could not meet the interest on its $1.3 billion of debt. What does this say about how a project's debt should be judged?
hints: The source says the tunnel was completed on time and on budget. What does it say went wrong?
Ask what the lenders' interest depended on, and what happened to it.
questions.onCorrect: Debt is judged by whether the cash that pays it survives the bad case, and good construction is only part of that.

extracts.text: Despite being completed on time and on budget, the tunnel has been an economic failure due to incorrect predictions of traffic volume.
extracts.kind: An encyclopedia article written by volunteer editors

acceptedIdeas: A project can be built to plan and still fail if the traffic its debt relied on never arrives
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A project can be built to plan and still fail if the traffic its debt relied on never arrives

choices.label: A project can be built to plan and still fail if the traffic its debt relied on never arrives
The builders are to blame, since a tunnel finished on time and budget should have earned enough
Road projects should never be funded with debt, because every one of them ends in receivership
The tolls were set too low for the traffic, and higher tolls would have solved the problem

misconceptions.feedback: The source blames incorrect predictions of traffic volume and says the tunnel was completed on time and on budget. The builders' work isn't the problem.
One failed project doesn't show that. The lesson is to judge debt against the worst case for the cash that must pay it.
The source gives incorrect traffic forecasts as the cause. It doesn't say higher tolls would have fixed it.

questions.prompt: A retailer in trouble faces these six costs. Which are direct costs of financial distress, and which are indirect?
hints: Direct costs are the payments that a bankruptcy itself brings. Which of the six would not exist without an insolvency?
Indirect costs can arise even if the firm never goes bankrupt.
questions.onCorrect: Many of the costs of distress arrive before any bankruptcy, which is why they count against borrowing even for firms that never fail.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Legal fees, auditors' fees and the insolvency firm's fees are direct costs, which bankruptcy brings. The higher interest rate, the managers' lost time and the dropped project are indirect costs, which can arise even if bankruptcy is avoided.

items.label: Legal fees paid during an insolvency
items.explanation: Legal fees are one of the payments bankruptcy itself brings.

items.label: Auditors' fees in a bankruptcy
items.explanation: Auditors' fees are named among the direct costs.

items.label: The fees of the insolvency firm appointed to run the business
items.explanation: A fee for the receivers is a payment that the insolvency itself brings.

items.label: Banks raise the interest rate as the firm's trouble shows
items.explanation: A higher cost of capital is Wikipedia's example of an indirect cost, and it arises before any bankruptcy.

items.label: Management time goes on the firm's trouble instead of on running the business
items.explanation: Wikipedia notes that distress takes management attention from operations, and the cost needs no bankruptcy.

items.label: A sound project is dropped because the firm cannot raise the money
items.explanation: The cost arises from the trouble and needs no bankruptcy. This is our reasoning, not a figure from Wikipedia.

questions.prompt: By trade-off theory, which features of a firm point towards carrying more debt, and which towards carrying less?
hints: Ask whether each feature makes the worst year safer or more dangerous for the interest bill.
The tax saving needs a taxable profit, and the distress cost grows when cash flows are unsteady.
questions.onCorrect: The same debt is cheap in tax and safe in a bad year for the first kind of firm, and costly and dangerous for the second.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Steady cash flows, a large taxable profit and cover that holds in the worst year lean towards more debt. Sales that follow the economy, losses in most years and a project resting on one forecast lean towards less.

items.label: Cash flows that barely change from year to year
items.explanation: Steady cash flows keep interest cover high even in a bad year.

items.label: A large taxable profit every year
items.explanation: The tax saving from interest needs taxable profit to exist.

items.label: Interest cover that stays well above 1 even in its worst year
items.explanation: The interest is covered in the year that matters most.

items.label: Sales that rise and fall with the economy
items.explanation: A bad year can leave profit below the interest bill.

items.label: Losses in most years
items.explanation: There is no taxable profit to shelter, and the interest is hard to pay.

items.label: One large project that depends on a single traffic forecast
items.explanation: If the forecast fails, the debt has nothing else behind it.

questions.prompt: A heavily indebted firm can choose between a safe project with a positive net present value and a risky one with a negative net present value. What does this sentence suggest about the choice its management is tempted to make?
hints: The sentence says what happens to management's incentive as the debt-to-equity ratio rises.
Ask which kind of project, safe or risky, the sentence says debt makes more attractive.
questions.onCorrect: Heavy debt can push owners towards gambles that destroy value, which is a cost of debt that no bankruptcy fee measures.

extracts.text: Asset substitution effect: As debt-to-equity ratio increases, management has an incentive to undertake risky, even negative net present value (NPV) projects.
extracts.kind: An encyclopedia article written by volunteer editors

acceptedIdeas: It may favour the risky project, because heavy debt gives management that incentive
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It may favour the risky project, because heavy debt gives management that incentive

choices.label: It will take the safe project, because heavy debt makes any risk too costly to run
It may favour the risky project, because heavy debt gives management that incentive
It will take whichever has the higher present value, because debt does not affect the choice
It will take neither, because a firm with heavy debt cannot start new projects

misconceptions.feedback: The sentence says the opposite. As the debt-to-equity ratio rises, management has an incentive to take risky projects.
The sentence says debt does affect the choice. It names an incentive to take risky projects, even ones with a negative net present value.
The sentence is about which project management prefers. Debt overhang is the problem that blocks projects, and this is a different one.

questions.prompt: Woolworths reports net debt of $14,980 million, including $11,316 million of lease liabilities, and a ratio of net debt to EBITDA before significant items of 2.5 times. A reader says that ratio alone shows whether its debt is safe. What else would you want to know?
hints: The cover table showed two firms with the same average profit and very different risk. What separated them?
A ratio says how much is owed compared with a year of earnings. Ask what it leaves out.
questions.onCorrect: A ratio describes the size of the debt, and the steadiness of the earnings behind it tells you whether the debt can be carried.

acceptedIdeas: How steady its earnings are, because the worst year decides if the interest is covered
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: How steady its earnings are, because the worst year decides if the interest is covered

choices.label: Nothing else, since a ratio below 3 times can always be treated as a safe level of debt
Only its size, since a firm as large as Woolworths cannot get into financial distress
Whether it has used the tax shield, since that alone decides how risky its debt is
How steady its earnings are, because the worst year decides if the interest is covered

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing in the lesson sets such a limit. Two firms with the same ratio can be in very different positions if one's earnings swing and the other's do not.
Size doesn't remove the need to cover the interest in a bad year. Large firms can be in distress too.
The tax shield affects what debt costs. The risk of distress depends on whether the cash flows would cover the debt in a bad year.

questions.prompt: A company has 100 million shares, each trading at $10, and $200 million of its value is cash. It pays a dividend of $1 a share out of that cash. If nothing else changes, roughly what is each share worth just afterwards?
hints: Ask where the $100 million of dividend cash comes from.
A company's value includes the cash it holds. Where does that cash go when it is paid out?

acceptedIdeas: About $9, because $1 a share of the company's value has left as cash
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About $9, because $1 a share of the company's value has left as cash

choices.label: About $10, because the dividend is paid on top of what a share is worth
About $9, because $1 a share of the company's value has left as cash
About $11, because a company that pays dividends is worth more

questions.onCorrect: Each share is now worth about $9, and the owner holds $1 in cash as well. The dividend moved value from the company to its owners and made none.

misconceptions.feedback: The $100 million paid out was part of the company's value, so it cannot be extra. Owners now hold that cash themselves and the shares represent a company with $100 million less in it.
Paying a dividend moves value from the company to its owners and creates none. The owner holds $1 more in cash and the share is worth about $1 less.

questions.prompt: A company has $50 million of surplus cash. Its best project would earn about 5% a year on it, and its owners could earn about 9% a year elsewhere on investments of similar risk. What should the company do with the cash?
hints: Compare the project's return with what owners could earn on the same money elsewhere.
The better home for the cash is the one that earns more at similar risk.

acceptedIdeas: Pay it out, because owners can earn more on it than the project would
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Pay it out, because owners can earn more on it than the project would

choices.label: Keep it, because paying cash out would give the owners' value away
Keep it and invest it, since a 5% return is better than none at all
Buy another business with it, so the cash stays at work in the company
Pay it out, because owners can earn more on it than the project would

questions.onCorrect: The project earns 5% and owners could earn 9% elsewhere, so the cash is worth more in their hands. Had the project earned 14%, keeping it would be right.

misconceptions.feedback: A payout moves value to the owners and does not destroy it. In their hands the money can earn 9%, which beats what the project would earn.
A project has to beat what owners could earn elsewhere at the same risk, not just earn something. At 5% against 9% the owners lose four points a year.
A purchase is a project like any other and has to clear the same 9% test. Holding cash does not make it worth spending.

questions.prompt: These two lines come from Lovisa's five-year table, with 2026 first and 2022 last. Dividends paid were above profit in four of the five years, and the amount drawn on its borrowing facility rose from $77 million to $87 million during 2026. What is the most useful next question?
hints: A payout above profit is paid for with cash the company already had or with money it borrowed.
Which figures in Accounting would tell you whether the cash is there?

acceptedIdeas: Whether its cash flow and borrowing can keep funding the dividends
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Whether its cash flow and borrowing can keep funding the dividends

choices.label: Whether its cash flow and borrowing can keep funding the dividends
Nothing, because a high payout is what shareholders want from a company
Whether the dividends carried franking credits, which would settle it
Whether the share price rose in the same years, as a sign of approval

extracts.who: Lovisa Holdings Limited, Annual Report 2026, five-year table
extracts.kind: A table in a company's annual report, written for shareholders

questions.onCorrect: A payout above 100% has to come from cash held or borrowed, so the useful check is whether free cash flow and the facility can keep supporting it.

misconceptions.feedback: A payout above 100% has to be funded from something other than that year's profit. Owners are better served by knowing whether the funding can continue.
Franking says who receives a tax credit with the dividend. It does not show where the cash came from, which is the question when payouts exceed profit.
A share price reflects many things. It does not show whether the cash behind the dividend is there.

questions.prompt: A company's share buyback lifts its earnings per share by 6%. Does that show the buyback made the business more valuable?
hints: Earnings per share is profit divided by the number of shares. Which part of that fraction does a buyback change?
Look at the owner's total in the table: did it differ between the dividend and the buyback?

acceptedIdeas: Not by itself, since fewer shares lift earnings per share anyway
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Not by itself, since fewer shares lift earnings per share anyway

choices.label: Yes, because higher earnings per share always means a higher value
No, because a buyback can never change what a business is worth
Not by itself, since fewer shares lift earnings per share anyway
Yes, because a buyback shows that managers feel confident

questions.onCorrect: Earnings per share is profit divided by shares, so a buyback lifts it even when profit is unchanged. Value to owners depends on the price paid and on what the cash would otherwise have done.

misconceptions.feedback: Earnings per share rises whenever the share count falls, even when the business is unchanged. In the table the owner's wealth was $10,000 whether the company paid a dividend or bought back shares.

A buyback at a price above or below what the shares are worth moves value between the owners who sell and the owners who stay, so it can matter. The rise in earnings per share is not the measure of that.
Managers may buy back shares because they think them cheap, which a later screen covers. The rise in earnings per share is arithmetic and says nothing about confidence.

questions.prompt: The ATO uses Rodney as its example. Once the grossed-up dividend is counted with all his other income and deductions, his tax comes to $200. What does the tax office do about the franking credit?
hints: Add the credit to the cash dividend to find the amount Rodney is taxed on, then compare the credit with the tax he owes.
If the credit is larger than the tax, what happens to the difference?

acceptedIdeas: It refunds the part of the credit that is above the tax he owes
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It refunds the part of the credit that is above the tax he owes

choices.label: It collects the tax in full, since the credit applies only to the cash part
It refunds the part of the credit that is above the tax he owes
It refunds the whole credit in cash, since credits are paid out
It does nothing, because a franked dividend is already taxed

extracts.text: On 11 December 2014, Rodney receives a franked distribution of $700 with $300 franking credits attached.
extracts.who: Australian Taxation Office, Refunding excess franking credits
extracts.kind: An official worked example for individual shareholders

questions.onCorrect: Rodney's income includes the $1,000, his tax comes to $200, and the $300 credit more than covers that. The tax office refunds the $100 difference.

misconceptions.feedback: The credit is taken off his tax bill of $200, and it is larger than that bill, so there is nothing to collect.
Only the part of the credit above the tax owed is refunded. The first $200 of it pays his tax bill.
The company paid tax on its profit, and Rodney is taxed on the grossed-up $1,000 as well. The credit is what stops the same profit being taxed twice.

questions.prompt: A company pays a franked dividend. Sort each holder by what it can do with the franking credit.
hints: Think about who is a resident taxpayer first. Anyone who is not cannot claim a credit.
Among residents, ask whether the holder can be refunded or can only reduce a tax bill.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The retiree, the complying super fund and the charity can use the credit and may be refunded. The Australian company can offset but not be refunded. The Singapore fund cannot use it.

bins.label: Can use it and may get a refund
Can use it but gets no refund

items.label: A retiree who lives in Australia and has no tax to pay
items.explanation: A resident individual gets back the part of the credit that exceeds the tax owed, which here is all of it.

items.label: A union's superannuation fund that is a complying fund
items.explanation: Complying superannuation funds are among the holders the ATO lists as eligible for a refund of excess credits.

items.label: A charity endorsed as exempt from income tax
items.explanation: Endorsed charities are listed by the ATO as entitled to a refund of franking credits.

items.label: An Australian company with a large tax bill that holds shares in another company
items.explanation: A company can use the credit to cut its own tax, down to nil, but it is not refunded any excess.

items.label: An investment fund in Singapore that holds Australian shares
items.explanation: A tax offset for a franking credit is open only to Australian residents.

questions.onCorrect: Residents who are individuals, complying super funds and endorsed charities can be refunded, a company can only offset, and an overseas holder cannot use the credit.

questions.prompt: A company that has paid a steady dividend for years announces in one month that it will double the dividend and also start a large buyback. Its chief executive's pay depends partly on earnings per share. Which reading is most reasonable?
hints: A payout may tell outsiders something managers know. What else could explain the buyback?
Earnings per share rises when shares are bought back. Who is paid on earnings per share?

acceptedIdeas: It may signal confidence, but check the cash and who benefits from the buyback
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It may signal confidence, but check the cash and who benefits from the buyback

choices.label: It may signal confidence, but check the cash and who benefits from the buyback
A confident sign and nothing more, since firms never promise cash they do not have
A bad sign, since cash that leaves the company can only hurt its owners
Meaningless, since managers know no more about the firm than outsiders do

questions.onCorrect: A dividend rise and a buyback can both signal confidence, but a buyback also lifts the earnings per share that pays the chief executive, so the cash and the motive both need checking.

misconceptions.feedback: A dividend rise can signal confidence, but the idea is contested and a company can pay out more than it can sustain. Check the cash before reading it as confidence.
Paying out cash is right when the company has nothing better to do with it. Whether it is good or bad depends on the alternative uses of the cash.
Managers know more about the business than outside investors, which is why a payout can carry a signal at all. The signal is not reliable, which is a different point.

questions.prompt: Coral Freight, an invented company, has $30 million of surplus cash. A new depot needing $10 million would earn about 13% a year. A second project needing $20 million would earn about 6%. Owners could earn about 9% a year elsewhere at similar risk. What should Coral Freight do?
hints: Test each project against the 9% that owners could earn elsewhere.
Cash that no project can use well is the cash to pay out.

acceptedIdeas: Build the depot and pay the remaining $20 million out to owners
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Build the depot and pay the remaining $20 million out to owners

choices.label: Build both projects, because each one earns a positive return
Pay out all $30 million, because paying out is the safer choice
Build the depot and pay the remaining $20 million out to owners
Build the larger project and pay out the rest, since it uses more cash

questions.onCorrect: Only the depot beats the owners' 9% alternative, so the company keeps $10 million for it and pays out the $20 million that no project can use as well.

misconceptions.feedback: A project must beat the 9% owners could earn elsewhere, not just earn something. The 6% project does not.
The depot earns 13%, more than owners could earn on the money elsewhere, so they are better off if the company keeps $10 million for it.
How much cash a project uses decides nothing. What counts is whether it earns more than the owners' 9% alternative, and the 6% project does not.

questions.prompt: Sandra is an Australian resident individual. She receives a fully franked dividend of $70 in cash from a company that paid 30% tax on its profit. What does she include in her taxable income for this dividend?
hints: Which two amounts did Rodney add together before his tax was worked out?
The credit stands for tax the company already paid on the profit. Where does that profit show up in the shareholder's income?

acceptedIdeas: The $70 plus the franking credit that came with it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The $70 plus the franking credit that came with it

choices.label: The $70 she received, since that is the cash she holds
The $70 plus the franking credit that came with it
Only the franking credit, since the cash was taxed at the company
Nothing at all, since a franked dividend is taxed at the company

questions.onCorrect: She includes the cash and the credit, which together are the profit the dividend came from, and the credit is then taken off the tax on that amount.

misconceptions.feedback: The ATO has her include the franking credit as well, which is the gross-up and credit approach. The credit stands for tax paid on profit that is treated as her income.
She is taxed on the whole of the profit the dividend represents, which is the cash and the credit together, and not on the credit alone.
The company's tax is not the end of it. The dividend is taxed again at her own rate on the grossed-up amount, and the credit is taken off that bill so the profit is not taxed twice.

questions.prompt: A company decides to return $20 million of surplus cash to its owners. Sort each consequence by whether it follows from a dividend, from a buyback, or from either one.
hints: Ask what each route does to the number of shares.
Some consequences come from the cash leaving, which both routes share.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A dividend: cash to every holder and a lower price per share. A buyback: fewer shares and higher earnings per share. Either: the company is worth less, and owners are no better off before tax.

items.label: Every shareholder receives cash in proportion to the shares held
items.explanation: A dividend is paid on every share, while in a buyback only the owners who sell receive cash.

items.label: Each share is worth about the cash paid per share less than before
items.explanation: The share count is unchanged, so the same value is spread over the same shares with the cash removed.

items.label: The number of shares in the company falls
items.explanation: The company retires the shares it buys.

items.label: Earnings per share rises even if profit stays the same
items.explanation: The same profit is divided across fewer shares.

items.label: The company is worth less afterwards, because the cash has left
items.explanation: Cash is part of a company's value, and both routes send it out.

items.label: Before tax, an owner is no better off in a perfect market
items.explanation: Either route moves the same $20 million from the company to its owners.

questions.onCorrect: A dividend leaves the share count and lowers the price, a buyback lowers the share count and lifts earnings per share, and both send value out of the company.

questions.prompt: A board is shown a model that gives a positive NPV on a traffic forecast like this one. What is the most useful thing for it to ask for next?
hints: A base case gives one answer. What would tell you how fragile that answer is?
Think about which number the whole project rests on and what happens to the NPV if it is too high.

acceptedIdeas: How far traffic could fall short before the project stops paying
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: How far traffic could fall short before the project stops paying

choices.label: How far traffic could fall short before the project stops paying
A more precise traffic figure, so that the base case is exact
The highest traffic the tunnel could carry, to see the upside
A longer model with more years of cash flow, to spread the risk

questions.onCorrect: A base case is one guess. The distance between it and the point where the NPV turns negative shows how much a miss on traffic would cost.

misconceptions.feedback: Adding digits to a forecast does not make it right. What the board needs is how much the answer would change if the traffic fell short.
The upside shows what is possible and not what the board stands to lose. The shortfall that turns the NPV negative is the figure a decision turns on.
More years add more forecasts, each with its own uncertainty. They do not show how the value depends on the traffic number.

questions.prompt: The table shows the project's NPV if each assumption turns out as badly as the firm thinks plausible, with the others unchanged. Which two assumptions should the firm investigate first?
hints: Look down the NPV column for the bad cases that do the most damage to the base figure of +$325,000.
A positive NPV after a miss means the project survives it. Which misses do not?

acceptedIdeas: Selling price and units sold, since a miss on either leaves the lowest NPV
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Selling price and units sold, since a miss on either leaves the lowest NPV

choices.label: Fixed cost and discount rate, since the NPV stays positive if either misses
Cost per unit and outlay, since the firm already knows them best
Outlay and project life, since they are the easiest figures to check
Selling price and units sold, since a miss on either leaves the lowest NPV

questions.onCorrect: A bad price leaves an NPV of about −$340,000 and a bad volume about −$273,000, the largest falls from +$325,000, so those two forecasts deserve the most effort.

misconceptions.feedback: A project that stays positive after a miss is the one to worry about least. The lowest NPVs show where a miss does the most damage.
How well the firm knows an input is a separate matter from what a miss would cost. A bad cost per unit leaves about −$41,000 and a bad outlay about −$75,000, far less damaging than price or volume.
Ease of checking says nothing about what matters most. A shorter life leaves about −$116,000 and a higher outlay about −$75,000, smaller falls than price or volume.

questions.prompt: In the table, a price of $90, which is 10% below the planned $100, leaves the NPV at about −$340,000, against about +$325,000 in the base case. Which statement about how far the price can fall before the NPV reaches zero is best?
hints: Price moves the NPV in a straight line. Between +$325,000 and −$340,000, where is zero?
Zero sits roughly halfway between those two values, so about halfway to a 10% fall.

acceptedIdeas: About 5%, because the base NPV is about half of what a 10% fall removes
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 5%, because the base NPV is about half of what a 10% fall removes

choices.label: About 1%, because the NPV is small beside the $2.0 million outlay
About 5%, because the base NPV is about half of what a 10% fall removes
About 10%, because the table's 10% fall is where the NPV turns negative
About 15%, because a positive NPV leaves room for more than the table's fall

questions.onCorrect: The NPV runs from +$325,000 to −$340,000 over a 10% fall in price, so it crosses zero about halfway, at a fall of about 5%.

misconceptions.feedback: The outlay is not what the cushion is measured against. A 10% fall costs about $664,000, so each 1% costs only about $66,000 of the $325,000 cushion.
The NPV is already about −$340,000 at a 10% fall, so it crossed zero before that point and the break-even lies well inside it.
A fall of 10% already takes the NPV to about −$340,000, so zero is reached well before 15%.

questions.prompt: Brisbane's CLEM7 toll tunnel gave the figures below. What do they show about testing volume and price one at a time?
hints: Compare the traffic with no toll and with the reduced toll. What moved when the price moved?
If two inputs move together in practice, what is wrong with varying them one after the other?

acceptedIdeas: They are linked, because the toll cut the traffic, so test them together
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: They are linked, because the toll cut the traffic, so test them together

choices.label: Volume does not react to price, so each input can be tested on its own
Only volume matters to this tunnel, so the toll can be left out of the model
They are linked, because the toll cut the traffic, so test them together
Tolls should be set at zero so that traffic stays near the forecast

extracts.text: The tunnel was predicted by Rivercity Motorways to carry around 60,000 trips each day. Without a toll an average of 59,000 vehicles used the tunnel and when the reduced toll was payable around 20,000 vehicles used the tunnel.
extracts.kind: An encyclopedia article written by volunteer editors

questions.onCorrect: The toll is the tunnel's price, and traffic fell by about two thirds when it applied. Price and volume come together, so they belong in one scenario.

misconceptions.feedback: The record shows traffic falling from 59,000 to around 20,000 once a toll applied, so volume reacts strongly to price.
The toll is what moved the volume, so leaving it out would hide the link that the model most needs to show.
A toll of zero earns no toll revenue at all. The aim is to test price and volume together so that the revenue each toll would bring can be seen.

questions.prompt: Wikipedia gives the Sydney Opera House as an example of the planning fallacy. What should a forecaster take from it?
hints: Is it likely that this is the only project whose estimate ran low?
What could a forecaster do that does not depend on the details of one project?

acceptedIdeas: Planned costs and dates run low, so check them against similar projects
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Planned costs and dates run low, so check them against similar projects

choices.label: Opera houses are unusual, so little of this carries over to other projects
Planned costs and dates run low, so check them against similar projects
Overruns come from bad luck, which no forecast could have allowed for
A delay changes the date and leaves the project's value as it was

extracts.text: The Sydney Opera House was expected to be completed in 1963. A scaled-down version opened in 1973, a decade later. The original cost was estimated at $7 million, but its delayed completion led to a cost of $102 million.
extracts.kind: An encyclopedia article written by volunteer editors

questions.onCorrect: The estimate was off by about fifteen times on cost and a decade on time. Planned costs and dates tend to run low, so the safer start is how similar projects ended.

misconceptions.feedback: Treating a project as unique is the inside view. Whether estimates for similar projects run low is the very question the outside view puts to the evidence.
Kahneman and Tversky found a consistent tendency to underestimate costs and times. A pattern is something a forecast can allow for.
A decade's delay moves every cash flow later, and later cash flows are worth less. The date is part of the value.

questions.prompt: Woolworths's note says a 1.0 point rise in the discount rate with a 10% cut to terminal-year EBIT would remove New Zealand Food's headroom, against 0.2 points and 4% for Petstock. Which valuation is thinner, and what does its note say about why?
hints: Which note needs the smaller change in the assumptions to bring the value down to its carrying value?
Read what each note says the valuation relies on.

acceptedIdeas: Petstock, which relies on growth and synergies after a recent acquisition
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Petstock, which relies on growth and synergies after a recent acquisition

choices.label: Petstock, which relies on growth and synergies after a recent acquisition
New Zealand Food, since it takes the larger change to remove its headroom
They are equally thin, since each one still has some headroom left
Neither can be judged without the share price on the day

questions.onCorrect: Petstock's headroom would go with a 0.2 point rise and a 4% cut, and its note says the value depends on continued growth and on synergies with the Group after the recent acquisition.

misconceptions.feedback: The larger the change needed, the more room the value has. New Zealand Food needs 1.0 point and 10%, and Petstock only 0.2 points and 4%.
Having some headroom says nothing about how much. Petstock's would go with a far smaller change.
The test compares a value built from the company's own forecasts with the carrying value. The share price is not part of it.

questions.prompt: A council's consultants forecast that a new toll bridge will carry 80,000 vehicles a day, and the council's finance team has checked the spreadsheet twice. Which step takes the outside view?
hints: The outside view looks away from this project. Where would you look instead?
Which of these steps would be the same whether the forecast was careful or careless?

acceptedIdeas: Collect what similar bridges carried against their forecasts and compare
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Collect what similar bridges carried against their forecasts and compare

choices.label: Have a second team check the arithmetic of the forecast again
Ask the consultants to revisit the forecast and be more cautious
Collect what similar bridges carried against their forecasts and compare
Raise the toll until the forecast traffic would earn the planned revenue

questions.onCorrect: Comparing similar bridges' traffic with their forecasts is the reference class method: it uses what happened elsewhere in place of the details of this forecast.

misconceptions.feedback: The arithmetic can be right while the assumptions are optimistic. Checking it again stays inside the project's own details.
Asking the same people to look at the same details keeps the view inside the project. The outside view brings in evidence from other projects.
A higher toll usually lowers traffic, so it does not make the forecast traffic arrive and may cut the revenue.

questions.prompt: Banksia Cafes, an invented chain, tests a plan for a new café by moving each input 10% in turn. A 10% rise in wages lowers the NPV by $300,000, and a 10% fall in customer numbers lowers it by $200,000. Wages are set by an award and are known to within 2%, while customer numbers could plausibly be 30% out. Which should the chain research first?
hints: The test moved both inputs by the same amount. Is that how far each could really be wrong?
Which input could miss by far more than the test assumed?

acceptedIdeas: Customer numbers, since they could plausibly be wrong by far more
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Customer numbers, since they could plausibly be wrong by far more

choices.label: Wages, since a 10% change in wages does the most damage to the NPV
Both equally, since each was moved by the same 10% in the test
Neither, because a 10% change is too small to matter to an NPV
Customer numbers, since they could plausibly be wrong by far more

questions.onCorrect: Priority goes to the input that could plausibly be wrong by the most, because the size of the possible miss and the size of the effect together decide where checking is worth the effort.

misconceptions.feedback: The 10% test is only a common yardstick. Wages are known to within 2%, so a 10% rise is far outside what could happen, and the larger risk is the input that could really be 30% out.
Moving every input by the same percentage makes them look alike. What differs is how far each could really miss.
A 10% change in either input already moves the NPV by $200,000 to $300,000, which is a large swing.

questions.prompt: A sensitivity analysis finds that a project's NPV reaches zero if the selling price is 3% lower than planned. The firm's own range for a plausible price miss is 10%. What does that say about the project?
hints: Compare the break-even with the firm's own range for the miss.
If the price fell by the plausible 10%, would the NPV still be positive?

acceptedIdeas: Its value is thin, because a plausible price miss would erase it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Its value is thin, because a plausible price miss would erase it

choices.label: It is safe, because a change of 3% is small beside most forecasts
Its value is thin, because a plausible price miss would erase it
The price forecast is probably accurate to within 3% of the plan
It should be approved, because its NPV at the base case is positive

questions.onCorrect: A break-even of 3% sits well inside a plausible miss of 10%, so a realistic shortfall in price would turn the NPV negative.

misconceptions.feedback: The size of a break-even matters only against how far the input could plausibly miss. A cushion of 3% against a possible 10% miss is thin.
The break-even says how far price can fall before the NPV is zero. It says nothing about how accurate the forecast is.
A positive base case says nothing about how much of the NPV survives a plausible miss. Here the miss is larger than the cushion.

questions.prompt: A company is testing the NPV of a new plant. Sort each check by the kind of analysis it is.
hints: Ask how many inputs each check changes.
A check that does not touch the plant's own inputs at all looks at other projects.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The discount rate and building cost tests change one input. The recession case and the price and volume change move linked inputs together. The overruns and the factory start-up times use similar past projects.

items.label: Raise the discount rate by two points and leave everything else as planned
items.explanation: Only one input changes, so it shows how sensitive the NPV is to that input.

items.label: Add 20% to the building cost and leave the rest unchanged
items.explanation: A single input moves, so this is a one-at-a-time test.

items.label: A recession case with a lower price, lower volume and higher interest rate at once
items.explanation: Several inputs that tend to move together change at the same time, which is a scenario.

items.label: Cut the price to win a bigger share and raise the volume it should bring
items.explanation: Price and volume are linked, so they change as a pair.

items.label: Collect the cost overruns of ten earlier plants of the same kind and compare
items.explanation: The evidence comes from similar projects that have already ended, which is the outside view.

items.label: Look up how long comparable factories took to reach full output
items.explanation: It uses a reference class of finished projects, and not the details of this plant.

questions.onCorrect: Changing one input is a sensitivity test, changing linked inputs together is a scenario, and comparing with finished projects is the outside view.

questions.prompt: Rio Tinto paid $2.9 billion in cash for Riversdale, wrote the value of its assets down by $3 billion two years later and then sold them for $50 million. What does that record support?
hints: Compare what was paid with what the assets were later sold for.
Remember what an impairment does and does not move: does it send cash anywhere?

acceptedIdeas: The assets proved to be worth far less than Rio paid for them
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The assets proved to be worth far less than Rio paid for them

choices.label: The assets proved to be worth far less than Rio paid for them
The price was fair, and bad luck accounts for all of the write-down
The write-down was $3 billion of cash paid out two years later

questions.onCorrect: Rio paid $2.9 billion and the assets later sold for $50 million. The record shows the gap and does not say what caused it, which the rest of the lesson looks at.

misconceptions.feedback: A price is judged against what the assets were worth. They were later sold for $50 million against $2.9 billion paid, so the price ended far above the value, whatever the reason.
An impairment lowers profit and the asset's recorded value and sends no cash anywhere. The cash left when Rio paid the $2.9 billion.

questions.prompt: A buyer offers $1,350 million, a 35% premium, for a company whose shares are worth $1,000 million, and it believes that the combination adds $120 million. If every synergy arrives, who gains?
hints: Compare the premium the buyer pays with the benefit it expects to get back.
The sellers receive the premium whatever happens to the synergies afterwards.

acceptedIdeas: The seller's shareholders, since the premium is larger than the synergies
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The seller's shareholders, since the premium is larger than the synergies

choices.label: The buyer, because paying a premium is how it wins control of the target
The seller's shareholders, since the premium is larger than the synergies
Both sides equally, because the synergies are shared out fairly in a deal
Nobody, because the synergies and the premium cancel each other out exactly

questions.onCorrect: The $350 million premium goes to the sellers, and the synergies are worth $120 million at best. The buyer is $230 million behind even if every synergy arrives.

misconceptions.feedback: Control is not a gain in itself. The buyer pays $350 million above market for $120 million of benefit, so it ends $230 million behind even if every synergy arrives.
Nothing in the deal shares the synergies. The premium is fixed in the price, and it is nearly three times the synergies.
The premium is $350 million and the synergies $120 million. They differ by $230 million and do not cancel.

questions.prompt: A buyer expects $120 million of synergies and offers a premium of 10%, or $100 million, for a company worth $1,000 million. Roughly what share of the synergies must arrive for the buyer to break even?
hints: The buyer breaks even when the synergies it delivers equal the premium it paid.
What fraction of $120 million is $100 million: less than half, or most of it?

acceptedIdeas: More than four fifths, since the premium takes most of the benefit
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: More than four fifths, since the premium takes most of the benefit

choices.label: About a fifth, since a premium of 10% is small beside $1,000 million
About a half, since only part of the expected benefit needs to arrive
More than four fifths, since the premium takes most of the benefit
All of them or more, since any premium needs the whole benefit back

questions.onCorrect: The premium is $100 million against $120 million of synergies, so about five sixths of them must arrive before the buyer is no worse off.

misconceptions.feedback: The premium has to be recovered from the synergies and not from the company's value. $100 million is most of $120 million.
The buyer has paid $100 million, so it needs $100 million of the $120 million back. That is far more than half.
Break-even needs the buyer to recover the premium it paid. $100 million out of $120 million is less than all of the synergies.

questions.prompt: A buyer is setting a price and has two lists of synergies: savings from closing duplicate departments, and extra sales from selling to the target's customers. Which list should it discount more heavily, and why?
hints: Which list depends on what the buyer does, and which on what customers do?
Where does the buyer have more control over whether the benefit arrives?

acceptedIdeas: Extra sales, because they depend on markets and customers
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Extra sales, because they depend on markets and customers

choices.label: Cost savings, because costs are the more uncertain figure
Neither, because every synergy is certain once the deal has closed
Both equally, because both are forecasts made by the same buyer
Extra sales, because they depend on markets and customers

questions.onCorrect: Extra sales depend on customers and markets, which a buyer does not control, so a prudent price discounts them more heavily than cost savings.

misconceptions.feedback: A cost saving depends on what the two firms do, which the buyer can plan. Extra sales depend on what customers do.
A synergy has to be delivered after the deal. Buying the company guarantees none of it.
The two lists differ in how much they depend on customers and markets, and treating them alike loses that difference.

questions.prompt: A company wins the bidding for a mine against six rivals, and the mine is worth the same to every bidder. Its estimate of the mine's value was the highest of the seven, and none of them knows the true value. What does winning tell it?
hints: The winner is whichever bidder's estimate was highest. How does that estimate compare with the other six?
If the estimates are right on average, is the highest one more likely to be too high or too low?

acceptedIdeas: That its estimate was probably the most optimistic, so it may have overpaid
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: That its estimate was probably the most optimistic, so it may have overpaid

choices.label: That its estimate was the most accurate, since it won the bidding
Nothing about the mine's value, since winning shows only who bid the most money
That its estimate was probably the most optimistic, so it may have overpaid
That its rivals were careless, since each of them bid less than it did for the mine

questions.onCorrect: Its estimate was the highest of seven, so if the estimates are right on average it is probably too high. Winning is bad news about the value.

misconceptions.feedback: Winning shows that its estimate was the highest, which is a different thing from the most accurate. If the estimates are right on average, the highest is probably too high.
Winning does carry information. It says that every other bidder thought the mine worth less.
Nothing says the rivals were careless. If estimates scatter around the true value, the lowest bids are as likely to be right as the highest.

questions.prompt: Which of these can the extract alone support?
hints: Which of these needs facts about Alcan's later cash flows, which the extract does not contain?
What does a rival's bid show about a price, and what does it leave open?

acceptedIdeas: That a hostile rival bid existed, but not whether the price was too high
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: That a hostile rival bid existed, but not whether the price was too high

choices.label: That Rio overpaid, since it paid far more than Alcoa's bid
That Alcan was really worth $27.5 billion, which is what Alcoa's bid showed
That the deal succeeded, since Rio beat its rival to the purchase
That a hostile rival bid existed, but not whether the price was too high

extracts.text: In 2007, Rio Tinto acquired Alcan in a US$38 billion deal. The offer served to undermine a hostile bid of $27.5bn from Alcoa, Alcan's US rival.
extracts.kind: An encyclopedia article written by volunteer editors

questions.onCorrect: The extract shows a hostile rival bid and a higher winning offer. Whether the price was too high depends on what Alcan later delivered, which the extract does not say.

misconceptions.feedback: A price above a rival's bid shows only that a rival was bidding. Whether it was too high depends on the cash Alcan later produced, which the extract does not give.
A bid is one buyer's offer for control, and it is not a measure of value. The extract cannot say what Alcan was worth.
Winning the contest says nothing about whether the price was justified. It is what the winner's curse warns about.

questions.prompt: A bidder knows about the winner's curse and is preparing a bid for a block that is worth the same to every bidder. Its own best estimate of the value is $100 million. How should that knowledge change its bid?
hints: Winning is news about how your estimate compares with everyone else's. How should the news change your view of the value?
What would you pay if you knew that your estimate was the highest?

acceptedIdeas: Bid below its estimate, because winning would mean its estimate ran high
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Bid below its estimate, because winning would mean its estimate ran high

choices.label: Bid its estimate exactly, since that is its best guess of the block's value
Bid below its estimate, because winning would mean its estimate ran high
Bid above its estimate, so that it is certain to win the block from rivals
Not bid at all, since the winner of a contest always ends up overpaying

questions.onCorrect: Winning means the estimate was probably among the highest, so a savvy bidder revises its view of the value down and bids below its raw estimate.

misconceptions.feedback: If it wins, its estimate was probably on the high side, so paying that estimate means paying at its own most optimistic reading. Savvy bidders shade their bids below their estimates.
A higher bid raises the chance of winning and the chance of overpaying together. That is the curse itself.
A winner overpays when it ignores the curse. A bidder that shades its bid can still win at a price that allows for what winning tells it.

questions.prompt: Two landowners each sell a parcel of farmland by sealed bid. A parcel would yield the same crop for any bidder, but no one can predict that yield exactly. The first sale draws 3 bidders and the second draws 12. Using the extract, in which sale is the winner more likely to have overpaid, and why?
hints: Which sale has more estimates for the highest one to stand above?
With twelve estimates scattered around the true value, how likely is it that at least one is far too high?

acceptedIdeas: The second sale, since more bidders make a very optimistic estimate likelier
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The second sale, since more bidders make a very optimistic estimate likelier

choices.label: The second sale, since more bidders make a very optimistic estimate likelier
The first sale, since fewer bidders means each bid is a bigger guess about value
Both equally, since each winner still bids its own estimate of the value
Neither, since winning an auction never says anything about value

extracts.text: The severity of the winner's curse increases with the number of bidders.
extracts.kind: An encyclopedia article written by volunteer editors

questions.onCorrect: The curse grows with the number of bidders, because the more estimates there are, the more likely it is that one is far too high, and that one wins.

misconceptions.feedback: Fewer bidders mean fewer estimates, so there is less chance that one of them is far too high. The extract says the curse grows with the number of bidders.
Each winner does bid its estimate, but the highest of twelve estimates is likely to be further above the true value than the highest of three.
Winning tells the winner that its estimate was the highest, which is information about how it compares with the others.

questions.prompt: A company is weighing reasons to buy a rival. Sort each reason by whether it can add value for the buyer's own shareholders.
hints: Ask whether the benefit is one that the buyer's owners could not get for themselves.
A reason that benefits the managers and not the owners cannot add value for the owners.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Bulk-buying discounts and closing the head office can add value if delivered. Diversifying, a chief executive's wish for size, pay tied to total profit and overconfident forecasts do not.

bins.label: Does not add value by itself

items.label: Combining the two firms' orders to win bulk-buying discounts
items.explanation: A purchasing saving is a benefit that owners could not obtain by holding both firms separately.

items.label: Closing the rival's head office once the firms are joined
items.explanation: Removing duplicated departments is a cost synergy, which is a real benefit if it is delivered.

items.label: A miner buying a chain of bakeries to even out its earnings
items.explanation: Shareholders can diversify in their own portfolios at much lower cost than a merger.

items.label: A chief executive who wants to run a bigger company
items.explanation: A bigger company gives the manager more power, and that benefit does not pass to the owners.

items.label: Executives paid on total profit and not on profit per share
items.explanation: The pay rewards buying companies even when profit per share falls, which hurts the owners.

items.label: Managers sure they will deliver every synergy in their forecast
items.explanation: Overconfidence about synergies leads to overpayment, and confidence is not a benefit.

questions.onCorrect: Purchasing savings and cutting duplicated departments are real benefits. Diversification, empire-building, pay tied to total profit and overconfidence are not.

questions.prompt: Harbourline Freight, an invented company, offers a 12% premium, or $48 million, for Dray Logistics, whose shares are worth $400 million. Closing overlapping depots would save an estimated $75 million in present value, and Harbourline has costed each closure. Which description is fairest?
hints: Compare the premium with the savings. Which is larger?
What would happen to the buyer's margin if only part of the savings arrived?

acceptedIdeas: It can pay off, since the premium is below the savings, if enough of them arrive
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It can pay off, since the premium is below the savings, if enough of them arrive

choices.label: It can pay off, since the premium is below the savings, if enough of them arrive
It cannot pay off, because the sellers always capture the whole gain from a deal
It will pay off, because cost savings are certain to arrive once the deal has closed
It pays off only if sales rise as well, since savings alone never justify a premium

questions.onCorrect: The $48 million premium is below the $75 million of savings, so the buyer keeps about $27 million if all arrives. Delivery is not certain, and a shortfall shrinks the margin.

misconceptions.feedback: The sellers capture the premium, which is $48 million here. The savings are worth $75 million, so $27 million is left for the buyer if all of it is delivered.
Savings still have to be delivered after the deal. They are more reliable than extra sales and they are not certain.
Cost savings alone can cover a premium when they are larger than it. Revenue is not needed for the sum to work.

questions.prompt: Lovisa's earnings per share rose 10.5% in 2026, and its share price fell from $30.91 to $23.25. What is the most likely reading?
hints: A share price is what buyers will pay now for earnings still to come. What could change that besides this year's profit?
Earnings per share looks back over a year. Does the price look back or forward?

acceptedIdeas: The price reflects expected future earnings and risk, which may have shifted
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The price reflects expected future earnings and risk, which may have shifted

choices.label: The price reflects expected future earnings and risk, which may have shifted
The market made a mistake, which later results will correct
Prices follow the latest profit growth one for one, so the fall must be an error
The earnings figure must be overstated, since good results cannot lower a price

questions.onCorrect: A price is what buyers will pay for expected future earnings, given the risk. It can fall in a year when reported earnings rise if those expectations or the risk change.

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing in the table shows a mistake. A lower price can follow from lower expectations of later earnings or higher risk, and the table shows neither.
A price looks forward at expected cash and risk, and last year's growth is only one input. The table shows the price rising and falling while earnings per share rose every year.
Nothing suggests the earnings figure was wrong. Earnings per share can rise while the price falls when buyers revise what they expect from here.

questions.prompt: Which statement is closest to what the efficient-market hypothesis claims?
hints: Think about what the hypothesis says a price contains and what that implies about trading.
Which of these statements would be false if news could lower a price?

acceptedIdeas: Prices reflect available information, so nobody can consistently beat the market
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Prices reflect available information, so nobody can consistently beat the market

choices.label: Prices equal true value at every moment, so a price can never fall
Prices reflect available information, so nobody can consistently beat the market
Analysis is pointless, since a price cannot depend on anything that analysts do or say
Prices move only on the days when a company's annual results are announced

questions.onCorrect: The hypothesis says that prices reflect all available information, so prices move on new information and nobody can consistently beat the market after allowing for risk.

misconceptions.feedback: The hypothesis says prices reflect available information. New information can lower a price, and a price built on information that proves incomplete can look wrong afterwards.
Investors trading on information is how information reaches a price, so the idea relies on analysis being done.
Prices move whenever new information arrives, whatever the day. Annual results are only one source of it.

questions.prompt: Analysts expect a company's profit to rise by 10%. Sort each announcement by what the share price should do.
hints: Compare each announcement with the 10% that was expected, and not with last year.
News that was already known, or that matches the forecast, leaves the forecast and so the price where they were.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A profit rise of 14% and a higher forecast for next year should lift the price. A rise of 7% and a rise of 10% with a warning about a new rival should lower it. A rise of 10% and the confirmed plan should change little.

items.label: Profit rises 10%
items.explanation: It matches the forecast, so forecasts do not change.

items.label: Profit rises 14%
items.explanation: It beats the forecast, so expectations of later earnings go up.

items.label: Profit rises 7%
items.explanation: Profit rose, and it fell short of the forecast, so expectations go down.

items.label: The firm confirms a plan it announced a month ago
items.explanation: Investors already knew about the plan, so it is not news.

items.label: Profit rises 10%, but the firm warns that a large new rival is coming
items.explanation: The warning lowers expected future earnings or raises the risk, which outweighs a result that matched.

items.label: The firm lifts its forecast for next year above what analysts expected
items.explanation: It is better than expected news about future earnings.

questions.onCorrect: Only the part of an announcement that differs from expectations moves a price, so a match or old news leaves it alone and a beat or a miss moves it.

questions.prompt: How does the efficient-market idea read the one-fifth fall when the figures came out?
hints: Ask what the price already contained before the figures were released.
What happens to a price when news is worse than the forecast it was built on?

acceptedIdeas: The figures were worse than expected, and the price fell to reflect that
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The figures were worse than expected, and the price fell to reflect that

choices.label: The figures were worse than expected, and the price fell to reflect that
The price had been mistaken before the figures came out, and they corrected it
Traffic has no bearing on a toll road's value, so the fall was random
Shares fall whenever any figures are released, whatever they say

extracts.text: After the poor patronage figures were released Rivercity Motorway shares immediately dropped by one fifth of their value, and have since declined to 0% of their initial value.
extracts.kind: An encyclopedia article written by volunteer editors

questions.onCorrect: The price reflected the forecast traffic. Figures that came in far below it changed what investors expected, so the price fell on the day.

misconceptions.feedback: On the efficient-market reading the earlier price reflected what was known then, including the traffic forecast. The new figures changed what was known.
Traffic produces the toll revenue that a toll road's owners are paid from, which is why the price fell when the figures came out.
A price moves on the surprise in news. Figures that matched what was expected would have left it alone.

questions.prompt: A researcher finds that share prices already reflect everything in company announcements and the financial press, but that people with confidential knowledge of a coming bid still profit. Which form of the efficient-market hypothesis do the results fit?
hints: Which kinds of information do the results say are already in the price, and which are not?
The three forms cover past prices, public information, and private information as well.

acceptedIdeas: semi-strong
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The semi-strong form: prices reflect all public information, though not private information.

questions.onCorrect: Prices reflect public information but not confidential knowledge, which is the semi-strong form. The strong form would require private information to be in the price too.

misconceptions.feedback: The weak form concerns only historical prices. These results say prices also reflect public information such as announcements and the press, which goes beyond the weak form.

questions.prompt: A bidder offers 30% above the market price for a listed company. Does that show the market price was wrong?
hints: Does the market price measure what it costs to gain control of the whole company?
What is the buyer getting that an ordinary shareholder who buys a few shares does not?

acceptedIdeas: Not necessarily, because a premium pays for control and expected gains
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Not necessarily, because a premium pays for control and expected gains

choices.label: Yes, because any bid above the market price shows the market was wrong
Not necessarily, because a premium pays for control and expected gains
Yes, but only when the target is a large listed company
No, because takeover bids are set at random by the bidder

questions.onCorrect: A control premium pays for control and for the gains the buyer expects, so it can sit above a market price that is right for an ordinary small stake.

misconceptions.feedback: A bid above the market price pays for control and for the gains the buyer expects, and neither is part of the price of a small stake. The gap alone does not show an error.
The size of the target does not change what a premium pays for. It buys control, and control is not what the market price of a small stake measures.
A bidder sets its price from the value it expects from control and the synergies, and a premium is needed to persuade existing shareholders to sell.

questions.prompt: After a product recall, a company's share price has fallen 20%. A director says the market has mispriced the company and that it should spend all its spare cash on a buyback. What is the best response?
hints: A buyback is a bet that the price is too low. What would the directors need to know for that bet to pay?
Could the 20% fall be the market's reading of the recall itself?

acceptedIdeas: Ask what the directors know that the price does not, and what drove the fall
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Ask what the directors know that the price does not, and what drove the fall

choices.label: Agree, since a falling price always shows that a company is undervalued
Agree, since a buyback will lift the price back to where it was
Disagree, since the market price is always right and managers can never know more
Ask what the directors know that the price does not, and what drove the fall

questions.onCorrect: A buyback bets that the price is too low, which needs knowledge the market lacks. The fall may be the recall's news, so the directors should say what they know that the price does not.

misconceptions.feedback: A fall can reflect real news, and the recall may be exactly that. A lower price does not by itself show that it is below value.
A buyback is a bet that the price is too low. It does not restore a price that reflects real news about the recall.
The hypothesis does not say that the price is always right or that managers know nothing extra. It says that beating the price is hard, so a claim to do it needs a reason.

questions.prompt: Ashgrove Mills, an invented company, announces a bid for a smaller rival at a 25% premium. On the day, Ashgrove's own shares fall 4% and the rival's rise about 22%. Using the extract, what is the best event-study reading?
hints: Which company's value did the market mark up on the news, and which did it mark down?
A price fall for the buyer means investors expect the deal to lower its value.

acceptedIdeas: Investors expect Ashgrove to overpay and the rival's holders to take the gain
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Investors expect Ashgrove to overpay and the rival's holders to take the gain

choices.label: Investors expect Ashgrove to overpay and the rival's holders to take the gain
The rival's price was wrong before the bid, and Ashgrove's own move is only noise
The fall in Ashgrove's price shows that the bid will fail and be withdrawn
Nothing can be read from one day's price moves, since prices follow no news

extracts.text: given rationality in the marketplace, the effects of an event will be reflected immediately in security prices. Thus a measure of the event's economic impact can be constructed using security prices observed over a relatively short time period
extracts.kind: An encyclopedia article written by volunteer editors, here quoting a 1997 paper by MacKinlay

questions.onCorrect: The rival's rise of about 22% is close to the 25% premium, which fits its holders collecting the premium, and Ashgrove's fall fits investors expecting it to pay more than the deal returns.

misconceptions.feedback: A bid above the market price pays for control and does not show that the earlier price was wrong. The 4% fall in Ashgrove's own price is the market's reading of the deal and not noise.
A price move shows what investors expect the deal to do for Ashgrove's value. It says nothing about whether the rival's holders will accept.
The event-study method rests on prices reflecting news quickly, so a short window around an event is the measure of its impact.

questions.prompt: Analysts expect a company's profit to fall 9%, and it falls 4%. Roughly what should its share price do on the news?
hints: Compare the 4% fall with the 9% fall that was expected.
Is the result better or worse than the forecast that the price was built on?

acceptedIdeas: Rise, because the result was better than expected
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Rise, because the result was better than expected

choices.label: Fall, because the company's profit went down over the year
Stay about the same, because a fall of 4% is a small one
Rise, because the result was better than expected

questions.onCorrect: The result beat the forecast by five points, so expectations of later earnings rise and the price should rise, even though profit fell.

misconceptions.feedback: Profit fell, and it fell by less than analysts expected. The price responds to the difference from the forecast and not to the direction of the profit.
The size of the fall matters only against the forecast. A fall of 4% is a better result than the 9% that was expected, so expectations rise.

questions.prompt: A company warns that its profit will be far below what analysts expected. Put these events in the order in which the news reaches the price.
hints: News has to be public before anyone can act on it.
Trading on information is what moves a price, and it stops when the news offers no more profit.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The announcement comes first. Forecasts are cut next, then some investors sell, their selling lowers the price, and the price settles once nobody can gain from the news.

items: The firm announces that profit will be well below what analysts expected
Analysts and investors cut their forecasts of the firm's future cash flow
Some investors sell, because the price is now above what they think the shares are worth
The selling pushes the price down
The price settles where no one can gain by trading on the news

questions.onCorrect: News changes forecasts, investors trade on the gap between the old price and the new forecast, and the trading moves the price until the news is no longer useful for trading.

flashcards.front: What do we call the value today of money due later, found by discounting it?
flashcards.back: Its present value. A payment due in a year has a present value of the payment divided by one plus the discount rate.

acceptedIdeas: present value
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Its present value. A payment due in a year has a present value of the payment divided by one plus the discount rate.

flashcards.front: Why can a firm prefer $108,000 in a year to $100,000 now when it can earn 5%, and prefer the cash when it can earn 10%?
flashcards.back: The rate is the price of waiting. At 5% the $108,000 is worth about $102,900 today, above $100,000. At 10% it is worth about $98,200, below it.

flashcards.front: What do we call the rate at which waiting and not waiting are worth the same?
flashcards.back: The break-even rate. Below it waiting wins and above it taking the money now wins.

acceptedIdeas: break-even rate
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The break-even rate. Below it waiting wins and above it taking the money now wins.

flashcards.front: What two things does a required return pay for?
flashcards.back: Waiting, which is the time value of money, and risk, the chance that the cash flow does not arrive after all.

flashcards.front: What do analysts call the value put on all the cash flows after the years they forecast in detail?
flashcards.back: The terminal value. It is often a large share of a valuation and very sensitive to the growth and discount rate assumed.

acceptedIdeas: terminal value
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The terminal value. It is often a large share of a valuation and very sensitive to the growth and discount rate assumed.

flashcards.front: Why does a rise in the discount rate cut the value of a 30-year stream by more than a 5-year stream?
flashcards.back: A higher rate is applied once for each year of waiting, so it cuts distant payments most, and the 30-year stream has far more of its value in distant years.

flashcards.front: What condition does the growing-perpetuity formula need, and why?
flashcards.back: Growth must be below the discount rate. Otherwise each year's present value is as large as the one before, the total never settles, and the formula gives no sensible value.

flashcards.front: What do we call a series of equal payments at regular intervals, such as rent or lease payments?
flashcards.back: An annuity.

acceptedIdeas: annuity
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An annuity.

flashcards.front: What do we call the present value of a project's cash flows less its cost?
flashcards.back: Its net present value, or NPV: the value the project adds, in today's money, over what investors could earn elsewhere.

acceptedIdeas: net present value
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Its net present value, or NPV: the value the project adds, in today's money, over what investors could earn elsewhere.

flashcards.front: A project returns exactly its cost over five years. Why is its NPV still negative?
flashcards.back: The cash arrives over time, and investors could have earned the required return on that money meanwhile, so in today's money it is worth less than was spent.

flashcards.front: What does a zero NPV mean for a project?
flashcards.back: It earns exactly the required return. It neither adds nor destroys value, so accepting or rejecting it changes the firm's value by about nothing.

flashcards.front: When should a firm accept every project with a positive NPV?
flashcards.back: When the projects are independent and capital is not short. If capital is limited, it picks the combination with the largest total NPV that the money can buy.

flashcards.front: What do we call the cash that changes because a project goes ahead, compared with the firm without it?
flashcards.back: The incremental cash flow. Only cash that differs between the firm with the project and the firm without it belongs in the NPV.
